Exclusive video of world’s first echidna puggle to be born at a university

New Scientist August 28, 2026

A baby echidna – one of Australia’s egg-laying monotremes – has been born and reared in a university for the first time. The baby, known as a puggle, was born earlier this month and has now been removed from its mother’s pouch for its first weigh-in. The scientists hope that, by researching this puggle and other echidnas, we will finally be able to understand some fundamental questions about the evolution of pregnancy in mammals.

The short-beaked echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus), also known as the spiny anteater, has proved to be an extremely difficult species to breed in captivity. In spite of numerous attempts, a dedicated research colony had never been successfully established, though several zoos and wildlife sanctuaries have bred the species.

Endangered echidna not seen in 60 years caught on camera

Now, Oliver Griffith at Macquarie University in Sydney and his team are successfully rearing a puggle, which is thought to be the first in the world born at a university. This week, it had become big enough that they felt confident in temporarily removing it from its mother’s pouch for weighing, which New Scientist was invited to witness.

Advertisement

T. aculeatus is one of only five known species of monotremes, a group of mammals that lay eggs. The others are three different species of echidna in New Guinea and the platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus). Most researchers believe monotremes are an ancient mammalian lineage that predate placentals.

Studying the chemical composition of echidna eggs may reveal how different they are to those of reptiles, which could give clues on when mammals and reptiles diverged, says Griffith. “We’ll look at eggshell proteins in the echidna and compare that to eggshell proteins in reptiles and try to work out: do they have the same origin or did they evolve independently?”

Five females and four males are in captivity at Macquarie University. In early August, Griffith and his colleagues noticed that the puggle’s mother, named Kootear, had stopped eating and moving for around 10 days, a sign that birth is imminent. Pregnant echidnas move their egg into a pouch, where it incubates while the female is fasting and immobilised.

“We had an inkling that she may have laid an egg,” says Griffith. “So, three weeks ago, we looked into her pouch and we found what was a very tiny, almost jelly-bean-sized baby that had hatched only a couple of days before.”

A week later, the team checked the pouch again and found the puggle had surged in size. “It had grown a crazy amount actually, and it was surprising to see it so much bigger in just seven days,” says Griffith.

Subscriber-only newsletter

When it was checked for the third time, the researchers anaesthetised Kootear so the puggle could be briefly removed. They found it weighed 36 grams and was starting to look like an echidna, albeit one without any spines or fur.

“Before this point, you couldn’t obviously see it was an echidna – you might confuse it with a platypus puggle or, maybe even, just because it’s a pink thing, you might think it was a kangaroo baby,” says Griffith. “But today you could really see the shape of an echidna – the beak, the feet, everything.”

Echidnas can live for more than 50 years in captivity. The university’s echidnas are unlikely to ever be released into the wild. “This is a long-term research programme,” says Griffith. “I’ve set this up to be sort of a career’s worth of research, and this puggle may well outlive me.”

Einstein thought time dilation was both real and not – he was right

New Scientist August 28, 2026

The passage of time often seems like the most malleable thing in the world. A minute may feel much longer when you’re asked to hold a plank position in a workout class, and an hour may fly by when you’re chatting with a friend. In these cases, your perception of time is altered. But real, physical time dilation also happens. According to Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity, clocks that are closer to Earth’s centre of gravity, say at sea level, tick more slowly than those at the top of a mountain. A similar slowing happens when a clock is physically travelling extremely fast.

Why banishing irrational numbers could trigger a revolution in quantum theory

Undeniably, this sounds bizarre, but decades’ worth of experiments haven’t managed to disprove it. Yet in what exact sense time dilation is real – and what it means for a physical effect to be real at all – has inspired philosophical debates ever since Einstein first formulated his theory in 1905.

In fact, in June, at the Foundations of Physics conference in Irvine, California, I heard Marco Giovanelli discuss how time dilation is both real and apparent at once. It sounds paradoxical, but when I called Giovanelli, who is a historian of philosophy and science at the University of Turin in Italy, to talk through it, I started to understand that it reflects the facets of our physical world that Einstein’s work first uncovered.

Advertisement

For Einstein, it was all about rods and clocks, explains Giovanelli. Suppose that you and a friend each had an identical clock and a metre-long rod. You stand still, while your friend gets into an incredibly fast spaceship and sets off on a journey. Compared with yours, their clock will tick less quickly and their rod will contract in size. If you want to know by how much, Einstein’s got your back: he worked out those calculations more than a century ago. If you happen to have a second friend who has a slightly slower spaceship and their own clock-and-rod set, the same trick will work again, except that their clock will slow and their rod contract a little less than your speedier friend. Finally, if you also acquire a spaceship and catch up with either of your friends, your clocks will start to tick at the same rate again, and your metre-long rods will again look the same length.

To discuss these effects, physicists use the language of “inertial frames”, similar to comparing a room at rest, or a rest frame, with a spaceship travelling at a constant speed, or a moving frame. In your individual frames, you and your friends can each establish a coordinate system, the familiar grid of width, depth and height. Your coordinate systems will match when you are all at rest or when your spaceships move side by side at the same speed.

When one of you moves more quickly, though, special relativity shows that their grid will deform, contracting in the direction of motion. It is this detail that bothered Einstein’s contemporaries. It seemed that the change in the rod length was uncomfortably intertwined with changes in the coordinate system used to situate it. But an effect that is a function of a coordinate system cannot possibly be real, critics argued. Ultimately, coordinate systems themselves are of dubious reality. They seem to simply be tools that we humans made up to help us organise our theories and observations of the physical world.

Does gravity create reality? A shocking path to a theory of everything

In 1911, physicist Vladimir Varićak argued that the rod’s length contraction “is only a psychological and not a physical fact, i. e., the body has not really undergone any change”. Giovanelli recounts another anecdote where, in the 1970s, physicist John Stewart Bell surveyed his colleagues at the CERN particle physics laboratory about whether length contraction could break a thread suspended between two spaceships accelerating at exactly the same rate. Most physicists said the thread wouldn’t break, endorsing the idea that nothing physically changes about the atoms in the thread. Could they have possibly been wrong? This made my head spin.

I will admit to having always been a rather terrible student of relativity, only learning it just well enough to pass my preliminary exams in graduate school. However, I’m certain I was previously taught that relativistic time dilation and length contraction are unquestionably real. We know they are, from experience in everyday life. The precise clocks on GPS satellites tick at different rates than those on Earth. This is partly because they move quickly and partly because of the gravitational effects explained by Einstein in his general theory of relativity. For GPS to be accurate, the difference in ticks must be corrected for. Failing to do so would have very real consequences, like ending up in someone’s backyard when I try to use my phone to visit a new café or bookstore. But here’s the crucial thing: the clocks on GPS satellites derive their precision from leveraging quantum control over atoms rather than some macroscopic clock gears, so it feels especially egregious to suggest that time dilation does, well, nothing to an atom.

Einstein himself was thinking about this, too, Giovanelli tells me. In fact, an atomic effect was at the centre of a 1906 debate he had with Johannes Stark, a physicist who was awarded the Nobel prize for discovering how electromagnetic fields can affect the energy states of atoms. Stark was studying fast-moving charged atoms and Einstein recognised that these experiments may display the transverse Doppler effect – in the same way that a siren changes pitch as it approaches you due to a shift in the frequency of its sound waves, a similar effect can happen due to time dilation. It is a distinct prediction of special relativity, an effect that doesn’t exist in other theories, says Giovanelli.

For the standard Doppler effect, you know that you could cancel it out by driving after the police car and that what is happening isn’t due to something changing inside the car’s speaker. The same question reared its head for the transverse Doppler effect. “Stark really thought, kind of naively but naturally, that something is going on in the atom,” says Giovanelli – in our analogy, the speaker in the car would be physically changing. Einstein rejected this. He posited that all the atoms remain the same and that their inner workings are unaffected by motion. Time dilation was the only explanation. Seemingly apparent, here it was confronted with a real, empirical test.

Ironically, when the transverse Doppler effect was experimentally verified in 1938, one of the two physicists involved was Herbert Ives, who never accepted special relativity. Ives thought that he had found signatures of the “luminiferous aether”, a hypothetical substance that some researchers thought permeated the universe and provided one preferred, true reference frame. A preponderance of other experimental evidence, much of it obtained even prior to Ives’s work, completely ruled out this option, and special relativity became the only game in town. For all the clamouring about the oddity of an effect related to an observer’s perspective, one that many physicists wanted to dismiss, time dilation withstood the test of time. Over the ensuing decades, ever-increasingly precise atomic clocks have never uncovered any evidence that something more “real” could be happening.

As far as Giovanelli is concerned, what happened was not so much a dispute over physics, but rather a run-in between physics and philosophy. Underneath the sticky question of whether time dilation is real hides another, even stickier philosophical one: what does it mean to be real?

Einstein killed the aether. Now the idea is back to save relativity

“At a certain point, you cannot avoid it,” says Giovanelli. “And so, Einstein was forced to address the question philosophically. OK, really, let’s define: ‘apparent’ means disappears for the co-moving observer, ‘real’ means empirically testable.” In some sense, the situation ought to never have become that complicated, he says. Scientific theories provide testable hypotheses – it is what they are designed for – and special relativity has passed every test we’ve put it to. What more could you ask from a theory?

Well, it’s hard to understand from an intuitive point of view, says Giovanelli. Einstein even had his own questions, primarily about how certain he could really be that two clocks, or two atoms being used as clocks, could be reliably identical. The advent of quantum physics offered some assurances, but Einstein had his qualms with quantum theory and spent time worrying about it way beyond how it applies to rods and clocks. But he never questioned the empirical reality of time dilation and length contraction, says Giovanelli.

As we talked, I wondered whether for me, like Einstein’s critics, it was my notable lack of relativistic intuition that made time dilation so hard to grasp. It may have been easier to accept that when atoms within a clock or a rod move at a certain speed, some as-yet-unknown mechanism physically changes them, leading to time dilation and length contraction. Instead, I have to grapple with there really being no such thing as absolute time.

Being a student of modern physics, however, I am not necessarily surprised by this somewhat frustrating duel between the words “apparent” and “real”. I gained my intuition about the behaviour of physical objects by interacting with mundane things like pens, oranges and soccer balls, never anything extremely small or cold, nor anything incredibly fast. Quantum theory, which governs all things tiny and chilled, taught me that I can’t always expect just one thing about an object to be unambiguously true at once. In fact, quantum objects can exist in states akin to clouds of probability that contain completely contradictory options. Absolute precision and absolute certainty are simply off the table. Special relativity may be teaching me a similar lesson about time.

The daring idea that time is an illusion and how we could prove it

Read an extract from Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s The Edge of Space-Time

New Scientist August 28, 2026

sε wo werε fi na wosan kɔfa a, yεnkyi

it is not incorrect to go back and get what you forgot

Advertisement

—Akan proverb

We are called to go back and get the history of space-time. And who am I to argue with the ancestors?

Even so, I do. Science in this society is often done for the wrong rea­sons, I find myself telling them. And they remind me that because it’s my job to study the origin and evolution of the universe and every­thing inside it, I know there is a location in space-time where the uni­verse became transparent to light: the first place where light could fly free. The ancestors insist: This is a story that I have learned so I could tell it to others. To do cosmology—to study the beginning and evolu­tion of space, time, and matter—is to be a griot, a keeper of stories and history. To do cosmology is to go back and get the beginning, to map out the future.

So: Quite nearly at the beginning, the universe said let there be light. And particles of light—photons—all of them traveling at the speed of light, the fastest in the universe, couldn’t get very far. They were stuck in a plasma stew where they constantly bumped into par­ticles, especially electrons, which swallowed their energy and spat it out in the form of new photons and other particles.

Humanity has only been aware of this cosmic light for eighty-two years. It has been there almost since the beginning of everything and has been traveling for nearly 14 billion years. It was there when the universe was cool enough for atoms to form. It was with the sun when it was just a cloud of gas, and it was there when the sun’s hydrogen ignited with fusion, turning the sun into a star. It was there when the leftovers from the gas cloud condensed into planet Earth. And it was there when carbon-based life forms evolved into apes.

Free newsletter

This light is a cosmic edge: We cannot look past it because at any time earlier than that, the photons were trapped, unable to get out. And this edge is a reminder that physics is a way of gaining deep insight into the universe, one we can add to the variety of overlapping forms of knowing that we have long used. To understand this bound­ary, and how we have come to know about it, is to deepen our rela­tionship with ourselves and the universe around us in a very specific and beautiful way. We should embrace it, for ourselves, and for future generations, because it is our history—and who are we to argue with the ancestors?

…

The book you are reading is about the queer, poetic wonder that is our universe and what we gain when we look at it from the margins. It is my version of what historian Aimé Dafon Sègla calls cosmovi­sions, a response to the question of why we should bother trying to get beyond the edges of human knowledge about the physical universe. The Edge of Space-Time is part of a larger tradition that includes not just scientists but also artists. People like jazz percussionist, artist, and technologist Milford Graves, who used percussion, sound, and observations of praying mantises and plant growth to understand a phenomenon he termed “cosmic energy.” Graves, a maker working in a long tradition of Black artists, was not formally trained as a scien­tist, and “cosmic energy” sounds a little like mystic talk. But when I listened to him describe his ideas in the documentary Milford Graves Full Mantis, I heard a familiar sensibility about how matter is linked with and through space-time, a relationship that takes center stage in this book.

As a set of knowledges and techniques, physics provides a path­way toward answering the same questions Graves asked about the fundamental nature of our cosmos and the relationship between matter, energy, and space-time. It allows us to specify in great detail the relationship between photons and the plants in Graves’s garden which transformed the photons into living particles. It is another entry point to what plant biologist and Black feminist theorist of intersectionality in science Beronda L. Montgomery calls lessons from plants.

When it’s at its best, physics is a kind of poetry, a story about the cosmos that is made from metaphors—and a producer of metaphors in its own right. We often analyze the world through metaphor, and I believe that seeing the universe through the perspective offered by physics strengthens our ability to understand what work metaphors are doing on us and how we might wield them. It is in this sense that physics works on us like poetry: a perspective on the world that provides insights not available to us elsewhere. This helps us under­stand why we should bother with it. We should bother with physics because it is, in part, how we as a species learn to use our minds. We should learn and teach poetry, physics, algebra, and other abstract ideas because they train us to think in symbolic and figurative terms. The same goes for calculus and quantum mechanics. And if we can­not learn to think in and through the abstract and the symbolic, then we are pliable. We are sitting ducks for the fascists and authoritarians who will use us for their ends, and their ends are ultimately catastro­phe for the rest of us. That’s always been true, and it always will be.

In a world where genocides (plural) can be live-streamed and still continue unabated, it is hard to imagine that society could be oth­erwise when what is broken about it feels so total and, in the case of the families shattered and lives lost, so final. I don’t think cosmology by itself can save the world. Even so, I believe in the ways that people experience a connection to the cosmos as nourishing. And I believe in preparing for the better world that is coming.

This is an extract from The Edge of Space-Time by Chanda Prescod-Weinstein (Canongate Books), the September read for the New Scientist Book Club. Sign up for the club here, and join the discussion on Discord here.

‘Thinking about the edges of space-time can help build a better world’

New Scientist August 28, 2026

If I could go back in time and tell my younger self something about life as a theoretical physicist, I might say: mind the gap between what’s exciting about physics and what the job actually is. My new book, The Edge of Space-Time, was born in part out of thinking about the physical questions that get pushed to the margins in professional physics. Big-picture questions like, what is the material nature of space? What is a quantum theory of time? It is very difficult to build a professional life working on these questions – even as books tout them as the most exciting ones in the universe.

I was recruited into the world of physics by the Errol Morris documentary about Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time. Eventually, I read Hawking’s book of the same name and my impression of a working life in physics was that, for the most part, physicists think big thoughts about wonders of the universe every day.

Free newsletter

Today, I’m a tenured professor of physics at a major research institution, and a lot of my job is sending emails about bureaucratic things, like asking whether anyone can tell me the policy that is governing changes that the university is making to my grant. On a good day, I get to have conversations about science with the postdoctoral fellows I employ in my research group – but that’s not every day. And in either case, the kind of research that we can get grant funding to do is quite limited. The sort of work Hawking did on the nature of time is financially out of reach for most physicists, a situation that is getting worse as the UK and the US both slash and burn basic science budgets.

Advertisement

The Edge of Space-Time was born in this gap between what we say science is and the reality of living it. I began it at a moment of transition. I had just been awarded tenure, which, in the US, historically has meant my position is permanent, and I am free to research whatever interests me without worrying about being fired. At the moment my tenure became official, I was thinking about what I had given up to get there, the strategic choices I had made.

Why dark matter is still one of the biggest open problems in science

I gave up working on quantum gravity, for example, both because of racism I experienced as a PhD student and because the job prospects weren’t good. I never took a class where we were asked to think deeply about time, space and the fundamental nature of space-time. Mostly, I learned to calculate and pursue questions that were broadly agreeable to the physics community, like understanding the nature of dark matter. And while I think these questions are important and interesting, they live at a kind of margin that physicists are pushed to by economic and social forces that determine which questions we can be paid to pursue and which we won’t be.

When I began working on the book in 2023, I was in the midst of a five-year stint working in US science policy, alongside colleagues from around the world (mostly the UK, Europe and Canada). As I learned more about the politics of science at the government level, it became clear to me that particle physics and cosmology were in trouble. Politicians were no longer sold on the fundamental importance of our research and didn’t see how it was beneficial to the capitalist economy or the military, which historically is how that support has been rationalised. The cultural arguments – that a well-cultured civilisation does things like try to understand the universe – didn’t seem impactful at all. And the general public, struggling with climate change and economies that don’t serve the 99 per cent, couldn’t see how we had anything to add.

You can’t put a price on the sense of awe particle physics inspires

I could see that we were about to be on the margins in a new way. And so The Edge of Space-Time became not just a return to my roots and the big-picture questions that once drove me, it also became a plea: don’t let me be the last of my kind. The cuts that are being made to science in the UK and the US right now seem like a political problem that is easily remedied, but it is more complicated than that. Even one year where there is a gap in funding means we haemorrhage workers who may never return. As those researchers leave, they take with them knowledge. Because the sciences work through apprenticeship, if there is no senior instructor to pass on knowledge, it doesn’t matter if there is money and an apprentice waiting in the wings.

With The Edge of Space-Time, I take readers on a journey through huge questions, like why does my favourite physics experiment foist the structures of quantum physics on us? And will we ever know what space-time really is, or is it always just going to be a useful mathematical construct that allows us to calculate motion in environments where gravity plays a significant role, like near black holes?

While thinking through the physics, I also try to make the case for why any healthy democracy needs people who live at the edge of what is known and what is unknown – the keepers of these cosmic stories that have fascinated humans for millennia. I make the case that, like poetry, physics gives us a viewpoint on the universe that we need because it is our ancestral inheritance. I also argue that spending time with what feels strange about physics can help prepare us to better reckon with difficult political questions.

Given the crises we face – genocides, climate change, attacks on transgender people – we need our critical faculties now more than ever. Thinking a bit about the various edges of space-time, like black holes and cosmic event horizons, can help us build the better world we need.

Wellington hospital called a ‘s***show’ as patients forced to wait 24 hours

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

Wellington Regional Hospital, and especially its emergency department, is under extreme winter pressure at the moment

By Ellen O’Dwyer of RNZ

Patients presenting at Wellington Hospital’s emergency department have faced wait times of more than 24 hours to be seen this month.

An ED nurse said that on a recent Monday night shift one man fell asleep and hit his head while waiting 12 hours to be seen.

Health Minister Simeon Brown said the current situation in Wellington ED was unacceptable, as it continued to be one of lowest-performing in the country.

But Health NZ said the hospital was under extreme winter pressure, and very long waits occurred for complex circumstances and weren’t the experience of most patients.

The New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) delegate said she feared speaking out would result in repercussions - RNZ agreed not to name her for this reason.

She said that on the overnight shift on Monday August 17 the hospital escalated to “code red” several times.

Health NZ said code red in ED referred to the amount of pressure the department was under - based on waiting-room congestion, staffing skill mix, changes in care hours and the seriousness of the patient cases.

The nurse said one man had come to the emergency department in the evening and wasn’t admitted until about 6am.

She said: “The only reason he was brought through then was because of him falling asleep and face-planting, and they were checking him for any injuries.”

The nurse said ED wait-times recently were extremely long - at times reaching 24 hours - although the peak was 18 hours more recently.

In internal Health NZ documents RNZ has seen, the agency said in early August that some patients exceeded 24-hour waits in ED, with high numbers of patients waiting more than six hours, due to medical bed shortages.

Hospitals throughout the country have a target that 95% of patients are admitted, discharged or transferred from an emergency department within six hours.

Latest results from Health NZ, between January and March 2026, show Capital & Coast hospitals only met that target 57.6% of the time.

An ED summary shift report from a staff member from August 17 said the department that night was operating under “extreme pressure”, experiencing “significant and sustained over-crowding”.

A mental health patient locked themselves in the bathroom and self-harmed, the nurse said, while a member of the public walked in and threatened to “kill staff”, assaulting a security orderly.

Police confirmed to RNZ they attended the hospital at 11.30pm to a report of disorderly behaviour - a person was arrested for breach of conditions, a spokesperson said.

Health NZ said it wouldn’t comment or confirm details about the specific patient incidents, without a privacy waiver.

The nurse said the hospital was full and bed-blocked that night, with at least 11 patients needing to be treated in corridors, although this was normal.

She said: “It’s just a s***show to work in at the moment. Lots of pressure.

“We’re getting high presentations, but the pressure’s coming from where we can’t get patients off to wards to free up our ED space, so that we can continue to see the new ones coming in.”

She said there could be up to 24 patients in corridors on other days, adding: “It’s awful, you know, and every day you’re seeing your corridors full and we’re all walking past these corridors. There’s no privacy for any of these patients.”

A Health NZ spokesperson said there were 27 full-time nurse vacancies at in the ED. In the coming months, 18 new nurses would come on board.

Michelle Sutherland, interim group director of operations for the region, said the hospital had 212 ED patients on August 17, following several days of high demand.

Winter was an extremely busy time for health services, so more patients were expected.

She said 66% of patients on August 17 were discharged from the ED within six hours, adding: “We acknowledge that a number of patients experienced very long waits. The longest waits tend to reflect particularly complex circumstances, rather than the experience of most people in the department.”

Brown said the current situation at Wellington Regional Hospital’s emergency department was not acceptable. He said: “It continues to be one of the lowest-performing in the country, and that is not good enough for patients or for staff.

“Our doctors, nurses and healthcare workers work incredibly hard every day, but they are operating in a facility that does not support safe patient flow or timely treatment.”

Brown said the government had prioritised a redevelopment of ED in the Health Infrastructure Plan and work was underway across the hospital campus.

His office said additional beds had been provided, among other planning measures made for the winter season.

Space in the hospital has been a long-standing issue, with the redevelopment likely to be complete by 2029.

Election 2026: National pledges lower student loan repayments for graduates staying in NZ, new penalties on Kiwis overseas

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

National is promising to lower compulsory student loan repayment rates for university graduates who stay in New Zealand, while increasing annual interest and buffing up penalties for those who move overseas, if re-elected.

National’s finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said in a statement the party would campaign on reducing the compulsory student loan repayment rate to 10 cents on every dollar earned above $24,128, down from 12 cents currently.

Simultaneously, Willis said National would introduce harsher penalties on Kiwis who move overseas in an effort to discourage defaulting and encourage graduates to stay in New Zealand.

This would see annual interest on overseas-based balances increased by 1 percentage point to 5.6%, with tiered penalties for sustained default on top of existing late payment interest rates.

If re-elected, the party would also restrict access to KiwiSaver so those living overseas permanently can only access their fund once clearing their student loan debt, while removing the need to prove a borrower had knowingly refused to pay before issuing an arrest warrant.

“National’s Back Pocket Boost for Graduates will reward young graduates who choose to stay in New Zealand, while pursuing those who leave and default,” Willis said.

“That is how we keep talent here, as part of our wider plan to fix the basics and build the future.”

New Zealand’s Student Loan Scheme (SLS) was introduced in 1992 by the Jim Bolger-led National government, replacing a long-standing system of near-free tertiary education.

Loans were initially interest-bearing for all borrowers until 2005, when Labour successfully tipped the election scales by campaigning to make student loans interest-free for those who remain in New Zealand for at least six months of the year.

In 2014, as offshore debt continued to balloon, National introduced “last resort” powers that made it easier for overseas-based defaulters to be arrested at the border.

The measure is still enforced, with arrests reported as recently as May, when a doctor living in Australia was arrested at Wellington Airport before flying home after defaulting on a decades-old student loan that had ballooned to about $180,000.

Data from Inland Revenue shows that more than 75% of the 114,347 Kiwis living abroad are behind on their repayments, owing $2.3 billion in overdue debt.

Nearly half of that default – approximately $1 billion – consists of accumulated interest and penalties.

In last year’s Budget, the Government confirmed an indefinite freeze on the repayment threshold at $24,128, effectively forcing 370,000 borrowers to pay more as inflation rises.

By not adjusting for inflation, the move is expected to save the Crown $65 million over four years by capturing more of borrowers’ income.

Earlier this year, the Government granted Inland Revenue the discretion to provide interest relief for overseas borrowers on a case-by-case basis, provided they commit to a lump-sum repayment or a short-term agreement.

Celebrated arts organisation Tautai Contemporary Pacific Arts Trust loses main funding source after 40 years

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

Then Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern helps open the Tautai Gallery, run by the Tautai Contemporary Pacific Arts Trust, in Auckland in July 2020. Photo / Tautai Contemporary Pacific Arts

A gallery and launchpad for contemporary Pasifika arts in New Zealand for four decades has lost its main source of funding and is reviewing its future.

The Tautai Contemporary Pacific Arts Trust is facing a “significant turning point” after its application to Creative New Zealand’s arts organisation and groups funding programme was unsuccessful.

Over the years, the trust has nurtured the careers of generations of Pacific artists, including John Pule, Michel Tuffery, Teremoana Rapley and Samoan master stone carver and painter, the late Johnny Reuelu Penisula.

The organisation receives support from other partners and funders but its main source of funding is from Creative New Zealand (CNZ).

The trust received $697,125 in 2023, $711,068 in 2024 and $725,289 last year. It will receive the latter amount again this year.

Tautai operations director Dr Olivia Laita said the funding outcome was “deeply disappointing”.

She posted a statement online confirming the loss of CNZ funding beyond 2026.

“This funding decision marks a significant turning point for Tautai,” she wrote.

“Our board and team have been taking the time to absorb what this decision means for our organisation, our artists and the communities we serve ... we will be reviewing what this means for Tautai’s future.”

Tautai has been a touchstone for many New Zealand-based Pacific artists and creatives since its founding in the 1980s by Samoan contemporary artist Papali’i Fatu Feu’u.

His goal was to support and promote Pacific visual artists while inspiring the next generation. At the time, he had been inspired by artist Colin McCahon.

Feu’u told the Herald he was still an emerging artist when another Kiwi artist and friend, Tony Fomison, introduced him to McCahon.

“I was so lucky. I was told I was the only Pacific artist who ever met McCahon before he passed away.

“He said: ‘We are waiting for you, Pacific artists, to make a contribution to the New Zealand art scene’. And here we are after 40 years.

“In the last 10 years, I’ve said to my friends: ‘I think we’ve done it – we’ve fulfilled his request’.”

Artist Michel Tuffery, born in Wellington, described the news about the trust as “heartbreaking”.

He remembers being a young artist, in the late 1980s, trying to get a break in the art world after studying at Otago’s School of Fine Arts.

He and fellow artist Lyle Penisula had their first exhibitions at what was then the Fale Samoa on Karangahape Rd, Auckland, thanks to Tautai.

“It’s done so much for all of us ... not just for starting artists’ careers, but also as an opportunity to meet the old ones.”

Tuffery has since completed many international art projects and is working on a piece for a war memorial in France. In 2008, he was made a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit for services to art.

He said Pacific art was still undervalued and it would be a huge loss if Tautai could not continue after this year.

“We’re denying that chance for those young ones ... the new ones that are coming through – my heart goes out to them.”

He said there was a huge demand for Pasifika in the art scene worldwide and encouraged budding creatives to continue their work.

“That’s why you need Tautai – so we don’t limit ourselves here to Aotearoa, because the world wants us.

“We can see from the Western perspective, but we can also go back to our Samoan or Cook Islands side. That’s our luxury,” he said.

In 2020, then Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern officially opened Tautai’s new gallery on Karangahape Rd, which showcases art and exhibitions by Pasifika artists year-round.

CNZ told the Herald in a statement that its arts organisation and groups fund is a contestable fund and applications are assessed on their merits.

“The quality of applications was exceptionally high, with demand for funding significantly exceeding the available support.

“At the same time, we are also navigating a constrained financial environment, managing reduced Government funding alongside a static lotteries funding path.

“We ... remain committed to supporting Pacific arts and artists in our ongoing work,” the spokeswoman said.

Feu’u is now 80 years old, a grandfather and great-grandfather. He is still creating artworks – albeit with the left hand helping to lift the right hand, armed with a paintbrush, because of a shoulder injury.

“It’s a slow process, but I’m still painting.”

He hopes young Pasifika will continue to look to the arts for a career and life purpose, he said.

“We believe in the arts. It can help heal the soul and get careers for a lot of young people. We can’t all be All Blacks and great athletes. So we turn to art to make a living.”

The news comes after organisers of another well-established Pacific arts entity recently called for donations as it grappled with financial issues.

Organisers of the Pacific Music Awards published a plea on Facebook, Instagram and its website in July, asking for public donations starting at $10.

The awards have run continuously since 2005, attracting audiences to its often televised and livestreamed ceremony.

“For 21 years, the Pacific Music Awards have been celebrating our artists, songwriters, producers and music,” trustee and event producer Petrina Togi-Sa’ena said.

“A number of factors [are] impacting the financial sustainability of the awards, not to mention the fact that public arts funding has been significantly cut, so the agencies that have long backed Pacific music now have less to give.

“This year, amongst continuing to look for sponsorship, we’re doing what our Pacific people have always done – turning to each other.”

Togi-Sa’ena told the Herald “it’s really survival mode each year”.

Contact journalist Vaimoana Mase

Vaimoana Mase is the Pasifika editor for the Herald’s Talanoa section, sharing stories from the Pacific community. She won junior reporter of the year at the then Qantas Media Awards in 2010 and won the best opinion writing award at the 2023 Voyager Media Awards.

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

Firefighters have contained a house fire on Forest Hill Rd. Photo / Hayden Woodward.

One person is dead after a fire engulfed a home in the West Auckland suburb of Henderson on Saturday night.

A Fire and Emergency New Zealand spokesperson told the Herald that multiple calls alerted them to the blaze on Forest Hill Rd at 8.37pm yesterday.

The single-storey home, measuring about 15m by 15m, was fully involved in fire when crews arrived.

Police confirmed this morning that one person who was originally unaccounted for had died.

Acting Detective Senior Sergeant James Kim said a scene guard was put in place at the property overnight.

“The cause of the fire remains unexplained at this early stage.”

Police will be carrying out a scene examination at the house today, including working with fire investigators.

Members of the community may see an increased presence while inquiries are ongoing, Kim said.

About 35 firefighters responded yesterday, supported by six fire trucks, a command unit, a hazardous materials unit and a breathing apparatus support vehicle.

Crews came from Henderson, Glen Eden, Te Atatū, Auckland City and Titirangi.

The incident was escalated to a second alarm response as firefighters battled the blaze and carried out a search and rescue operation for the missing person.

Assistant Area Commander Katie Pocock told the Herald at the scene that on arrival, crews found a well-involved property fire and were advised that a person was reportedly inside.

Heavy rain overnight drenches North Island communities after Northland flooding

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

Paddocks along Wayby Valley Road in Wellsford flooded yesterday. Photo / Hayden Woodward.

Heavy rain that drenched the upper North Island from Northland to Auckland and the Bay of Plenty has subsided.

Yesterday, flooding in Northland closed several roads while police asked the public to avoid unnecessary travel as river levels rose.

The heaviest rain fell in Whananaki overnight, with the area getting 93mm between 1-11pm, following warnings from MetService to watch for localised heavy rain that could cause flash flooding in Northland, the Coromandel Peninsula, Auckland and Bay of Plenty.

Kerikeri received 54mm in the same time period, while 28.2mm fell over Auckland from 1pm-12am, MetService meteorologist Maddy Neal told the Herald.

During the worst of the weather, rainfall rates reached as high as 25mm an hour on the Coromandel Peninsula.

Elsewhere, 25mm/h fell on parts of Auckland, 15mm/h in Bay of Plenty and 20mm/h in Northland.

It is now forecast to be cloudy with some isolated showers today and tonight for the rain-affected areas.

Looking ahead, a strong wind watch is in force for southern areas of Southland and Clutha for 27 hours from 9am today until noon on Monday. Westerly winds could approach severe gale in exposed places, with a moderate chance the watch will be upgraded to a warning.

The same watch comes into effect on the Tasman district from 4pm today until 1pm tomorrow.

A strong wind warning has also been issued for Hawke’s Bay south of Hastings and the Tararua district from 7pm tonight until 5pm Monday. Westerly winds could reach 120km/h in exposed places.

MetService said the gusts could damage trees, powerlines and unsecured structures, while driving could be difficult for high-sided vehicles and motorcyclists.

On Saturday, heavy rain caused flooding and travel disruption across Northland before the weather moved southeast towards Auckland, Coromandel and the Bay of Plenty.

Several Northland roads were closed or restricted, including Whangārei Heads Rd, where a blocked culvert was suspected of contributing to flooding.

Flooding was also reported at Helena Bay, Kawakawa and Kāeo, and across paddocks north of Auckland.

Police urged people to avoid unnecessary travel in Kāeo and Kawakawa as rivers rose, while some road restrictions were expected to remain in place today. MetService recorded rainfall rates of up to 25mm/h in parts of Northland and about 20mm/h in parts of Coromandel.

In Auckland, rising water in the Mahurangi River near Warkworth triggered the region’s flood alert system, with people warned to avoid flood-prone sections of Falls Rd.

Rotorua apartment fire: Man charged with wilfully setting fire to property

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

A man was charged in relation to a fire at a Fenton St apartment. Photo / Kelly Makiha

A man has been charged following a late-night fire at a Rotorua apartment complex.

Residents escaped the residential block of apartments on Fenton St when an alarm sounded shortly before midnight on Friday.

The apartments, on the corner near Carnot St in Glenholme, have long-term tenants.

A police spokesman said all residents and neighbouring occupants were safely evacuated and no one was injured.

The spokesman said at least two of the units were engulfed by fire.

He said a 29-year-old man was arrested and charged with wilfully setting fire to property and endangering life.

He made a brief appearance in the Rotorua District Court on Saturday morning and was remanded to reappear on September 11.

Police confirmed they were not looking for anyone else.

The fire caused debris from the apartments to drop onto the nearby footpath.

A couple who live at the apartments told the Rotorua Daily Post they appreciated how quickly emergency services arrived.

The woman said she was asleep when her partner came in telling her they needed to get out.

“We heard the alarm sound and some smoke coming out of the room … I was fast asleep and my husband was watching a movie. All of a sudden we had to get out and when we did the police were already there.”

The man said they were moved to the Novotel Rotorua for the rest of the night and their landlord made arrangements yesterday for alternative accommodation at neighbouring Park Central Rotorua, formerly Four Canoes Hotel.

A Fire and Emergency New Zealand spokesman said the apartment, which was about 30m by 8m, was well involved in fire when they arrived about midnight.

Five fire trucks and firefighters were called to battle the blaze – including two from Rotorua, two from Ngongotahā and one from Mamaku.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Nepal flood: The tragedy that ‘nobody expected’ – Editorial

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

Nepali Army personnel comfort twin babies during rescue operations in the aftermath of the deadly flash flooding. Photo / Prabin Ranabhat, AFP

As the death toll rose and the missing remained unfound, their families, wretched with grief and uncertainty, waited.

We have watched in horror the footage that emerged from the calamitous flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet-China border. Remote communication systems meant to warn those in low-lying areas were no match for the speed and size of the landslide and glacial avalanche.

As rescuers scrambled in the mud, dust and chaos, we watched.

Those missing include New Zealanders, some on pilgrimages, and hordes of foreign tourists.

The violence of a ruinous landslide that began with a melting glacier from the Langtang Lirung peak, near the border with Tibet, was unfathomable. When that vast chunk of ice loosened, it hauled a murderous freight of boulders and debris several storeys high. Towns and villages, once vital hubs of culture, community and resilience, now resemble wastelands submerged by mud and the heaviness of tragedy.

The Nepalese call Everest Sagarmatha, or Forehead of the Sky. The Tibetan name is Chomolungma, or Mother Goddess of the Earth.

Aotearoa New Zealand has an abiding bond with Nepal. It began with Sir Edmund Hillary, who, with Tenzing Norgay, summited Mt Everest in May 1953. Since then, the Himalayan Trust, founded by Hillary, has built schools, medical clinics and airfields. Many New Zealanders travel to Nepal to volunteer, to adventure and to connect with a culture defined by its rich literature, folklore, languages and philosophy.

The bridges we have built, both material and metaphorical, are made to last. Each year in May, Everest Day honours the bonds between Kiwis and Nepalis.

Many Nepalis have settled and established communities in New Zealand, with Auckland the largest hub, according to the 2023 Census.

Some of them joined in a candlelit vigil in Aotea Square yesterday as the search continues for the missing.

Scientists from around the world have said this was the largest glacier flood they have witnessed, warning that it is the catalyst for more to come from human-driven climate change.

Witnesses said, “Nobody expected that.”

Except science has warned us of this repeatedly. We are just not listening, even in the face of such horrors and of irrefutable evidence.

Nepal’s carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions are among the lowest in the world per capita: 0.01% of global CO2 emissions since the mid-1750s.

In 2024, the average person in Nepal emitted two tonnes of CO2 equivalents. In the same year, the average New Zealander emitted 6.23 tonnes.

Despite its low share of emissions, Nepal’s geographical virtues also make it vulnerable: mountainous and landlocked, it has suffered from deforestation and global warming.

Nepal, like many remote, developing countries, is also vulnerable to the decisions of leaders around the world. Its towering, jagged peaks and lush forests, combined with a fragile ecosystem, are no match for rising global temperatures caused by burning fossil fuels. The people of Nepal and Tibet live in a high-risk environment highly susceptible to natural disasters.

So, when we consider our connections and friendship with Nepal, its origin story and its legacy, we might reflect that the greatest friendship is not characterised by festivals (while lovely) or a building (while important), or even one viewed through the tender lens of nostalgia. It is most defined by decisions we make as a developed nation, environmentally, so we can carry that important legacy relationship, and the responsibility that comes with it, into the future.

This disaster cannot be undone, but it must not be relegated to an aberration; a clamour on social media; a brief season in the news cycle; a time in which we all stood, transfixed by it, feeling powerless.

What we decide to do next, environmentally, as informed human beings, and as steadfast friends, can change the course for generations.

That is a real friendship between nations.

Rotorua rafting merger wins approval through split Commerce Commission decision

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

The Commerce Commission has approved the merger of Rotorua’s three commercial rafting operators, much to the pleasant surprise of those behind the bid.

The ruling, finalised in June, came after months of investigation, during which Rotorua Rafting director Sam Sutton became so resigned to defeat that he and his fellow applicants came close to ditching the proposal.

After two decision extensions amid the commission’s concerns that the merger might lessen competition, Sutton was prepared for bad news.

“So it’s cool that they came through in the end,” he said.

“It’s exciting for Ōkere Falls to see what we can create as a destination.”

The decision clears the way for Rotorua Rafting, Kaitiaki Adventures and Kaituna Cascades to merge their rafting and sledging operations.

The proposal, first lodged in November 2025, was presented by the operators as a response to mounting pressures facing the sector, including rising operating costs, compliance expenses and increasing uncertainty around river conditions and visitor demand.

The application was backed by the Rotorua Lakes Council’s tourism arm, RotoruaNZ, and the local tourism sector.

RotoruaNZ chief executive Andrew Wilson told the commission the merger represented a “proactive and collaborative approach to ensuring the long-term sustainability of the rafting sector”, and would help preserve “a cornerstone of Rotorua’s adventure tourism identity”.

After the commission released a statement of unresolved issues in April, Sutton considered ending the bid.

But support soon arrived from the Tourism Export Council of New Zealand and New Zealand Māori Tourism.

The groups argued the industry faced rising costs and operational pressures, and that a combined business would be better placed to remain viable while continuing to invest in safety, staff and visitors.

Eventually, the regulator accepted that rafting operators compete not only with each other, but with a much broader range of visitor experiences across Rotorua.

For Sutton, the support from across the tourism industry reinforced his view that the merger was about strengthening the sector.

“I haven’t had too much negative feedback from it, so that’s good,” he said.

“There’s obviously the odd keyboard boys worrying about a rafting cartel, but I think there’s bigger cartels that they should be concerned about.”

Commerce Commission deputy chair Anne Callinan said the decision was “finely balanced”, with two of the three deciding commissioners approving the bid.

Associate commissioner Rakihia Tau was not supportive, saying he was not satisfied he could rule out the possibility of a substantial lessening of competition.

Tau argued the three operators were direct competitors and remained unconvinced other tourism experiences would sufficiently constrain the merged business once it controlled commercial rafting on the Kaituna River.

But he was outvoted by Callinan and fellow commissioner Bryan Chapple.

“Although these rafting providers are close competitors, we are on balance satisfied that the loss of competition resulting from the merger would be mitigated by a range of competitive constraints in aggregate,” Callinan said.

Sutton said work was now underway toward finalising the merger, but it would not be completed in time for the upcoming peak season.

The companies still need to resolve how the joint venture will operate and determine the level of involvement from each business.

He could not yet provide a timeline but said it would be finalised before the following peak season.

“It’ll be good for the customers,” he said.

“If we are able to pull this all off and pull it together, it’s going to be a better operation.”

Longer-term, he believes the merger will allow operators to focus less on competing with one another and more on attracting visitors from around New Zealand and abroad.

“Rather than fighting over a slice of the pie,” he said, “we’ll be actually able to grow the pie.”

Mathew Nash is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based at the Rotorua Daily Post. He has previously written for SunLive, been a regular contributor to RNZ and was a football reporter in Britain for eight years.

Tauranga City Council orders removal of protected tree on ex-mayor’s property

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

A nearly 150-year-old protected tree on an ex-mayor’s property faces the axe after Tauranga City Council ordered it felled under emergency powers.

The Bunya Bunya pine at 167 Grange Rd, Ōtūmoetai, is listed on the council’s Notable Trees Register.

Former Tauranga Mayor Greg Brownless owns the heritage property, known as Woodhill.

He said the tree was “demonstrably unsafe” for people and property after several limb falls.

The removal order has been criticised by Avenues resident Phil Green, a member of the council’s Urban Design Panel, and NZ Notable Trees Trust trustee Brad Cadwallader.

They have asked the council to stay the order while options for retaining the historic tree are explored.

The New Zealand Tree Register estimates it is 146 years old and measured it at more than 26m tall in 2017.

Council chief executive Marty Grenfell made the removal order under Section 330 of the Resource Management Act (RMA).

It comes as the council’s risk management practices are under intense scrutiny after a probe into January’s deadly Mount Maunganui landslide tragedy found systematic failures.

Green said an August 18 letter from Grenfell referred to a single recent limb failure and acknowledged previous arborist reports described the tree as “generally healthy”.

“To my untrained arborist’s eye, it appears the branch came down during a storm, not because of rot, disease or root instability,” Green said.

He questioned whether the tree had been regularly maintained and said it was not directly over homes or other structures.

Removing a protected tree without resource consent or clear evidence it posed an immediate risk to people or property was unjustified, Green said.

“Even if there were safety concerns, there are protocols that must be followed through the resource consent process.

“We need to draw a line in the sand and halt this process until there is clear evidence of an immediate danger that cannot be managed through alternative arboricultural measures.”

He described the removal of a healthy tree listed on the NZ Notable Trees Register as “a serious matter”.

Tauranga had already lost many mature and notable trees and Green said there was a steady decline in the city’s streetscapes.

He questioned whether similar trees at historic property The Elms would face the same fate if branches fell in storms.

In his view, the council should consider alternatives to felling historic trees and be more transparent about decisions affecting them.

Cadwallader said the emergency RMA powers required an “objectively reasonable opinion” that immediate action was necessary to prevent or remedy an emergency, and the response must be limited to what was necessary to address the threat.

“In our view, evidence of a single branch failure does not, on its own, justify removing the entire tree, particularly when previous arboricultural assessments found it to be generally healthy.”

He said he had asked for the removal to be halted until the council could demonstrate that removal of the entire tree was “proportionate and necessary” to address the identified risk.

Brownless, who was mayor from 2016 to 2019, owns the Category 2 Historic Place property with the Woodhill Trustee Company.

He said in recent years incidents of the tree’s limbs falling and endangering people had dramatically increased – not only in storms.

Several large branches had fallen since January, including on to power lines, he said.

“One branch smashed a fence, left a branch rammed into the earth and fell against power lines.

“More importantly than property damage, there have been near-miss incidents this year of people walking up the driveways and even on the adjacent footpath.”

Brownless said he and two neighbouring property owners had contacted the council several times this year about the tree.

“Initially, the council suggested a resource consent application to remove the tree, but later decided it posed an imminent danger and ordered me to remove it.”

He said the issue was not the tree’s health, but the danger it posed to public safety.

“Sadly, the tree has to go, but it is demonstrably unsafe. These 9m-long branches do pose a serious threat.”

He said the wood was “extremely dense and heavy”.

“Maintenance has been carried out over the years, usually after a branch falls, but there is no way to predict which branch will fall next.”

He said it was taking time to find a contractor able to remove the tree safely, and he would pay the removal bill.

The council’s general manager of operations and infrastructure Reneke van Soest confirmed Grenfell authorised the tree removal using emergency RMA powers.

“Council was satisfied there was a real and imminent risk that further limb failure could cause death, serious injury, or serious property damage.

“That assessment took into account a history of repeated large limb failures, recent photographic evidence of a substantial limb falling through a fence and across a driveway, and the tree’s position over entranceways, a public footpath and the road.”

Van Soest said Brownless raised his safety concerns with the council on April 8, seeking authorisation to remove the tree.

She said he was responsible for arranging its removal.

The council will meet on Tuesday to discuss its next steps in responding to the systemic issues raised in a review by former judge Paul Davison, KC, into the landslide tragedy.

Te Ranga Pamu dairy farm wins biodiversity and primary sector awards in Bay of Plenty

New Zealand Herald August 29, 2026

A 60ha Te Ranga block has been in the Mark family since 1912.

One hundred and fourteen years on, the family have won the Bay of Plenty Bayleys People in Primary Sector Award and the Ministry for the Environment Biodiversity Award at the 2026 Ballance Farm Environment Awards.

John Mark was the first European owner of the initial grazing and firewood block farmed in conjunction with his home farm on Mark Rd.

The property was expanded across the road in the 1960s, where his great-grandson Peter Mark now farms with his wife Megan Richards.

Their daughter Niamh Mark is the fifth generation of the family to farm there.

The farm was converted to sheep and beef by Jack Mark in 1964.

It was converted back to a dairy unit by Peter and Megan in 2014.

“It was a small one-person sheep and beef farm, and I love contact with people so it wasn’t really working for me,” Peter said.

“We leased the farm out for eight years, and I enjoyed tutoring for Toi-Ohomai and Primary ITO.”

Immersed daily in dairy information, Peter felt that the farm needed to be made more viable.

He decided on a dairy unit, with Jersey cows as they are lighter on the land and can manage a long walk to the shed.

“Getting finance from the banks for the conversion proved difficult as everyone who came on site said it was too hilly.”

A chance conversation with a BNZ staff member who was selling Peter a motorbike led to the family acquiring finance.

Milking started twice a day in the new 30 ASHB shed with 260 Jersey cows on the 100ha milking platform on the 170ha (127ha effective) property.

“The first year the payout was $3.90 per kg/MS, and the second year it was $4.20 per kg/MS, so the process to manageable debt and profit took a little longer than hoped.”

Now around 275 Jersey cows are milked once a day and average 319kg/MS per cow annually.

“What’s lost in production, we gain in cow reproduction, condition score and worker wellbeing.

“I work on the farm, Megan does the books and our daughter Niamh is the farm manager. Contractors do the extra jobs.”

In 2019, Niamh Mark was working for AsureQuality after finishing a degree in agriculture.

“I came home to help dad after a staff member resigned,” she said.

“During Covid-19, I stayed on through all the lockdowns.

“Towards the end of 2020 I met my now husband, Breno Codognolla, who works in the kiwifruit industry. We live on the farm.”

Niamh was in the running for the New Zealand Dairy Industry Awards 2022 Bay of Plenty Dairy Trainee Award and runner-up in the 2025 Bay of Plenty Farm Manager Award.

During Niamh’s time at the farm, the team have implemented new technology, including contracting in drone technology for precise weed control.

A virtual fencing system manages their grazing patterns and monitors cow health and behaviour.

“We’re definitely getting more out of our pasture this way, pushing the cows further uphill into new areas,” she said.

“It’s also reduced the workload by half a man-power.”

The judges praised the family’s robust succession planning, saying it provided a transparent, long-term framework for family continuity.

“We are moving the business structure from a partnership to a company to allow future generations to hold shares in Te Ranga Pamu.

“My sisters, Abi and Gwyneth, can all own shares.”

The steep terrain has prompted sophisticated management, including the recent installation of a 60m x 30m composting barn that provides shelter and significantly reduces the risk of soil damage and nutrient leaching.

Solar panels on the cowshed roof reduce environmental impact. Sustainability is deeply integrated into the farm’s structure.

“Over the past four years, we’ve planted over 10,000 native trees on steep, unproductive land, aiming to create a vital wildlife corridor in conjunction with neighbours that could eventually link regional kōkako breeding groups in Kaharoa and Otanewainuku Reserves.”

The team’s commitment to biodiversity is backed by intensive pest control efforts for possum and rats across the property and neighbouring areas.

Forty hectares of the farm were put under QEII protection in the early 1980s.

A bush classroom has been developed on 0.8ha of native bush, complete with its own glowworm track, and is used by the local primary school.

“A grant-funded specialist environmental teacher.”

The Marks are involved with the Paraiti Catchment Care Group with other like-minded local landowners.

Focusing initially on pest control and native tree planting, they received funding and assistance from BOP Regional Council and other environmental organisations.

The judges said that Te Ranga Pamu dairy farm demonstrates how exemplary leadership can merge profitability with environmental stewardship, ensuring the land looks set to thrive for future generations.

Leah Purcell is renowned for being tough on screen, but it’s what lies beneath that is the secret to her success

Sydney Morning Herald August 30, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Laughter might not come easily to the characters Leah Purcell plays: taciturn police sergeant Andie Whitford in High Country; fierce but distraught Molly Johnson in The Drover’s Wife; double-crossed undercover cop, now prisoner, Rita Connors in Wentworth.

But asked why she thinks audiences have embraced her High Country character, she erupts in raucous and infectious laughter. “Maybe they just like me … everyone fell in love with me!”

As an actor, director, producer and playwright, Purcell has forged a remarkably varied and successful career playing fierce and tough-minded women battling adversity and hardship. It’s what lies beneath that hard surface that is key to her appeal.

What Lies Beneath is also the subtitle of the returning season of the mystery thriller High Country, which sees Whitford back in uniform and investigating dark deeds in a small, close-knit town.

For those coming in late – no spoilers – High Country evolves around Purcell’s police officer Andie, who is transferred to a picturesque but insular mountain township of Brokenridge to replace retiring cop Sergeant Sam Dyson (Ian McElhinney, the veteran Northern Ireland actor best known as Barristan Selmy in Game of Thrones).

It’s a town filled with grievances, suspicion and vendettas and a handful of missing-person cases. Those disappearances dovetail with the discovery of a far-reaching conspiracy involving many of the town’s residents.

Alongside the mystery-thriller element, High Country also dealt with Andie’s new-found connection to her Indigenous ancestry and relationships with partner Helen (Sara Wiseman), teenage daughter Kirra (Pez Warner) and ageing mother (Melissa Jaffer).

It was filmed in Victoria’s high country, mainly around the township of Jamieson, which is where John Ridley – who created the show with Marcia Gardner – grew up and continues to live. The dramatic mountain landscape is a key element of the show. It also happens to be a region associated with many real-world events, from missing hikers to the cult known as The Family and most recently the notorious fugitive Dezi Freeman.

Purcell wears many hats on High Country. In addition to playing the lead, she is an executive producer, which allows her to have input to the script and key production decisions. She is also the cultural consultant, ensuring all protocols are correctly carried out. That haunting voice on the opening soundtrack is hers as well.

The new season takes up months after the events of the 2024 debut. It kicks off with a double murder on a houseboat, but there are many continuing storylines and characters, most notably Sam Dyson and Andie’s family.

Purcell says that many decisions regarding the new, eight-episode series were based on audience feedback. “Everyone fell in love with their relationship,” she says of Andie and Sam.

“We both thoroughly enjoyed working with one another. So we kept [the storyline] open and everyone’s diaries aligned and away we went,” she says. “He’s a great bloke and phenomenal actor and the story lent itself to opening up that relationship. It’s a thriller, so there’s many threads to the story, and it’s a great thread to have him being a part of.”

Audiences also felt that Andie’s domestic relationships were authentic. “Pez [Warner] reminded me of myself,” says Purcell. “She had no training, comes from Newcastle, is a little go-getter. We all have a great relationship and I think that comes across clearly in the first season.”

Andie has now settled into her job and has begun to understand the lay of the land. But she remains very isolated. Work is her life, her family. We only see her wearing her dark blue uniform. “That was all part of trying to show her isolation and what she’s put herself in at home.”

The new cast includes Brendan Cowell as a gnarly, surly and possibly shifty detective who has a contemptuous history with Dyson, as well as a troubling personal connection to the victims of the houseboat murder.

Purcell has played opposite Cowell on stage, describing him as deep and very smart. She credits Ridley and Gardner for allowing actors to “mould the words to suit their mouths. Brendan is very clever with that shorthand, which suits his character … the abruptness and poeticness around some of his lines.”

Season two of High Country has a noticeably different palette and setting to the first, which was dictated by the seasons in which the filming took place. “The lakes were down. So you utilise what you’ve got. He [John Ridley] said it’s a great way for any secrets that are hidden in that man-made lake [to be revealed]. When the water goes down, the secrets will rise and that’s what happens.”

Where season one was all lush and damp forests, season two is a baked and receding lake (the actual Lake Eildon), a barren mine and the glare of summer.

“We utilised that in the story, the change of landscape,” says Purcell. “The hardness of a mine, the masculinity in this story. It was all a hardened approach to the various landscapes up there. Turn one way and you’ve got lush mountains. Turn and you’ve got a mine shaft. That was all deliberate, just working with the landscape and the time of year we could shoot.”

Purcell believes that the success of High Country in the UK and US, where it aired on BBC and Hulu respectively, was due to it breaking the mould of what Australian stories are normally about. Instead of red-hot desert, viewers saw snow, mountains and greenery.

But mostly, she says, it was down to the character. “That’s what you want from your leading lady, that the audience falls in love with the character and what she was going through. And it’s a First Nations story, that was something else that makes this different. A woman trying to work out who she is and there happened to be this First Nations connection to Country.

“It wasn’t just the landscape; the landscape was talking. A lot of people thought that was a great addition to our cop story.”

Purcell recently added librettist to her extensive list of credits, having written the opera adaptation of her play, film and novel The Drover’s Wife, which is also being turned into a TV series. The series “is not what people think. It starts with Molly Johnson’s six-times granddaughter in 2020. We’ve flipped it, coming at it from a different perspective. It’s not just the movie in six episodes. We always try to find a different way into those stories.”

There’s nothing accidental about Purcell’s confidence and skill as a TV creator.

“People have said, ‘Leah you’re so easy to shoot’. Because I understand what they need, what the camera person needs. It’s experience, and time. It’s a talent to be at one with the camera, just me and it. It’s a talent that you learn if you’re aware of it. Some people can be in the industry forever, and it’s not quite their thing, but I’ve had a couple of DOPs come up to me and say you’re so easy to shoot because you understand what the camera is doing.”

She recalls one of her first roles on Police Rescue. “It was my training ground. I would sit and watch and understand when the camera was moving or crept in for a close-up. When Steadicam came in, that was magic, that was like dancing.

“I love that challenge. Sometimes you can get caught up for a very long time trying to get the take if you don’t understand what they’re trying to achieve with the camera. So I would ask them, what do you need from me? It’s all very clinical, it’s maths when you break it down. It’s our job to make it look natural. I learned very early that the relationship other than [with] your fellow actor is with the camera.”

But even after 35 years in the business and despite a full slate of future projects, she takes little for granted. “It’s a tough industry, but you’ve got to believe. I’ve created paths and proven myself that I can hold a show. We’re a small industry, so everyone wants a piece of a very small pie. We keep chipping away and hoping that our stories come through and rise to the surface.

“As they say – what lies beneath,” which prompts another hearty laugh.

High Country: What Lies Beneath premieres on Monday, September 14, on Binge.

Palestinian woman and NBC News team reportedly attacked in West Bank

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 21:55:08 GMT

Matt Bradley and crew assaulted while interviewing woman who said settlers had driven family out of home

A Palestinian woman and an NBC News team are reported to have been attacked and injured by masked Israeli settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday, amid worsening confrontations in the area.

Benjamin Netanyahu said he condemned the violence committed “by a handful of rioters”.

The attack occurred when four members of the news team were interviewing Aida Ahmed Abdullah and her family in the Palestinian town of Jalud, near Nablus.

Abdullah told the outlet that they had been driven out of their home by settlers, and the team was walking down a hill toward the house.

A car with Israeli license plates reversed up the hill toward them. At least four men with their faces covered leapt from the vehicle, hitting them with sticks and throwing rocks.

“They jumped out, beat us, then jumped back in the car,” said NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley. Bradley was hit twice in the arm and treated at a nearby clinic.

Abdullah, 51, was taken for medical care by the Red Crescent. Her injuries were not life-threatening. Three other members of the news team were also injured and treated.

“Suddenly a car came to us,” said producer Lawahez Jabari. “The settlers had sticks, I saw a gun, but they didn’t use the gun.”

Camera operator Khaldoon Eid said the team had not expected to be attacked in a village.

Several violent incidents in the area were reported on Saturday. Palestinian workers were pepper-sprayed in nearby Qusra by masked Israeli settlers.

Israeli security forces told the outlet they had received reports that “violent clashes had occurred, including stone-hurling toward Palestinians and additional civilians”.

They said “security forces identified dozens of rioters who had barricaded themselves inside a Palestinian home while Palestinian residents were inside”, the statement said.

“The security forces who arrived at the scene initially operated to remove the rioters from the home and separate the groups, in order to protect the residents inside. In addition, the security forces confiscated vehicles belonging to the Israeli rioters that were suspected of having been used to reach the area,” the statement said.

“IDF soldiers and Israel Border Police forces continue to operate in the areas of Qusra and Jalud to prevent further disturbances and restore order in the area,” it added.

Earlier this month, a group of settlers began blocking supplies from entering Palestinian houses on the outskirts of the village near Nablus, trapping residents inside and drawing strong criticism from the US ambassador.

Israeli forces continue to operate in the area while settlers still roam the surrounding hills.

Netanyahu, whose government has been accused of turning a blind eye to the settler attacks, condemned the “criminal acts of violence” and blamed “a handful of rioters who violate the law, cause enormous injustice to the law-abiding settler public, hinder the IDF in fulfilling its missions and harm Israel’s standing in the world”.

According to the United Nations’ office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank in the year to 24 July. Three Israelis were killed over the same period.
