Lavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of a soul or spine

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 20:33:33 GMT

It might be too early to push the panic button but Roberto De Zerbi faces a huge task if he is to turn Spurs around

Time for Tottenham to start panicking? This is, of course, a subtle trick question. Tottenham is one of those clubs that never actually stops panicking. They panic when they concede and they panic when they score. They panic when they have the ball and they panic when someone else does. They have a coach in Roberto De Zerbi whose face evokes a state of permanent alarm, the expression of a man perpetually having a toilet door opened on him. One year they even managed to panic their way to the Europa League. For the ever-rattled Spurs fan, this club is less a treasured devotion and more a lifelong haunting, broken up by occasional panic substitutions.

You could intuit that sense of encrusted resignation pretty much from the moment Anthony Elanga’s improvised shot kissed the post and trickled over the line to give Newcastle the lead. Since beating Aston Villa 4-1 in late 2024, Tottenham have gone behind 44 times in all competitions and come back to win precisely zero of them. There is something innate and endemic here, a chronic case of Long Tottenham for which – despite the new coach, the new leadership structure and more than a third of a billion pounds in transfer fees – there remains no proven cure. Yoane Wissa’s clincher was of zero surprise to anyone.

And so welcome back to the temple of pain, the Theatre of Everyone Else’s Dreams, a stadium that fittingly still has no naming rights because pretty much every visiting side gets to own the place. Over the past 12 months, Aston Villa have won the same number of domestic fixtures at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (two) as Tottenham. Unai Emery’s men may well get the chance to retake their lead here in three weeks’ time. In the meantime it was Newcastle, with one clean sheet in their last 18 matches, who feasted on Tottenham’s neuroses, stayed tight and stayed patient, waited for the train that always arrives.

Perhaps as Matthias Jaissle’s team climbed all over the duels and the second balls there was also a certain reassuring symbolism here: a lesson in the enduring value of culture over commerce. Newcastle have lost half a team but kept their soul; Tottenham have bought half a team and are still searching for theirs. There were inevitable boos for Sandro Tonali, who was actually fine: one of those rare Tottenham players who actually treasures the ball and wants to do interesting things with it. Alongside him Mateus Fernandes was restless, classy, excellent. Omar Marmoush on his debut looked fit and sharp. But of course the individuals were never the problem here.

The problem was the little things: the lost headers, the fractional pauses on the ball that kill momentum, the rushed shots, the extra touches, the tackles not quite committed to, the barely perceptible signs of a deep-rooted softness. Take Elanga’s goal, which sprang from an unpressed Nico González long ball, a poorly challenged Amar Dedic header, a cool turn and finish. Three very simple things in a row, at least two of which should probably have been prevented. No screaming howler or smoking gun here. Just a run of lost battles, a sum of marginal flaws, a team that for all its moments of promise and competence has not yet been welded together into a coherent whole.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

How De Zerbi fixes this is anyone’s guess. It feels increasingly clear that for all the new blood there is still a kind of generational trauma here, perhaps dating back to the injury crisis of 2024-25, when a threadbare squad was pushed beyond the boundaries of wellness and sanity. For the veterans of that campaign, your Archie Grays and Micky van de Vens, your Destiny Udogies and Rodrigo Bentancurs, you occasionally glimpse that accumulated tension in the 50-50 tackles and big physical clashes, the sense of players still not quite trusting their bodies. And oppositions really do pick up on this stuff. Right now there is a clear blueprint for beating Tottenham: compete, do the simple things well, and eventually bully them into playing your game.

How much worse does this get before it gets better? Are Spurs fans ultimately in for another season of discontent and disgruntlement, of taking an unhealthy interest in the latest score from the Coventry Building Society Arena? The instinct here is still to be patient and wait for the required chemistry to develop. But what if two defeats become four, or six? What if it’s November and the top scorer is still somehow Richarlison with two? How does a club so medicinally addicted to panic possibly avoid it?

Quietly, there is now some ridiculous creative talent at this club. The signings of Marmoush and Sávio, the new-look midfield, the return of Mohammed Kudus and Dominic Solanke, the prospect of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons to come. A World Cup finalist in Marcos Senesi sitting unused on the bench. It feels inconceivable that Tottenham could be in relegation trouble again. But as with so many clubs before them, Tottenham are discovering that buying new footballers is the easy part. Growing a spine will take considerably longer.

The moment I knew: I’d never had romantic feelings for a man – then he touched my hand and it felt electric

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 20:00:37 GMT

As a widower and a newly single father of three, Jim Rogers was struggling. Then on a poolside holiday, he sat next to Tyler – and his life changed

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

In the mid 90s, I was in the prime of my life. I was in my early thirties, married to my soulmate, Lorna, with three kids under three. We’d emigrated from our small town in Worcestershire in the UK to Perth, and life was wonderful. Then Lorna was diagnosed with melanoma. We returned to England and less than a year later she was gone. It was completely unbelievable, as though someone had just come along and smashed my life into a million pieces.

The following months were a blur: I was a grief-stricken widower and newly single parent struggling to keep the kids’ life on track and my own head above water. As time went on, it was obvious I wasn’t doing well and my parents insisted on treating me to a holiday in the sun. I didn’t want to go.

I remember arriving at this beautiful hotel in the Canary Islands and sitting on the balcony. I was so miserable looking out at all the happy people holding hands.

Every day I’d drag myself down to the pool and sit in the same spot. There was a large group of British tourists there each day who would look at me sympathetically and invite me to join them. I turned them down a few times but eventually I thought “sod it” and joined in, careful not to burden anyone with the tragic details of why I was there all alone.

Over poolside beers I found myself chatting to this lovely English chap, Tyler. When I asked if he was married he surprised me by telling me he was gay. I’d never met an openly gay person in my life.

The day went on and as my spirits lifted I agreed to join them for the evening. Tyler and I spent the night chatting and laughing and one by one the group dwindled until it was just the two of us. As we eventually wandered back to the hotel he threw his arm around my shoulder and I just felt this connection. Over the next couple of days, I noticed I was thinking about him all the time. We went out for lunch one day, and I spilled my whole story.

Back in England we began chatting on the phone for hours every evening. It became clear that this friendship was lifting me out of the doldrums – our conversations each night made me feel like I wanted to get up the next morning.

One day I drove to London to surprise him at work. We went for lunch in this lovely restaurant with views over the Thames. As he reached out and touched my hand in the elevator, electricity ran through me. Then he leaned in and kissed me. I’d never had romantic feelings for a man before. It was so strange; it felt so right, yet so wrong. I was desperately confused but I couldn’t let go of it because it was making me feel something I hadn’t in the longest time – happy.

In those days, and in my conservative village, the idea of being openly gay was a complication I couldn’t add to my life. I’d been on a few dates with women, but they were always spoiling the kids and making me cringe; and I never wanted to feel like I was replacing Lorna.

Whatever was going on between Tyler and me was different. It didn’t feel like it was spilling over into the children’s lives: it was just for me. When I introduced Tyler to the kids, it was just as “dad’s friend”. They never questioned it, and Tyler didn’t want anything from us: he just wanted to give. He made everything fun and his upbeat personality lifted this dark cloud that had been hanging over us all. He was so comfortable in his own skin, so kind and so spontaneous; it changed everything.

Eventually, I told my parents. While my mother was sceptical, my father was amazingly supportive. Still, this was small-town England in the early 2000s and I felt the only way we could be together was if the house next door came up for sale. Miraculously, it did!

Ty is the most impulsive person you will ever meet. If he’s in, he’s fully in. He went back to London and called to say if I saw a “sold” sticker on the sign, it was him. A year after we met, he moved in and we became neighbours. Ty’s dad came over and popped a panel out of the garden fence. Out the front, we were a widower and a bachelor living side-by-side; out the back, we were together. We lived like that for years.

Several years later, friends from Australia came to visit. They went on and on about how much they loved it there, and how much Lorna had wanted the kids to grow up there. My kids seized on this and would not let it go. For a while I pretended I was looking into it, then I gave in. We returned to Perth when the kids were 12, 13 and 15; they finished high school there and then headed east for their careers. Ty and I soon followed.

We made a beautiful life for ourselves in Sydney. It was everything you could want from Australia, wrapped up with a bow on it. But I was starting to have problems at work. I’d been managing large scale property projects for decades, but I was getting forgetful – something wasn’t right. At the doctor’s one day, they asked me to turn my phone to silent and I was completely blank; I simply couldn’t work out how to do it. Tests would reveal I had early-onset dementia. I was only 55.

I fell into a serious depression. But Tyler has a very positive outlook on life: even in the worst of times you’d very, very, rarely catch him down. It’s just his natural way; some people are lucky enough to be like that.

No matter how maudlin I can get, he stays calm, and you will never hear a shortness in his voice. One day, as I continued to wallow about my diagnosis, he said: “Listen, you have to draw a line in the sand and you have to step over it. Because if you stay here in this moment, you’re gonna miss what is right under your nose and all the fun we could have.”

We’ve been travelling the world celebrating our 25 years together. Tyler has rescued me more than once. I feel so very lucky that we crossed paths.

Jim Rogers is a dementia advocate and author of Holding On To Happiness, co-written with his daughter, Millie Robinson, available on 1 September through Pan Macmillan (RRP AU$36.99).

AI vaginas, customisable personalities and fake bruises: the sex doll market is booming. Does it matter how the dolls are treated?

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 20:00:35 GMT

As the sex doll industry grows and AI changes the products available, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?

Two weeks ago, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman, stuffed into a suitcase in a small town about three hours south of Sydney. They called the local police, who in turn issued a statement that a body in a suitcase had been found. The wider public waited sombrely for Australia’s tally of dead women to tick up by one.

But instead, a day later, after forensic analysis, it was determined that the woman in question wasn’t a woman at all. The “body” was that of a sex doll, marked with fake bruises, left to rot on a lonely dirt road. In Australia, as in the UK and some other European countries, it is not illegal to own a sex doll unless it resembles a child. Given the doll’s seemingly mature presentation, police investigations were called off.

The sex doll trade is flourishing. A 2026 market analysis estimates that the global market currently was valued at US$6.6bn in 2025, with a projection that it will more than double, to US$13.4bn, by 2033. As the market booms, and involves increasingly lifelike facsimiles of women, does how these dolls get treated matter?

And when a sex doll with “bruises” and rain-matted hair is tucked into a suitcase and left on a roadside, should we be concerned?

Johannes Fuss, chair of forensic psychiatry and sex research at the University of Duisburg-Essen, tells the Guardian that “the disposability and desecration of the female form in these contexts cannot be viewed entirely in isolation from broader cultural hostilities toward women”. Working with researcher Jeanne C. Desbuleux, Fuss has published papers on the link between the anthropomorphisation of sex dolls and gender-based violence.

The research remains inconclusive. “We currently lack robust longitudinal data to definitively prove whether such doll use is protective or, conversely, is a behavioural stepping stone that increases real-world offending risk. I think we urgently need research on this question as more and more technologies enter the market to simulate human sexuality,” Fuss says.

However, he is suspicious of their appeal. “To put it provocatively: it boils down to total availability, a youthful and attractive body, and zero emotional demand or dialogue.”

A quick scroll on The Doll Forum website finds members regularly pit real-life women against their silicone knock-offs, one writing that “girlfriends are for guys who haven’t found the right doll yet”, and that “no matter how pretty she is, there is a man out there who is sick of her shit”.

Tammie Paine, owner of Naughty by Nature Adult Store, a sex doll retailer based in Adelaide, regularly engages with sex doll enthusiasts. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that they all fit a particular stereotype, or that owning a doll automatically says something negative about someone’s character,” she says. “This hasn’t been our experience at all. The recent image from Goulburn [a town near where the sex doll was found in the suitcase] understandably attracted attention because, without context, it looked confronting. But I don’t think one unusual image should be used to characterise an entire group of consumers.”

While the market for sex dolls may be heterogenous, what does it mean to engage in any kind of relationship with a woman-shaped thing?

“From my conversations with professionals and police, there are definitely men with adult-like companion dolls who see that doll as a person. They might see their dolls as women,” Prof Kelly Richards, a criminologist in the School of Justice at the Queensland University of Technology Centre for Justice says. “But do they see women as humans?

“This is going to sound really dark. But in a global context, where I believe gender equality has gone backwards, sex dolls are actually just the extreme end of that.”

Central to the industry’s rise is sophisticated technology. Lifelike sex dolls are now increasingly customisable. Prospective buyers can render themselves an ideal companion from scratch, courtesy of 3D printers. In 2017, the sex-doll brand RealDoll paved the way for the future of AI-generated sex robots by introducing “Harmony” to their coterie. In its newest model, which its website says will be available this year and for which it is running a waitlist, buyers can assign personality traits to her – attributes like “spiritual” or “insecure” – from an app on their phone. “She’s far more than a beautiful body. Harmony listens to you,” the website reads.

The new Harmony also has an AI vagina – described on the RealDoll site as “an electronic insert that pairs via Bluetooth to the X-Mode App. It detects touch, movement, and speed, transitioning naturally from mild arousal to climax, with synchronised vocal responses that make every moment feel real.”

At the 2026 annual Consumer Electronics Show, a major international conference that unveils breakthrough technologies, the Singapore-based sex tech company Lovense introduced Emily, an AI-powered companion doll, to participants. She is customisable, offering “personality switching” from modes including “co-worker”, “gym crush” and “tradwife”, is able to send AI-generated selfies on request, and remembers past conversations. The Lovense website outlines built-in sensors around the doll’s body which elicits a moan when touched, and suggests the doll can offer “routine companionship”, help with “building confidence through judgement-free connection” and allow for a “safe expression of your wildest fantasies”. The site is running a waitlist, with shipping expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Coeros, an online sex doll accessories brand based in Los Angeles, offers customised sex doll heads. According to their website, they are able to model each head on “photos of a real person, an original character, or an AI-generated image”. Customers are able to upload reference photographs to a submission form on their site, when ordering their very own ersatz woman. The Coeros website claims they are able to “achieve around 90% resemblance” to the woman in photographs provided, depending on the quality of the images. The entire process of making the doll’s head, it says, is about one to two months.

Asked about the company’s responsibilities or processes if a doll was asked to be modelled on a real person without their knowledge, a spokesperson at Coeros told the Guardian: “The fact that a custom design can be created from reference images should not be interpreted as permission to use another person’s likeness without their consent. We do not encourage or support the use of our customisation service for harassment, impersonation, or other non-consensual purposes.” Details for prospective buyers on the website include specific services from eyebrow hair implantation to shipping, but do not appear to include any directions as to obtaining the permission of women in any photographs uploaded. One member of The Doll Forum wrote of Coeros’s invention: “The most obvious candidates are the ones who turned you down, the ones that got away, the ones you had no hope of winning.”

A custom sex doll head is available for approximately US$1,790. Caitlin Roper, Australian author of Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, calls these kinds of dolls “replica female sex slaves”.

Roper actively campaigns for adult sex dolls to be prohibited as well as childlike sex dolls. “There’s an understanding, in the case of child sex abuse dolls, that their use extends to the harm of actual children. This same recognition of harm does not extend to adult women dolls. Women are being reduced to a set of penetrable orifices,” she says, before referencing a case currently being tried in South Korea involving Jang Yoon-gi, a 23-year-old man who last month admitted to the rape and murder of a 16-year-old high school student in May. A damaged sex doll was reportedly found in his apartment, with damage to its neck and chest.

There was much speculation about why the sex doll was abandoned on the quiet country road south of Sydney. Was it a prank? A dark, violent fantasy? Or possibly, even, a clumsy way of discarding a large and bulky item – garbage?

As a large, potentially embarrassing, item, disposal of a sex doll can present its own set of issues. In March, a man from Adelaide posted an advert for his 5’6” tall sex doll on The Doll Forum. This is because it can be easier to give away a doll, even one with a mutilated vulva, than it is to dispose of one. This particular owner had cut holes out of his doll’s vagina and had never gotten around repairing it by glueing new thermoplastic elastomer to the area.

On Reddit, there are many other dolls looking for adoption, and a trove of pictures can be found. Their list of injuries are interminable: macerated nipples, perforated limbs, mouths encrusted with mould. The users authenticate listings for their used sex dolls by positioning them next to blank pieces of paper, inscribed with username details and the date. It makes for a grisly tableau of lifeless hostages.

Jerry Siew, owner of SxDolled, a sex doll retailer in Australia, has seen the same listings. “I went through forums – I saw the demand of people wanting to dispose of their dolls. I see it as very important,” he tells the Guardian. Siew’s company is the only one in Australia that offers a discreet lifelike doll disposal service.

“For owners, it gives them a dignified way to part with a beloved doll, whether the doll is beyond repair or they are simply moving and unable to take the doll with them. You just have to look at the incident in Goulburn,” he says. “It caused 20 hours of police time, and stress for the community. I’ve also seen articles of dolls thrown into oceans and rivers. That causes panic and wastes emergency resources.”

These glass-eyed companions have little to say about their treatment, but their owners frequently do. While discussing how best to dispose of a lifelike doll, one member of The Doll Forum recommended investing in a chainsaw. “Live out your wildest chainsaw massacre fantasy!” he wrote.

Bill Lee, the Tennessee governor, on Friday said he favored a proposal to rename Nashville’s international airport after legendary country singer Dolly Parton, who died three days earlier at age 80.

In a statement, Lee said he and the managers of the airport in Tennessee’s capital city – where Parton resided – wanted to create “a lasting tribute to her indelible legacy and the generations of people she inspired”. He said he had spoken previously to the 11-time Grammy winner and her team, who were “touched by the idea”.

“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said, noting that Nashville airport is where Tennessee welcomes the world.

He added: “It is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”

The proposal was scheduled to be addressed at a meeting of the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority (MNAA) on 17 September. A statement from Doug Kreulen, MNAA president, said the Nashville airport shared Parton’s understanding that “dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status”.

“Whether you are boarding a private aircraft or taking your first flight, you deserve to be welcomed, respected and served with the same level of care,” he remarked.

Parton had requested a private funeral for immediate family, and there is not going to be any public memorial. She will be buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, at Nashville’s Woodlawn memorial park and mausoleum.

The singer told Entertainment Weekly in 2014 that she expected Whitney Houston’s rendition of I Will Always Love You to be part of her service. Parton also said she wanted an old gospel hymn, If We Never Meet Again, which was her father’s favorite.

In a video statement announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver, her longtime head of security, remarked: “Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”

Lee discussed the proposal to rename Nashville’s airport after a plane tugging a banner urging the name change buzzed over the Tennessee state capitol on Friday. A petition was also launched, and it has since gained more than 150,000 signatures.

“Everybody is looking for a way to honor Dolly and her legacy,” petition organizer Dan Dion told the Tennessean. “Our airport is so important, and there’s symbolism in flying into Parton Airport. With Dolly’s message of love, acceptance, music, kindness, humor and all these things, people feel that she is representative of what Tennessee truly is.”

If it comes to be, renaming Nashville airport will be at least the second airport in a matter of months to make a switch. Palm Beach airport was recently renamed for Donald Trump, with mixed reactions from travelers and locals about naming the facility after the president.

Freddie O’Connell, the Nashville mayor, hinted that the proposed name change is only the start of metropolitan tributes in the city. He said the 9 to 5 and Jolene singer had been in the process of developing a hotel and museum called SongTeller “that she called her love letter to Nashville”.

“Now it’s our turn to share a love letter to Dolly – by renaming Nashville International Airport to Dolly Parton International Airport in Nashville,” O’Connell told the Tennessean.

He also said the city was “working closely” with Parton’s team and family “on appropriate public recognition”.

Omar Badawy: Guided Detour review – dizzying tales of decision paralysis

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 19:31:10 GMT

Pleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThe comic’s unique tale of assimilation and romance-related limbo has a high joke rate and emotional intelligence

I want to tell Omar Badawy to take a breath. This debut moves at a frantic, almost dizzying pace, so much so that you could easily miss a few details in a show that zooms in and out of the time he was accidentally caught in the middle of a Tommy Robinson march while en route to a fancy dress party. But with writing this sharp, does it matter? You can see why SNL: UK came calling.

The Cambridge-raised Badawy lays out his identity conundrum: he’s an Anglo-Egyptian Muslim who, as a pupil at a Christian school, was teased for his background. Differences surfaced during Nativity plays, where his culturally accurate interpretations of innkeepers and wise men’s assistants weren’t quite what his teachers had in mind. He also knows his well-spoken accent makes it easier to assimilate. Because of all this, Badawy often feels stuck in the middle. Once, a stranger even asked his ethnicity because he wanted to call him his “correct racial slur”.

Perhaps this state of limbo is also why he has a severe case of decision paralysis. He’d rather be pulled into things than actually have to choose a side. But, at university, he started going out with the only Arab girl, and now he’s got a big choice to make. Using the march as the linking framing device feels too neat, but it also gives Badawy a heart-tugging, romcom-style ending.

With his delivery veering towards the shrill and over-astounded, he doesn’t yet look totally at ease on stage. The more he tells us he hates leaving the house, the more you start to actually believe him. And yet Badawy possesses a budding star quality and the hour with him is a joy. His voice is unique, emotionally intelligent and generous. He shoves a hell of a lot of jokes in along the way – from having to police his divorced mother’s suitor list to using football chat to placate angry men. It’s an hour about detours, but there’s no question Badawy is going places.

Dan Lawrence said he was “desperate to establish myself in an England shirt” after taking some solid steps in the right direction on a rain-affected third day of the second Test against Pakistan.

In a chill breeze and with frequent interruptions from the weather, the battle for England’s batting spots heated up in the continued absence of the injured Jacob Bethell. Emilio Gay’s hard-fought 31 was ended by a grubber before Lawrence scored his second half-century of the series – matching Jordan Cox on that metric – to put England in control, 177 for seven at stumps to stand 357 ahead.

“I’ve really tried not to think about that,” Lawrence said about the contest for places, after finishing the day unbeaten on 50. “I’ve tried to just enjoy every day of being here and trying to contribute to the team. It’s pointless looking into the future. I’m just trying to give a good showing of myself and thankfully I think I have done.

“Thoughts creep into your head and I’m desperate along with all the other boys to establish myself in an England shirt. It’s just about trying to take every opportunity you get instead of feeling nervous about the occasion, just have fun and play the cricket that’s got me here this summer.”

Lawrence’s last run in the team, three Tests against Sri Lanka in 2024, came as opener and without great effect, three single-digit scores and three in the thirties. “I got wrapped up in a lot of things and I was thinking about my position and what I needed to do to stay in the team, instead of just enjoying it and realising how lucky I am to play for England,” he said.

“My mentality since coming back has been completely different. Hopefully, we get a good series win and then we’ll see what happens in the coming months and years.”

As a middle-order batter by preference he does not covet Gay’s position as opener – “It has been great fun batting in a position that is a little bit closer to what I’m used to,” he said, after a third outing at No 6 – and certainly took no pleasure in the 26-year-old’s dismissal, trapped lbw by a Mohammad Abbas delivery that kept low. “He played beautifully last night, dug in really hard and fought for the team.

“Hopefully that bit of bad luck he got, he gets all the good luck next week. He can take a lot of confidence in how he played.

“To get off the mark I had a massive big whooshka and edged it over the slips. That could easily have been caught and I’d have looked really stupid.”

No country for old men: Premier League grind is why managers are getting younger

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 19:00:34 GMT

The boss in the dugout is typically no longer an ageing former player – most are in their 40s on an exhausting treadmill

One of the problems with getting older is that you’re never quite sure whether it’s you or them. Is the world really changing, or is it just you, struggling to adapt? There’s a milestone in life, probably as you’re contemplating university or a first job, when you realise you’re watching a footballer who is younger than you. Then, 15-20 years later, you realise you’re watching a manager who is younger than you. And 15-20 years after that, especially if you’re watching the modern Premier League, you realise that almost every manager is younger than you.

At which you do two things: give thanks for David Moyes; and check to see whether it’s actually happening, or whether this is just the football equivalent of the policemen-getting-younger cliche.

It turns out it is true. Managers used to be ashen-faced men with nicotine-grey hair dressed in the sports jackets of grim experience. They spoke with a rasping melancholy of the depths of human fallibility and of fates that were not to be trusted. Now they’re trim, sprightly figures in T-shirts, convinced that analytics can explain the world.

There are fewer Premier League managers now aged 50 or over than at any point in the past 20 years: only four, and two of those have only just made it over the threshold. Moyes is 63 (three months younger than José Mourinho, which, like Aberdeen being further west than Bristol, is a fact both true and too counterintuitive to be worth believing). Then there is Unai Emery at 54, Oliver Glasner at 52 and Régis Le Bris at 50. Most Premier League managers are in their 40s, with the youngest two Matthias Jaissle, 38, and Fabian Hürzeler, 33.

This is not coincidence; rather it seems the result of two interconnected trends. Even at the turn of the century, when Mourinho was starting out, it was unusual for a manager not to have played the game to at least a reasonable level, which meant they were starting their managerial careers in their mid-thirties. That’s still the route many take – Andoni Iraola, Michael Carrick, Gary O’Neil or Álvaro Arbeloa, for instance.

But there’s also a recognition, to use Arrigo Sacchi’s phrase, that a jockey does not need first to have been a horse. Coaching is regarded as a job in its own right, requiring a very different skillset to playing. Hürzeler came through the youth systems at Bayern Munich, Hoffenheim and 1860 Munich but, aged 22, in part because of an ankle injury, decided to focus on coaching.

Jaissle was a member of the Hoffenheim side that soared through the divisions to win promotion to the Bundesliga before knee and achilles tendon injuries ended his playing career at 26. The early switch into coaching seems particularly common in Germany: Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann have similar stories.

That greater receptiveness to career coaches explains the wave of younger managers. But there are also fewer older coaches.

In part it may be coincidence: an experienced generation – Sam Allardyce, Tony Pulis and Alan Pardew – grew old together. That the process occurred just as many of their tactical characteristics – low blocks, direct play, a focus on set pieces – re-entered the mainstream may not simply be irony. The old must be cast out before it is reinvented as new; the modish cannot be represented by a 60-something football man.

But it’s also because modern management is exhausting. At Ipswich, Kieran McKenna would have his coaches present their plans to him for the day at 6am, altering anything he felt wasn’t quite right. That plan would be sent to the staff at the training ground to set up all the various pitches and drills. McKenna would then go to check everything was laid out properly. It was all extraordinarily detailed; everything was marked out, down to where players should stand when they weren’t directly involved and where water bottles would be placed.

During sessions, McKenna would walk between each unit, stepping in to offer advice and make amendments. After sessions, coaches would watch them back and report to McKenna on what could be improved before planning the next day’s drills to be presented at 6am the following morning.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

During 11 v 11 practice games, McKenna would be the only one who coached. Over his five years at Ipswich, no drill was ever repeated in exactly the same form; repetition and possible staleness were to be avoided at all costs. Little wonder that after a third promotion in five seasons at the club, he felt exhausted, in need of a break rather than taking on an uneven fight in an ungrateful Premier League that could only sap his reserves further.

Brian Clough would take holidays during the season. He would turn up only infrequently at training. His input was sharp, erratic, impressionistic. Four decades on, a top-level manager is running a team of coaches and analysts that probably outnumbers the players with whom he has direct contact.

He cannot simply ignore the board until he needs money for a signing but has to manage up to whatever structure of sporting directors exists above him. He often will have little autonomy, although the success of Mikel Arteta, who has a more traditional role and seems to micromanage everything at Arsenal, may change that. And he is liable to be sacked after a month of poor form. The pressure is enormous, the margin for error minute.

That perhaps explains why so many top managers are now drifting into international football. Management, it’s commonly said, is a drug, but perhaps that fix is more palatable when it is delivered in five doses spread over a season, plus a major tournament every other year, rather than in the relentless drudgery of the club game. Carlo Ancelotti took his break from the club game at 66, Jürgen Klopp at 56, Tuchel at 50. None have demonstrated any great desire to return to the remorselessness of the league.

The Premier League may be the greatest stage in management. It may be where the best salaries are paid. It may be where every manager wishes to test himself. But it is an exhausting and capricious world that requires extraordinary reserves of energy, physical and mental. It is no theatre for old men.

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 18:32:55 GMT

If ever you wanted to understand the distinction between “winning the transfer market” and winning an actual football match, then this was the game for you. Tottenham’s first home fixture of the Premier League season began with adulatory focus on all their new players. It ended in decisive defeat by Newcastle as recruit after recruit failed to make their presence pay, while Newcastle’s forgotten forwards made hay. “Tottenham Hotspur, it’s happened again,” sang the Toon Army as if it needed pointing out.

Tottenham should have taken the lead in a first half they had the better of, but they had no response to impressive second-half strikes by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa. What had looked like green shoots of positivity withered to nothing. For a Newcastle team themselves a work in progress under Matthias Jaissle, this was a heartening victory achieved with many of their own additions to come in.

Rarely can there have been a club so desperate to show their fans that they have flashed the cash as Spurs this summer. Vinai Venkatesham, the Tottenham chief executive, wrote a two-page letter in the programme that led on the spending and proclaimed: “We have attracted the names we wanted to attract.” Before kick-off there was a brief ceremony to welcome all eight signings to the club. “We spent and we spent, and we’ve got lots of top players,” sang the club announcer.

Time will tell on the latter point, but there was no arguing over the former. The £92.5m purchase Sandro Tonali started in midfield and was booed on his every touch by the Newcastle fans in a performance that only spluttered. The Italian was not the only player finding his feet, with four other summer recruits in Roberto De Zerbi’s XI and £60m Omar Marmoush starting 24 hours after signing for the club. For Jaissle’s Newcastle, there was a debut for Nico González, signed this week for £50m from Manchester City, and another showing for new goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek and right-back Amar Dedic.

Newcastle started the brighter, with Wissa full of energy at the tip of the visitors’ attack. Spurs were sloppy and looked porous, but they did not give up a true opportunity and – as the half wore on – they took control of proceedings. On the left-hand side Mathys Tel began to combine with Andy Robertson. The midfield three of Tonali, £85m Mateus Fernandes and Rodrigo Bentancur began to interchange positions. Even the wildcard selection of Pedro Porro at right wing showed flashes of success with the Spaniard seeing his close-range shot well blocked in the 17th minute. Spurs had decent chances for both Tel and Jan Paul van Hecke too, but Hornicek did well to save both efforts.

Jaissle asked his team to be more assertive in the second half, to be fully committed in the press with the confidence that they would succeed. His analysis turned out to be correct and the resulting shift in the dynamic of the match is likely to have been a familiar experience for Spurs supporters. Whatever energy had been visible in the home team, whatever nascent understanding between players, fell away after the break. Newcastle were more compact but also more aggressive and began to see more of the ball. Just after the hour they took the lead from a move beautiful in its simplicity.

It began with Gonzalez, 10 yards outside his box, hitting a 60-yard switched pass left to right and to the corner of the Tottenham area. There it was met by Dedic, who had run beyond his winger to head the ball down into the path of Elanga. The Sweden international, whose future at the club has been under scrutiny but who has begun the season in sterling form, took a touch to steady himself, span on the ball and drove a left-foot shot inside the far post for his second goal in two matches.

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 17:28:29 GMT

Second Test: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand

Head coach changes front-row just before start

The Boks are back. Level at one apiece in the series after a return to what they do best. Blending power and directness, blood and thunder, to edge far enough ahead of New Zealand and withstand a gutsy comeback from the All Blacks. Throw in some brazen mischief from Rassie Erasmus, who swapped his entire front-row just an hour before kick-off, and this was much closer to a trademark Springboks performance after they were unrecognisable a week ago.

South Africa were far from flawless but constantly ferocious. It was not a knockout blow – not least given how the All Blacks finished the match – but it was some counterpunch after last week’s humbling. The third Test is scheduled for Johannesburg but they may consider relocating to Manila.

Erasmus had been up to his usual games all week. Naming his team on Monday, swapping his fly-halves 24 hours before kick-off by recalling Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and then coming up with his front-row switcheroo, starting with Gerhard Steenekamp, Deon Fourie and Thomas du Toit and relegating Ox Nché, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw to the bench. Nché and Marx were introduced on 36 minutes and promptly won two penalties to set up Siya Kolisi for a crucial try and stretch their half-time lead to 10 points. Marx was inspired thereafter while Cheslin Kolbe, who was drafted into the side on Friday, kicked 18 points.

Whether Erasmus should have been allowed to switch his front row so soon before kick-off ultimately depends on the fine print of the tour agreement between the two unions. That he would not have been able to without medically justifying the decisions in the World Cup demonstrates how close to the wind the head coach is sailing.

What is not up for debate is just what a savage intensity this Test was played at. The All Blacks were braced for a Bok-lash but could do little to stop South Africa’s opening score inside two minutes. Jordie Barrett did not get enough distance on his clearance after New Zealand received the kick-off and from the resulting lineout, the Springboks’ maul went into overdrive. Jessie Kriel was soon over. Statement of intent made.

For all that South Africa were fired up, the All Blacks were not to be cowed. They demonstrated last week how slick they can be showcasing their ability to use the rapier in response to the bludgeon. After a series of wonderfully dextrous passes, Will Jordan found himself in space on the right, releasing Cam Roigard inside him.

The most significant difference in South Africa’s performance was how direct they were and Kolbe nosed South Africa back ahead with a penalty before the Springboks struck again with another maul leading to Damian de Allende’s close-range score. Again New Zealand responded with a devastating score – Ardie Savea busting up the guts before Damian McKenzie was sent clear to the right-hand corner on the angle. It was another demonstration of how lethal the All Blacks can be.

Just as was the case at Ellis Park, the Springboks came on strong towards the end of the first half and some nifty footballing skills from Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Kolbe forced a scrum five metres out. Cue the introduction of Nché and Marx and Kolisi’s try on his comeback to the side. Marx then proceeded to make a thunderous tackle on Luke Jacobson, with the All Blacks threatening on the left, to bring an end to a pulsating half.

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 17:08:43 GMT

Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency

Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order.

Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE.

A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.

The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.

The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West.

West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper.

Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News, previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status.

At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency.

He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13.

Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart.

Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk.

A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.

He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency.

The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.

The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead the Conservatives to Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”

He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success in London,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”

Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.

According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.

Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.

Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028. Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.

If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.

Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.

‘It’s no surprise’: the manosphere mogul convicted of attacking pregnant girlfriend

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 16:00:31 GMT

Podcaster James English is one of many men with far-right ties to have been found guilty or accused of domestic violence

In many ways, the case heard this week at Glasgow sheriff court was, unfortunately, not out of the ordinary. It was one of thousands of domestic violence trials to have passed through the Scottish courts since new legislation was introduced in 2019 to clamp down on a grimly persistent problem.

A woman had testified that her former partner had waged a campaign of terror against her, and that she suffered abuse while she was pregnant with his child. The court heard that her partner had grabbed her by the throat, pinned her to a door, kicked her off a bed and sent her abusive texts, sometimes calling her a “fat slag” and a “little bitch”.

What caught the eye of onlookers, however, was the identity of the man convicted.

James English may not be a household name, but in the online world he is a star, a podcaster with millions of followers across several social media platforms for his interview show, Anything Goes.

English has won plaudits for securing high profile guests, such as the footballer Paul Gascoigne and Rebecca Loos, who allegedly had an affair with David Beckham.

However, he has also attracted controversy for his ties to figures from the far right, particularly the English Defence League founder Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, more commonly known as Tommy Robinson. Last September, English appeared at Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally, describing the event as “legendary” and praising Robinson for organising it.

During the course of his podcasting, English has also platformed personalities from what has become known as the manosphere.

Other guests on English’s podcast have included men accused of serious sexual offences, such as Andrew Tate, the internet personality recently charged with rape and sex trafficking, and the footballer David Goodwillie.

Goodwillie and his former teammate, David Robertson, were ordered to pay £100,000 in damages to Denise Clair after a judge in a civil case ruled they had raped her after a night out in 2011.

English, a 42-year-old father of three from Larkhall, Lanarkshire, reinvented himself as an independent journalist after appearing on Glow, a failed reality television show billed as a Glaswegian Towie.

Although he says he does not necessarily share the views of his guests, he has given a range of far-right activists a sympathetic platform. As well as hosting Robinson several times, he has interviewed the commentator Katie Hopkins and the Raise the Colours founder Ryan Bridge.

The Unite the Kingdom march was “beautiful” and “very patriotic”, English said. “The people that have been on stage speaking, Katie Hopkins, Tommy Robinson, it’s been unbelievable,” he said, on a clip posted on Robinson’s X account. “It’s been great to see so many people getting behind each other and uniting for a better future.”

English is one of many men with ties to the far right who have found themselves accused of intimate partner violence.

Project Starlight, a 2021 study commissioned by Counter Terrorism Policing, found that about a third of people referred to the government’s Prevent programme had links to a domestic abuse incident, either as an offender, victim, witness or a combination of all three. In 18% of these cases, extreme rightwing ideology was present.

Deniz Ugur, the deputy director of the End Violence Against Women Coalition, said police data had “consistently shown that a significant proportion of men arrested during far-right riots are already known to the police for domestic abuse”.

The Guardian previously revealed that 41% of those arrested in the 2024 riots, prompted by the murders of three young girls in Southport, had been reported to the police for alleged domestic abuse. After the riots, 21% were accused of similar offences.

English had already been charged with abusing the woman, a model he met on Instagram, by the time he travelled to London for the Unite the Kingdom protest. One of its central themes was the threat supposedly posed by migrant men to British women and girls. “It’s all about saving the children,” English said.

Some speakers promoted conspiracies about migration, including the “great replacement theory – the suggestion that there is a plot to replace white Europeans with people from other races. While English described the march as “peaceful”, the Metropolitan police said its officers faced “unacceptable violence” from some demonstrators, more than 20 of whom were arrested.

This week, Sheriff David Hall, who heard English’s case without a jury, convicted him of engaging in a course of abusive conduct towards his former partner between July 2022 and November 2023. The single charge included 19 allegations, six of which Hall judged to have been proved. He described the woman as “credible and reliable”.

Alice Russell Harris, public affairs lead at the domestic abuse charity Refuge, said: “The manosphere, which significantly overlaps with far-right communities, has helped amplify misogynistic narratives that objectify and seek to control women, casting women as subordinate to men and suggesting that those who reject male expectations deserve punishment. These ideas can directly promote abuse – both online and offline – by encouraging men to engage in coercion, control and related harms.”

English, who will be sentenced next month, was not in court to hear Hall’s verdict on Tuesday. However, the next day, he used his social media platforms to issue a rallying cry to his followers, sharing misinformation about the legal basis for his conviction.

“Men need to be worried, especially in Scotland,” he said. “Ladies, if you have a brother or a son, you should also be worried, because women can say anything and it’s a man’s job to prove his innocence.” He added that, in Scotland, “accusations are enough to get the man charged”.

In fact, Scottish law is underpinned by the principle of corroboration, where two independent sources of evidence are required to prove a criminal accusation. Defendants are innocent until proved guilty and the testimony of a single witness – no matter how compelling – is not enough to secure a conviction.

Neither English nor any of the nine people he claimed could support his version of events took the stand. English said this was because he was “so confident” he would be cleared. “I should never have been charged, never mind convicted,” he said.

Ugur said: “It is no surprise to see a convicted perpetrator of domestic abuse and prominent figure in the far right promote deeply harmful misinformation about violence against women and girls.

“Most victims do not report to the police, and those who do, know how many hurdles there are to seeing a conviction due to institutional cultures of victim blaming and failures to treat violence against women and girls with the seriousness it warrants.”

Despite the headlines his case has generated, English has remained defiant, criticising the mainstream media for covering it. “People need to be wary, because if they want you, they’ll find something to get you on,” he said, adding that he was “tired of men getting fucked over”.

He did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian, but vowed on his social media channels to continue broadcasting. “I’m still going to keep doing what I’m doing,” he said. “If anything, it’s just fuelled me to keep raising the bar.”

A year after his conviction for child sex crimes, Ferguson thanked Epstein for being the “brother” she had “always wished for” in an email.

Last September, the Mail on Sunday published emails from 2011, in which Ferguson privately described Epstein as her “supreme friend” and apologised for “letting him down”, despite having publicly called her association with him “a gigantic error of judgment”.

The messages were sent less than two months after she had insisted she would “never have anything to do with [Epstein] again”, amid pressure over the ties she and Mountbatten-Windsor had maintained with him – including a £15,000 payment Epstein made to help settle Ferguson’s debts.

Epstein has been the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of “serious lapses of judgment” over his friendship with the late child sex offender and allegations of sexual assault against him by one of Epstein’s victims, Virginia Giuffre.

‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 14:11:10 GMT

Family members pin photos of Nepal’s missing to hospital wall as people try not to give up hope on loved ones

Nepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updates

Posters of missing people line the wall of the hospital, the glue still fresh beneath. A schoolgirl smiling in her uniform; a beaming, chubby-cheeked baby; a couple smiling on their wedding day; a young man, hands on hips, atop a mountain peak; a young girl with flowing hair, peaking out from behind a door.

These faces are just a fraction of the thousands who have not been seen since deadly flash floods coursed through the Himalayas and wiped away entire villages. By Saturday morning, the toll of the missing had risen to almost 3,000, in both Nepal and Tibet.

So far, Nepal has recovered 669 bodies, but many remote areas have only been accessed by army helicopters on the hunt for survivors. Rescuers said it was too difficult to assess how many more people might be buried beneath the mud.

The task of identifying the dead is also gargantuan.

In the Nepali city of Chitwan, the morgues have been overrun by the sheer number of bodies and a makeshift building has been set up to house the dead.

Some of the bodies were carried so far down the river by the force of the floods, they were recovered in neighbouring India.

At Tribhuvan University teaching hospital in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, desperate relatives gathered in the hope of news. Four days on since the disaster struck, people continued to crowd round the police desk to register the names of missing family members. Hundreds of the injured are recovering in the hospital’s wards and people were frantically checking lists of patients, desperate to find a sign that their loved ones were still alive.

In the absence of information and with affected areas almost completely cut off, many families have resorted to making posters to appeal for information. Yavraj Lama said his sister, her husband and their two children were missing after their village of Jaydada, in Rusawa district, had been entirely washed away.

His eyes filled with tears as he glued a photo of one-year-old Sijan Tawang, a baby in the arms of his mother, to the hospital wall. A picture of 12-year-old Sahil, his brother, hung next to it.

“We are numb, we don’t have words to say how sad and distraught we are,” said Lama. “Our main focus is trying to find baby Sijan. He was so sweet and innocent; it’s impossible for us to think he is not with us any more.

“But their whole village has disappeared,” he added, “so we have no hope left that any of them survived.”

Monita Nepali, 22, howled in grief as a poster of her missing husband, Vishal Nepali, 30, was pinned to the hospital wall. They had married six months ago and his work as a driver regularly took him to the border between Nepal and Tibet. She had spoken to her husband an hour before the floods hit when he was out for a morning walk in Rusawa. He had promised to call her that evening, but his phone has been ever off since.

“I don’t want to live on the face of this earth without him,” she said. Four days may have passed, Nepali said, but she had not stopped believing in her husband’s return. “I feel it in my heart he will come back.”

For some families, the scale of the loss was too hard to comprehend. Tulmaya Tamang, 36, came to the hospital bearing posters of some of her 12 family members, including her five-month-old niece, who lived in a village in Rusawa and have not been seen since the floods.

“Our family is under tremendous stress,” she said. “So many are gone, and those of us who are left behind are struggling.”

As hopes for their survival faded, Tamang said they were now just hoping the bodies could be retrieved. “If we had the bodies, then at least we could have peace,” she said. “Otherwise, the family will never stop wondering and this pain will go on for a very long time.”

At least 900 of those still missing were working on the vast hydropower projects along the Trishuli River corridor, high up in the Himalayas, which were decimated by the floods and mudslides. Many of the workers were low-paid labourers, including at least 63 from India.

On Friday, dramatic footage showed Nepali soldiers pulling several survivors out through a thick wall of mud from a tunnel in the Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The Nepali army said they believed at least another 100 people were still trapped inside the tunnels, as well as dozens more stuck underground in the Trishuli-3 hydropower plant.

Among those missing was 24-year-old Sujan Nepali, who had just finished his night shift at the hydropower project and was asleep in bed when the wall of water came gushing down the valley. At the hospital trauma centre in Nepal, his sister, Sushisha Maluwar, had returned anxiously every day to check if his name was listed.

“We haven’t lost hope,” she said. “We are writing down his name at the hospitals and putting up his photographs everywhere, hoping that we might find him somewhere. Maybe he has already been rescued. Maybe he had managed to escape and survive.”

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 12:00:28 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Too cloying, too sweet or just right? Our tester works through the shop shelves to find the best slaw for your next barbecue, picnic or packed lunch

The best supermarket veggie burgers

I find shop-bought coleslaw hard to stomach because it’s sharp, gloopy and often made with copious amounts of poor-quality mayonnaise and spirit vinegar. Pungent ingredients, such as cabbage and onion, are better eaten fresh, otherwise they break down and give off a disconcertingly sulphurous and sweaty aroma.

I judged each product in this test on appearance, aroma, texture and, above all, taste, and awarded extra points for value. I marked down for an off-puttingly strong raw onion aroma.

Preservatives and stabilisers aren’t essential (the better-tasting products don’t use them), and often give a slaw an unappealing, moussey texture. All that said, I was surprised to find some great products out there and most retained a surprisingly satisfying crunch.

★★★★☆

A lovely, crunchy, finely shredded slaw with a creamy sauce and with no stabilisers or gums. Red onion and chives are present, but not dominant. The mayo includes a little whipping cream, free-range egg yolk and UK dairy.

★★★☆☆

A creamy, chunky coleslaw that’s unctuous and moreish. Fresh, crunchy and well balanced with sweetness and acidity, this is cabbage-forward, with a little carrot and a subtle onion flavour, and a relatively straightforward mayo made with guar and xanthan gums.

★★★☆☆

A veg-heavy, fine-cut cabbage and carrot slaw with a subtle onion twang and a refreshing sauce. A little tart, but arguably that’s what one wants from a slaw. Free-range egg, too. Flavoured with mustard, but also includes a preservative (potassium sorbate) and stabiliser (xanthan gum).

★★★☆☆

A medium-thick, crunchy coleslaw in a rich, free-range egg mayo. Sweet with some mild acidity and a subtle onion flavour. One of the simpler recipes (carrot, cabbage, onion, mayo), but it does contain xanthan gum.

★★★☆☆

A thinly shredded slaw that’s simple, creamy and crunchy, and has a nice balance of sweetness and acidity. Onion present, but not overpowering. No cream, but the thick mayo is thickened with citrus fibre, guar gum, xanthan gum and pectin.

A rich, saucy, medium-thin slaw that’s sweet and crunchy but has a dominant onion and chive flavour. The mayo, made with xanthan gum and citrus fibre, is slightly moussey, though.

★★☆☆☆

Finely shredded crunchy carrots, lots of sweet sauce made creamy by the addition of creme fraiche, and a sharp finish. Contains acetic acid, stabilisers (guar gum, xanthan gum) and a preservative (potassium sorbate).

★★☆☆☆

A finely shredded slaw with heaps of flavour, a warm dijon undertone, nice acidity from white-wine vinegar and great crunch. Colourful, with pink cabbage, carrot, red onion and chives, and a relatively strong onion flavour, but a slightly overcomplicated ingredients list, including potassium sorbate, maize starch and xanthan and guar gums.

★★☆☆☆

A ribbon-cut, saucy coleslaw made with a splash of single cream. Subtle acidity from lemon juice, but a complex recipe including stabilisers (guar gum and xanthan gum), potato starch and citrus fibre.

‘I’ve £80k in the account, here’s my pin’: turning the tables on the scammers

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 12:00:27 GMT

Plagued by bank impersonation scams, one Guardian Money reader got even by stringing the fraudsters along … for hours

“A couple of Sundays ago at just past 11am my mobile rang. An automated message purported to be from Barclays Bank, querying a payment to Argos for more than £1,000. Not only had I not made a payment to Argos recently, nor do I bank with Barclays.

I am plagued with these kinds of calls. Usually, when possible, I make it clear to the scammers that I know their game. Usually, that call ends there and then.

But this time I realised there was a chance to string them along. It was just a question of how soon they realised I was bluffing. I assumed it would be a couple of minutes. In fact it was three hours.

I called the number shown on my phone and, pretending to be a confused, doddery old man – not that difficult for me – I expressed the expected alarm at the bogus payment.

The man who answered, who had more or less a received pronunciation accent, went through what I understand is the usual story: my credit card had been compromised, bankruptcy was on the horizon, remedial action essential. Someone from the investigations team would call me back, he said. Thirty minutes later someone calling himself “Adam” rang. From here on in the number always came up as “No caller ID”.

Several times Adam ended the call, presumably to consult his fellow crooks, and rang back later.

First, Adam went through several security-like questions. When did I last use my credit card? “Can’t remember,” I replied. What was the last transaction I made? “Dunno.” Did I use internet banking? “No”. Then came the big one: how much is in your current account? “Around £80,000,” I said. (If only.)

There wasn’t a sharp intake of breath. I couldn’t hear a licking of lips. But I could sense that Adam’s vocal cords had tightened, and he was from now on more intense.

He explained it was a matter of the utmost urgency my credit card should be cancelled and a new one issued. Would I like to keep the same pin, he asked? I said “yes” and he asked for it. I’d already written down a made-up pin on a bit of paper, and gave it to him. I thought I could sense him trying hard to remain matter of fact.

He asked if I had my debit card and credit card with me. I said I couldn’t find my credit card. Adam was stern, insisting I look for it. I couldn’t be bothered to fabricate two false 16-digit numbers, and so I told him my wife must have it and she was out. He let this go.

I had already taken out one of my debit cards from my wallet, one issued by HSBC, jotted down the first eight digits and made up eight more. To my surprise, and some alarm, Adam read out the first six digits, correctly, saying the card was issued by HSBC. (How did he know I had an HSBC account?)

He didn’t bother to explain why he needed the debit card, too – or why he needed the numbers – and, being in character I didn’t ask, just went meekly along. I guess the implication was that both cards were compromised and so the investigations team needed to cancel that one as well.

I gave him the made-up number, thinking this would be the end of it. But within a minute he came back and said the number I’d given didn’t seem to be a genuine one.

I assumed concerned bafflement and told him that all I could say was that I was reading out the number on the card in front of me. There was another pause, presumably while he consulted one of his scammer colleagues. To my surprise they decided to keep going.

As this was Sunday, as Adam pointed out, the banks were closed. So the only safe procedure was to send round a courier to pick up my debit card – right now. It couldn’t wait until tomorrow. Was that OK with me? I told him it was fine.

He said I should put the card in an envelope and address it: HSBC Investigations Team, what he thought was my name, Ref HS844677.

He was most insistent on two things: he repeated several times that the courier must, on no account whatsoever, be able to see that a bank card was in the envelope, and that I must seal it extremely carefully.

He insisted three times that I read the address back to him. I pretended to be getting a bit fed up with all this but he explained, quite firmly, that banking security was at stake here and there was no room for error.

A new thought then occurred to him. Did I have a current bank statement, and could I find the most recent one? I noisily opened and shut a drawer. He asked for the balance. I had already written down a precise made-up amount. I told him £81,224.93.

Adam told me he’d ring back when he had booked the courier and got an ETA. He’d already asked me for my postcode and I’d given him one where I lived several years ago. Now he asked for my exact address and I gave him a house number that I knew was too high to exist in that street.

Fifteen minutes later he rang back, sounding a little flustered. A blue Prius was outside the address I’d given but it seemed to be a block of flats. “That’s not right,” I said, “I live in a house.” Another hiatus, as he communicated with the courier. Could I see a blue Prius? he asked. I paused long enough to have looked out of an imaginary window and said “No, I can’t see a blue car”.

What can you see outside your house? he asked. “Nothing,” I said. He rang off again.

Five minutes later he called back. Would I mind going out and trying to find the blue Prius? I explained that I had a bad leg and couldn’t leave my house at all. But I would gladly open the front door and have a look. Then another call. The driver was absolutely adamant that the address was in a block of flats.

I’d kept this charade up for a lot longer than I’d expected and I was about to go out. “Oh dear,” I said in my best whispery voice, “it looks like I’ve been wasting your time.”

What? I switched into my own voice to deliver the – unprintable – coup de grace, and hang up.

Adam even had the cheek to ring back later. I didn’t answer. I wish I had. I could have thanked him for the afternoon’s entertainment.
