Switching channels: will the Edinburgh TV festival’s magic survive the move south?

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 12:00:27 GMT

After 50 years the annual shindig is heading to Manchester – but a new rival could keep the industry’s fringe link going

The summer sojourn to Edinburgh has been a highlight of TV executives’ calendars for half a century, allowing them an annual trip to the UK’s most spectacular city during the world’s biggest arts festival.

So there was sadness when it was announced that this year’s 50th Edinburgh TV Festival would be the last to be held in the Scottish capital.

High costs fuelling concerns about accessibility – accommodation in the city in August is the most expensive in Europe – prompted the TV Foundation, the charity which runs the annual industry shindig, to consider a new venue last year.

Campbell Glennie, its chief executive, said the move was about “exploring how we can reduce costs for delegates and make the festival open to more people”.

However, critics of the decision pointed out that while holding the conference alongside the Edinburgh fringe and international festivals made it so expensive, the chance to see world-class theatre, arts and comedy was a huge part of the draw for attenders.

Off the record, some TV figures blamed the Scottish government for the failed attempt to keep the event in Scotland. Glasgow had initially been on the table, requiring only a 40-minute train ride west, but Holyrood ministers threw their weight behind a campaign to keep it in Edinburgh.

It was ultimately Manchester that had the winning proposition, backed by Andy Burnham, then the Greater Manchester mayor, who promised the necessary “infrastructure, talent, ambition and creativity” to host the festival from next year.

At Edinburgh’s valedictory gathering, many delegates did not hide their disappointment.

One Scottish television producer said the decision reflected a problem in the industry, where production companies south of the border have brought London-based workers to film in Scotland and failed to hire local talent. “It’s a fucking joke,” they added.

The TV Foundation said relocating would “radically reduce the costs” for attendees. The charity makes no profit from running the festival and instead invests the funds into programmes to improve training and widen access, with several sessions this year aimed at tackling the class gap in the industry.

Sydney Lima is a documentary presenter and co-founder of the Rich Parents Club, a group providing support to working-class people in arts and media. She said members were reporting that TV was becoming “an increasingly gatekept industry”, suggesting that recent hits from working-class writers such as the Channel 4 series Big Boys would no longer be commissioned.

“As funding cuts continue, employers rely on smaller pools of talent, more often than not, from within their own networks – or even gene pool,” she said.

In 2024 the scriptwriter James Graham used the festival’s keynote MacTaggart lecture – past speakers have included Armando Iannucci, Dennis Potter and Rupert Murdoch – to lament how impenetrable the industry was for working-class people.

A subsequent TV Foundation report found nearly a quarter of TV executives were privately educated. Graham’s views were echoed by the presenter Carol Vorderman, who grew up working class, in the alternative MacTaggart slot the same year. (That lecture was delivered by Amol Rajan this year).

The move also comes at a time of enormous financial pressure on the industry, with the BBC shedding up to 2,000 staff, ITV and Sky merging broadcast operations and Channel 4 under pressure.

Traditional UK broadcasters are struggling to compete for audiences and advertising money against the rise of deep-pocketed US-based streaming titans, such as Netflix and Amazon.

In a sign of the times, this year’s main MacTaggart lecture was delivered by YouTube’s Pedro Pina, who hit back at proposals to make public service content more prominent on his platform, now the second most-watched media service in the UK.

As British commissioners cut their TV production budgets, freelancers are bearing the brunt, making it harder to find funds for networking events like the TV festival.

A full-price ticket cost more than £1,500, though there were bursaries and lower rates for freelancers, Scottish delegates and those under 30. Among this year’s attendees were graduates and freelancers, some of whom had bitten the bullet and forked out in the hope of making connections that would lead to work.

Adeel Amini, a freelance executive producer who founded the campaign group The TV Mindset to support casual workers in the sector, said: “The price of the ticket is already ridiculous and unaffordable, especially when the industry has been going through a crisis and so many people are out of work.”

Amini, who has produced entertainment shows such as Who Wants to Be a Millionaire, Lingo and Catchphrase, praised the TV Foundation’s work but said the conference itself highlighted how “two-tier the industry is”, with a divide between those who pay their own way and executives whose companies pick up the tab.

Amini added: “It’s there for commissioners and production companies to go and mingle and have these parties and either lament the state of the industry without doing anything much about it or just give themselves a round of applause without acknowledging the workers at the heart of it.”

Daran “Jonno” Johnson, the head writer on this year’s surprise hit SNL UK, spoke on a TV festival panel on Friday morning as part of its new Funny Business strand, focusing on comedy. It was in between performances of his successful nightly Edinburgh fringe standup run.

He said the benefit of the two festivals being in the same city was that “so many industry people are suddenly in town in the last week” that it was helpful “to have that pipeline between fringe comedy and telly”.

Performers were nervous that their shows – many of which cost tens, if not hundreds, of thousands of pounds to put on – might no longer have the same chance of being seen by commissioners. Kimberly Hart-Simpson, a Manchester-based writer and actor whose one-woman play Amnesia won a Scotsman Fringe First award this year, said her concern was “whether TV industry professionals will continue to commit to attending the arts festival to discover and support emerging talent”.

However, the fringe was so integral to many TV executives’ diaries that they would still be here if the schedules clashed, reassured Alex Cartlidge, co-director of Country Mile Productions at an event at the fringe venue Shedinburgh.

“The reason you’re coming to Edinburgh, if you’re a TV producer, is for the fringe. The TV festival happens to be on, and you can convince your boss to put a few of those things through company expenses … but if TV companies have the choice next year between going to Manchester or coming here, 99% of people will come here.”

There is hope on the horizon for those who do not want to see the link between the fringe and television severed. On Thursday evening, television executives, performers and fringe organisers gathered in a hot room at Edinburgh Fringe Central for the launch of an initiative for the media and creative industries from 2027, funded in part by the Scottish government.

Speaking to the Guardian at the launch, David Smith, director of Screen Scotland, which is partnering with the Fringe Society on the project, said it was not a replacement for the TV Festival. “It will be inclusive of TV, but it won’t be a TV festival,” he said.

Having two events risks splitting attendance, but with dates for Manchester yet to be announced there is still the prospect the gatherings could avoid a clash if the TV Foundation does not go for the traditional last week of August slot.

The Scottish culture secretary, Màiri McAllan, said that while it was “hugely disappointing that a London-based company took the decision to move the Edinburgh International TV festival”, the SNP government was now focused on Screen Scotland’s alternative and was “working with the TV, media, and festivals sectors to ensure that we deliver an unmissable event”.

Smith said plans were still being formed on what that event would look like but added: “I hope to get back to some of the chaos of the original TV Festival, the fact that it was slightly more seat-of-your-pants.”

The rebranding of ‘Lake America’ is Trump’s desperate attempt to distract us

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 12:00:26 GMT

Ignore Iran, the Epstein files, and your wallet – not to mention Trump’s plummeting approval ratings

Don’t mention the war! Or the economy, for that matter. Or the Epstein files. Or Natalie Harp. Or “affordability”, which, as Donald Trump recently said at a rally, is a word that was “never used” by the media before he took office. Best not to talk about anything that affects ordinary people or embarrasses the president, really. Instead, let’s all rejoice in Trump’s latest triumph: renaming Lake Ontario, which is shared by Canada and the US, as Lake America.

On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to America-fy the lake’s name on US maps and documents, which is an excellent use of time and resources. I suppose we can at least be thankful that the president, who is trying to slap his own name on everything from airports to the Kennedy Center, didn’t decree that the body of water be called Lake Trump.

This is not an isolated embarrassment: the Lake Ontario name change follows the president’s rebranding of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America last year. “We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” Trump told reporters.

Give it a few more months of the disastrous war in Iran and a bruised Trump may well make good on that threat: the man will do anything to distract from his failings.

As well as being a distraction, this pathetic maneuver is supposed to be a middle finger to Canada. Trade negotiations between the US and Canada recently collapsed, with the Trump administration imposing a 50% tariff on some goods and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, promising a “dollar for dollar” response. One suspects that Trump thinks Lake Ontario is named after the Canadian province it borders. Ergo he reckons a unilateral name change is a good way of showing the US’s northern neighbour who is boss.

However, as Carney was forced to point out on social media, the name Lake Ontario has been used for more than 400 years and comes from the Indigenous Wendat/Huron word Ontari’io, meaning: “The lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” It predates both the Confederation of Canada and the US Declaration of Independence.

A US president ordering the name change of a Great Lake in order to antagonize one of its closest allies would have been headline news for weeks in a normal timeline. Now it’s just another Thursday. Still, this is more than a silly stunt that both Canada and the governor of New York have made clear they are going to ignore. It’s a glaring demonstration of just how desperate, isolated and out of ideas Trump is. His approval ratings have hit a new low, sliding 14 points from 47% at the start of his second term to 33% now amid rising costs. The Iran war, which was sold as a “little excursion” that would only last a few weeks has hit the six-month mark, and there isn’t a decent off-ramp in sight. And Canada isn’t the only former ally angry with Trump’s US; the country’s reputation has plummeted globally. A 36-country survey conducted by Pew earlier this year found overall ratings for the US are largely negative; only seven countries rate the US positively, with Israel at the top of the list. Trump is weak and floundering: because he lacks the intellectual and diplomatic ability to reshape reality to his liking, he’s trying to rebrand it instead. But it doesn’t matter how many executive orders he signs; people will be calling Lake Ontario by its original name long after we can all stop calling Trump “president”.

Brevard county’s 2025 deputy of the year has now resigned from the sheriff’s office after an investigation found numerous examples of “egregious misconduct”, including images of him putting a gun in his ex-girlfriend’s mouth and a claim he used the Flock license plate readers to look up his ex-girlfriend. He also appeared to have posted a photo of himself sporting a Hitler-like moustache while performing a Nazi salute. This is not a one-off: there are numerous allegations involving law enforcement officers using Flock to stalk people. The self-styled misogynist Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan were arrested in the US in July as part of a UK police investigation into alleged sexual offences. Part of their lawyers’ strategy to fight extradition seems to be to paint them as posers who just pretended to be “uberwealthy” online in order to generate attention. “[T]he $2.1m Aston Martin and $5m and $7m Bugattis featured in Tristan’s videos were rented,” one legal submission notes. “The valuation of Andrew’s watch collection is based on a third-party enthusiast publication.”

A study tracked 183,450 postmenopausal women in the UK and found that those who had used hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for at least a year were 10% less likely to develop any form of dementia.

This is more than 10 months into a “ceasefire”. Still, that kill count is not enough for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party and the minister of national security. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night,” Ben-Gvir recently said on a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. Hittner ruled on the basis that the law was so vague that it was unconstitutional. As the New York Times noted in a piece last year: “Vagueness has become fundamental to the way Trump operates. It is not so much a legal strategy as a power dynamic.” People are more likely to self-police and comply in advance because they’re terrified they’ll get in trouble.

‘I wanted to find the slowest fashion imaginable’: the woman growing her own dress

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 11:00:26 GMT

Looking for an alternative to fast fashion, Eve Ogden Schaub decided to create a garment from homegrown flax

From crop tops to shorts and brightly patterned dresses, many of today’s clothes are the result of fast fashion. But one woman is taking a radical approach to challenging this trend by growing her own dress.

Eve Ogden Schaub is in the midst of a project to create a linen garment made from flax she is growing at home, documenting the process in videos shared on her Instagram account.

“I had this idea that I wanted to find the slowest fashion imaginable. And that’s when I had the idea I could grow a dress from seed in my back yard,” she says.

Schaub began the project in April 2025 when she turned a 600 sq ft vegetable garden in Vermont into a plot for growing flax. Having harvested the first crop, Schaub sowed and harvested a second. She is also learning to process the material in steps that would not sound amiss in a Grimms’ fairytale – sometimes enlisting family and friends to help.

“We retted it, which is a sort of decomposition process, and then you do breaking and scutching and hackling, and you have to spin and scour and then maybe dye your yarn,” she says, adding that she has yet to get to the latter step, but is growing indigo plants for the purpose.

Once the flax is spun into linen yarn, Shaub will weave it on a huge loom – not unlike Penelope in the Odyssey – before cutting out and sewing a dress. “So it’s an enormous undertaking, but something that not all that long ago was completely commonplace, and I found that a very attractive, interesting facet of the project,” she says.

As Schaub says, it has never been easier to get a cheap, convenient garment delivered to your door.

However “fast fashion” has become an environmental and health catastrophe, with garments ending up on huge rubbish dumps in Ghana and workers in India’s recycling factories experiencing ailments including lung disease.

In our current culture, “if you can do something cheaper and faster, it’s always the preferred option,” Schaub says. “And I want to step back and say: but is it? What might we stand to gain if we were to slow down and try to find things that are more meaningful to us, that bring us something that we can’t get from this fast-paced commercial world?”

Schaub also wants to explore the value of creativity, and question what benefits people may gain from making more things.

A self-described “fibre-person and maker”, Schaub is no stranger to lifestyle experiments, having written books on a number of projects, including her family’s attempts to give up sugar for a year, and to go 12 months without producing any rubbish.

The latter, says Schaub, dovetails with her new endeavour, noting that in avoiding waste, she learned about synthetic materials and the issues plastic poses for our environment and our bodies.

“Unfortunately, we’re all walking around wearing plastic bags most of the time, and we don’t even realise it,” she says.

Schaub hopes her project will shine a light on the implications of modern clothing – including the poor treatment and low pay of those producing such garments: “The whole system, I want to question and say, is this what we want?”

In her efforts to go from ground to garment, Shaub has picked the brains of myriad experts, adding that valuing shared knowledge is another facet of the experiment.

But she admits some steps have proved easier to get the hang of than others: in one of the many videos capturing her attempts at spinning Schaub is left grimacing at the camera.

“There’s something inherently funny in the learning process, because you screw up and you screw up, and you know you’re going to screw up,” she says.

The project, she adds, has been an eye-opener for many. “I get so many people commenting on my social media posts saying, ‘now I understand. Now I understand why clothes were so expensive, why cloth was a valuable commodity, why people only owned one or maybe two outfits, because it was so hard to get’,” she says.

Schaub says her own views about clothing have changed too, noting she no longer finds department store clothing appealing, and has a greater motivation to appreciate and mend the clothes she already has.

As for the final dress, Schaub admits her previous experience in sewing has only run as far as making Halloween costumes. But she is planning to work with an experienced friend to design the linen garment based on historical dress patterns.

“I cannot predict when this project will end, but I promise I’m going to wear something at the end of this,” she says, adding that whatever she produces, it will be deeply meaningful to her. “Because of that, I hope it will be beautiful,” she says. “I know it will be beautiful to me.”

Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 10:00:24 GMT

Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took over

In mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.

They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.

That was precisely what the former president Gustavo Petro’s “total peace” plan had sought to achieve: negotiating with and disarming all of Colombia’s criminal groups, which are estimated to have nearly 30,000 members.

But the group of just 99 people was the only one to disarm, and did so just three days before the presidential runoff, which was won by the far-right millionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who had campaigned on a promise to end “total peace” and return to a full-on strategy of jailing or killing criminals.

Now, several weeks after the new president took office – and amid efforts to deal with the aftermath of the 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as his government has already begun the promised airstrikes against criminal groups – the 99 do not know what will happen to them.

“We’re in limbo,” said Natalia Bríñez, 29, one of 13 women among the group staying in the temporary location zone, or ZUT by its Spanish initials, a government-controlled zone where, under surveillance and unable to leave, they were supposed to make the transition to civilian life over the following months.

The former guerrillas are housed in beige brick buildings decorated with drawings they painted themselves, including doves of peace, with a communal dining hall where three meals a day are served. No weapons are allowed inside and soldiers guard the ZUT from a perimeter less than a mile away.

One former combatant built a makeshift gym with weights made from metal pipes and tins filled with cement and sand, and there is an improvised football pitch, but most of them spend their days on their phones.

De la Espriella has repeatedly said his government will no longer negotiate peace agreements and has yet to announce what he intends to do regarding the people at the ZUT. The president has not responded to requests for comment.

In theory, any arrest warrants against the group are suspended, and they remain under state protection until 25 December, when Petro’s decree establishing the ZUT expires. But De la Espriella could revoke the decree at any time.

Armando Novoa, the former government official who led peace negotiations with the group, said “the worst-case scenario would be for the new government to close the ZUT, launch a military operation and try to capture or kill them. That would be a crime against humanity, because these people are unarmed.”

Between 2 and 4 August, days before De la Espriella’s inauguration, Novoa led journalists including the Guardian through the ZUT. The Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, where he worked, has since been absorbed into the newly created National Security Commission – a move expected to result in more than 200 job losses – and Novoa has resigned.

For now, at least, the ZUT remains in operation and has a small library run by Bríñez, who has a phoenix tattoo on her left shoulder as a symbol of her rebirth away from the armed conflict.

“The hardest thing for me has been being away from my children,” said Bríñez, who has a seven-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son and speaks to them on video calls, but will only be able to see them in person once her “transition” is complete, a process that includes vocational training and psychosocial support.

They were also supposed to receive financial support of about £425 a month, which had not yet been paid. In the meantime, some of them were planning to start a chicken-rearing business.

The 99 made up a small part of a group of about 1,000 combatants called Commandos of the Frontier – most of whom remain armed – and are part of the National Coordinator of the Bolivarian Army (CNEB), a former dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) with about 2,500 members which controls the border with Ecuador.

The Petro administration said negotiations were also under way with other members of the CNEB, who published an open letter addressed to De la Espriella saying they were willing to continue talks with him. It is not known whether the president responded.

The CNEB’s chief “peace negotiator”, Geovany Andrés Rojas, known as “Araña” (Spider), had been in custody since February under a US extradition request for drug trafficking, which Petro had delayed. Last Wednesday, De la Espriella ordered extradition.

Although such groups emerged in the 1960s as leftwing rebels fighting government abuses and seeking revolution – followed soon afterwards by far-right paramilitary groups – ideology has long since been overtaken for most of them by economic interests, above all drug trafficking (Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine) and illegal mining.

“Here in the ZUT, the vast majority were not in the group because of any ideological commitment, but for economic reasons,” said Novoa. “It even surprised us that most of them simply called the group ‘the company’.”

Petro repeatedly tried to negotiate peace agreements with larger groups. The armed factions took advantage of temporary ceasefires to continue expanding, a process that had already begun before he took office. They also clashed among themselves for control of territory and illicit economies, which many security experts say contributed to a rise in homicides, kidnappings and massacres.

“Total peace” was an attempt to address what the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc failed to resolve, as other armed groups and Farc dissidents remained active.

Petro’s administration failed to reduce violence, which instead reached its worst levels in a decade, and to reach the disarmament stage with any of the gangs, apart from the 99 former combatants – who handed over their weapons only on the eve of an election that every poll indicated the government-backed candidate would lose.

“They [the government] told us: ‘If this works, you’re opening the door for other groups and will set an example,’” said Bríñez.

Some security experts saw the agreement as rushed.

“It was a somewhat irresponsible decision,” said Paula Tobo, a senior researcher at the thinktank Ideas for Peace Foundation, which published an extensive report on why Total Peace failed.

Tobo said the 99 were now in a “legal limbo” because their protection rested on decrees that could be revoked and there is no legal framework for their transition to civilian life. All of the Petro administration’s proposals to regulate surrenders failed in Congress and, under current law, anyone who has committed crimes such as kidnapping or drug trafficking is not eligible for amnesty.

“It’s positive that these people wanted to lay down their arms, but it really wasn’t the right time for the government to take that decision … The previous administration clearly put them at risk of this government suddenly deciding to abolish the ZUT and arrest them,” said Tobo.

The group wrote a letter to De la Espriella reaffirming its “irreversible decision to commit to peace” and inviting him to visit the ZUT. At the time of publication it had received no response.

The youngest member of the group, a 19-year-old who asked to be identified only as Adrián, said they wanted “to have a home, a family”.

However, he knows what he will do if things do not go according to plan. “Honestly, I’d take up arms again, because we’re keeping our side of the bargain and the government should do the same, shouldn’t it?” he said.

Daniela Díaz travelled to Valle del Guamuez at the invitation of the Colombian government’s former Office of the High Commissioner for Peace.

Lando Norris agrees new deal until at least 2030 with ‘second family’ McLaren

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 09:26:53 GMT

Norris: ‘I want my whole career to be with McLaren’

F1 title holder says other teams have approached him

Lando Norris has said he would like to see out his career with McLaren, as the defending Formula One world champion announced he has agreed a multi-year deal until at least 2030 with the team he described as like “a second family”.

The 26-year-old, who won his first F1 title last season, joined McLaren to make his debut in the sport in 2019. He has been with them ever since and his current contract was due to run until the end of this year. Norris emphasised that he had not countenanced leaving McLaren and had made no approaches toward other teams – although some had made advances towards him.

“It really was the easiest decision I’ve had to make in my career so far,” Norris said. “I’ll be very, very happy at the end of my career to say that McLaren is the only team I’ve been with. I kind of want my whole career to be with McLaren, because I’m happy here and I don’t want to change.

The British driver added: “Even when we go through a harder year, such as we’ve had so far this year, there’s no thought comes to my head of: ‘Was this the right decision or not?’”

Norris joined McLaren as part of their young driver programme in 2017 and stepped up to the team two years later alongside Carlos Sainz. McLaren were still undergoing a rebuilding process after an extended period of underperforming. He took his first podium at the Austrian Grand Prix in 2020 during difficult years for McLaren.

Under the leadership of the chief executive, Zak Brown, and, more recently, the team principal, Andrea Stella, McLaren have returned to the front of the grid. Norris took his first GP win in 2024 in Miami and the team went on to claim the constructors’ championship that year. Last year, with Norris winning the title, McLaren took the drivers’ and constructors’ double. He has taken 13 wins for the team and, with 163 grands prix raced, he is their longest-serving driver.

This season, the team have struggled somewhat under the new regulations but with comprehensive upgrades to their car are once more in the mix, as Norris’s victories in the last two races at Zandvoort and the Hungaroring have demonstrated.

Norris made the announcement at a friends and families day held at the McLaren Technology Centre in Woking, where the team also confirmed he was to be presented with one of the MCL39 cars he drove to the title in 2025 as part of the deal. Norris emphasised it was the environment at McLaren that played a central role in him sticking with them.

“I always want to be where I’m happy first and foremost, closely followed by the fact I want to be where I believe there’s always going to be good results,” he said. “I still believe through the harder periods that what we achieved over the last few years was possible, and obviously all of that came true.”

“People is the most important thing for me. Of course the leaders – but every individual. I’ve built very good relationships with so many people here over the years. People that work here every day, to the mechanics, to the engineers. It just very much feels like my home. They just feel like my second family in some ways.”

No details of how much Norris will be earning were released, but he did concede it was not as much as Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen have been reported as making in their recent contracts. Hamilton’s deal with Ferrari is thought to be worth $60m (£44.3m) a year. Verstappen’s new contract with Red Bull, announced at the Dutch GP last weekend, prompted speculation it was worth as much as $100m a year.

“It’s certainly not close to the level of Lewis or Max,” Norris said. “It shouldn’t be because I’ve not achieved as much as they have in their career. In a way, I believe it should be, because I believe I can fight against them whenever I need to and I can do a better job whenever I need to. So I guess I have the two opinions on it.”

Last year Norris’s teammate Oscar Piastri also agreed to a multi-year contract extension with McLaren.

Stella said: “Lando is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.”

The hill I will die on: The barbecue is fundamentally unenjoyable. Please, put a lid on it

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 09:00:22 GMT

Dress up the barbie however you like – it’s toxic, tiresome and, more to the point, malnourishing

“If you’re invited to a barbecue, have your dinner before you go.” It is the wisest advice my dad has ever given me. Barbecues are one of life’s perennial disappointments. The romance of eating outside quickly degenerates into a recipe for mucky fingers, smelly clothes and more mess than you bargained for, with grills that you can never get clean, uncomfortable seating that makes your back ache or, dafter still, eating while standing up. Worst of all is the true barbecue legacy – the nagging hunger that follows bitty dining, leaving you with the aggrieved sense that you missed a mealtime you’re never getting back.

I grew up in Cornwall, where beach barbecues were a rite of passage. The flame under the sandy grill was blown out by the Atlantic wind, so these gatherings were impractical, unpredictable and interminable. One minute the sausages were raw and looked like they’d never be ready, the next they were hard and black and basically inedible. Rain frequently sent us scrambling to pack up and flee for shelter.

Even when it doesn’t rain, and the scene is a suburban garden where something that looks like it belongs in a gastropub kitchen has been installed to char halloumi three times a year, I find myself wondering: “How is this fun?” Barbecues are terrible for socialising because the food trickles out, with kids served first (why, when they have the most energy?), so guests don’t eat at the same time and instead dine in silos, wondering if they’ll get home early enough to make pasta. As for drinks, they’re warm because ice buckets don’t work – they’re too small and the ice melts almost instantly in the kind of temperatures we’ve seen this summer – and nobody wants to dash back and forth to the fridge.

The popularity of barbecues is inexplicable yet undeniable, with black smoke puffing from back gardens at the first sniff of a sunny day. When I broached my hatred with an Australian, she reacted as if I wanted to deprive her of her birthright. But just because people keep doing something doesn’t necessarily mean they actually enjoy it.

Barbecues are antisocial in other, more important ways. I used to live above a man who liked to come home from work and barbecue steak on his patio, directly below my kitchen. I had to close every window to stop my whole flat stinking of beef. If you live in a densely populated area, it’s not particularly socially conscious to fill the air with meaty smog during hot weather, just so you can clog your arteries.

Disposable barbecues, which have been factors in wildfires during this summer’s heatwaves, are the worst. This month, one caused a forest fire in the North York Moors, while Dorset and Wiltshire fire and rescue recently told people to go to the pub instead. A spokesperson added: “I’d certainly challenge anybody to say whether they’ve ever had a good meal from a disposable barbecue.” An excellent point which, if we’re honest, applies to all variations of barbecue.

Max Liu is a freelance writer

‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to Rotherham

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 07:00:21 GMT

Country star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation scheme

Shane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school where he was deputy headteacher when he got a call asking him to come to Rotherham hospital ASAP. It was December 2007 and Jarman’s wife, Claire, had given birth the previous day to their first child, a girl called Emma, so of course he rushed to the phone. All was well, he was told, but that “everything would become clear” when he got to the hospital.

Once there, his wife told him – somewhat unexpectedly – that they were going to meet Dolly Parton. “And literally within what felt like five minutes,” he recalled, “there were great camera flashes, lots of noise, lots of clicking and in walked this real big bundle of energy.”

Jarman said that as his wife handed over their tiny 4lb 6oz baby to the country star, “all I remember is seeing Dolly Parton with my little girl’s head in her hand and these great big red nails”.

Was he a little nervous about the nails? “I was very nervous about the nails to be quite honest.”

Parton was in the South Yorkshire former mining and steelworking town – not principally known for its razzle-dazzle – for the British launch of the Imagination Library, the book donation programme the musician had started in her Tennessee home of Sevier County a little over a decade earlier, and which she had been invited to extend to children in Yorkshire.

If Rotherham – or at least a gathering of local dignitaries that assembled later in a disused steelworks – was a little bemused by the singer, Parton knew places like this, and of course knew how to charm.

“I gotta make sure I say your town name right – it’s Rother’m?” she said, flattening the famous southern twang to something approximating flat Yorkshire vowels. “Did I get it right? I’ve been practising because it don’t look like that on paper. In the States, anything that’s h-a-m we have to say Rother-ham.”

Among the torrent of tributes to the entertainer, businesswoman and philanthropist since her death on Monday, Rotherham too has been remembering the impact of a woman who, for all her own glamour, cared deeply about places that had a little less of it.

Parton may have jested when she said she had considered buying a South Yorkshire pied-à-terre (“so you may be walking down the streets of Rotherham and see me coming out of a little cubbyhole somewhere”), but her description of the post-industrialist town as “a heart spot for me” was sincere, thanks to the similarities she saw to her own outsider upbringing.

“I totally related to Rotherham,” she said some years later. “I know that it’s out in an industrial area … When they were making fun of me for going out there, I thought, you know what? Don’t make fun of me.”

The scheme ensured that every child in Rotherham was posted a free book, in their own name, for each month of their life until they were five, funded partly by Parton’s foundation and partly by the local authority and other local funders. Deborah Bullivant, who took over leading the Rotherham Imagination Library shortly after Parton’s visit as part of a wider literacy drive, said that despite some initial scepticism from locals, it “changed the culture” for many.

“Some people were very suspicious: Why Dolly Parton? What is this thing?” she said. “[But] can you imagine receiving a book, from registering your child’s birth, your baby in their own name receives the book every month through the letterbox? For many families who didn’t really have a background in reading, it changed the culture within their homes to being more of a reading culture and embracing books and using books and sharing books.”

The fact that the literacy drive was so personal to the singer was “the best way to counter any of the suspicion or worries that people had about it”, Bullivant said. “Why is Dolly Parton doing this? Who is she? She doesn’t know about this? Well, she does. She understood she needed to drive her own work herself from scratch. She got the importance of the imagination, of reading, of telling stories.”

Though the Rotherham scheme was wound up in 2015 after the council withdrew support, it would be rolled out to other places in Britain, including Doncaster, North Lincolnshire, the London borough of Southwark (“Hello Suth’rk! This is Dolly!”) and Nottingham (which even coaxed an “Ay up me duck!” from the singer).

In total, 6.3m books have been given to children across the four UK nations since one-day-old Emma Jarman received the first one in 2007, a copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, which Parton autographed for her. (Globally, the figure is 300m).

Emma, now 18, will shortly be going to university to study biomedical science, “and, if I know Emma, [the book] will go to university with her so that she can show her friends there,” said her father.

‘Now is a good time for players to speak up’: Lucy Bronze on Fifa and helping refugees

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 07:00:20 GMT

Chelsea defender reflects on spending time with refugees in Colombia this summer and her passion for helping people on and off the pitch

Lucy Bronze does not stop. Her brain runs a hundred miles a minute. She does not need traditional entertainment. “I’m not good at watching TV – I can’t sit still,” Bronze says, sitting sort-of still, on a bench shielded from the wind, overlooking Chelsea’s training pitch at Cobham. “Someone recently asked me what I listen to in the car and someone else jumped in and was like: ‘Lucy has her own podcast going on in her own head.’ I don’t listen to music, I don’t listen to podcasts, I just have a million thoughts going on.”

Bronze’s late ADHD and autism diagnosis help it make sense, but her mum had always suspected she might have one of the conditions, so it wasn’t a surprise. “Naomi Girma said to me: ‘I’ve never met someone who trains so hard in the gym with zero music on; it does not make sense.’ I was like: ‘It’s literally in my head, I don’t need anything else.’”

Walking her dog, Nala, is the main thing Bronze does to relax, but otherwise she is “just involved in so many things, different businesses, PFA boards, stuff for Fifpro and Uefa at the minute. There’s obviously a lot going on behind the scenes and I’m just keeping up to date with things like that.”

“Things like that” are hugely rewarding and Bronze gets pleasure out of elements that could seem tedious but contribute to the wider game and its growth. “I love growing-the-game stuff, but it’s emotionally draining as well,” she says. “Myself and Kim Little are on the PFA players’ board and we speak to each other a lot. We’re in quite similar positions as older players who’ve lived so much of the game and want to give so much back and we feel like we’ve got so many great ideas to help so many people and that there’s so much to be done but you just want to do it all tomorrow.

“Sometimes you’ve just got to keep pushing and pushing but I do enjoy it and I feel like I’ve got endless energy so it does help that I’ve got like all these different avenues to push myself.”

Recently, that has involved being vocal about Gianni Infantino’s rogue and scuppered plan to sell off the World Cup, and his tenure as Fifa president. At the start of the month the defender backed the threat of a European boycott of Fifa competitions, regardless of what it meant for her football ambitions, telling the New Zealand Herald: “It’s for the future of the game and not just for me today and tomorrow.”

In a press conference on Tuesday before Chelsea’s 5-2 victory over Real Sociedad in the first leg of their Champions League qualifier, Bronze explained why she had shared the social media post of the former France defender Mikaël Silvestre, who is on Fifa’s players’ voice panel, which said “change is necessary” at the top of the game. “The football comes first no matter what, no matter who’s in charge, who’s playing … and it feels like now is a good time for players to speak up.”

A summer with no major international women’s tournament has given Bronze time to focus on some of the issues she is most passionate about. “I’ve been trying to go to Colombia for four years to do stuff with refugees,” says Bronze, who was asked to help with fundraising for the UNHCR (UN Refugee Agency) during Covid and has been involved since. She says, with a wry smile: “Sarina [the England head coach, Sarina Wiegman] is the one who’s always blocked it because she said that she didn’t want me travelling there before a tournament and getting jet-lagged, especially before the World Cup in Australia. She blocked it then and she blocked it before the Euros because we didn’t have a lot of time. She was like: ‘Lucy, it’s not a good idea for your body.’ So, that’s been planned for a long time.”

The trip to Colombia, which according to the UNHCR is facing a humanitarian crisis and has about 2.8 million Venezuelan refugees and migrants and seven million people who are internally displaced, was worth the Wiegman-enforced wait.

“It was crazy,” she says. “I had had a bit of the background explained to me beforehand. A lot of people don’t necessarily know so much. I guess now that there’s been the earthquake in Venezuela people know a bit more, but it’s generally not spoken about as much because it’s Venezuela to Colombia compared to like, Ukrainians to wealthier countries like England or Germany.

“Being on the ground and especially around kids was special. They don’t know why they’re in that position and it’s not their fault, it’s just the life that’s been put in front of them and they just make the most of the smallest of things. It was a tiring time, emotionally and physically, but it was powerful seeing so much good work being done too.”

Experiencing the resilience and joy of children in the worst of circumstances is “really moving” says Bronze. “At the same time, when we went to leave, there were kids saying: ‘Take me with you,’ which is really devastating.”

after newsletter promotion

Bronze went with shirts, including some from Girma. “There was a refugee girl there who was the captain of this football team which was all boys,” says Bronze. “Nay’s [Girma’s] parents were refugees too. So I told this girl Nay’s story, and this kid’s face just lit up. I showed her pictures of Nay playing for America and I gave her her shirt. This girl was so excited because while it’s not someone in the exact same situation, it’s someone whose family had to rebuild their lives and she could see her own life in it and how amazing she’s doing now.”

Helping people on and off the pitch gives Bronze energy. There is excitement for the new season with Chelsea’s changed and young team under Sonia Bompastor after a high-energy pre-season.

“I feel like it’s taken Sonia till now to do everything she’s wanted to do behind the scenes, in terms of her staff and putting the trust into her staff to do the things that are part of her vision,” Bronze says. “There’s been a hard transition and balance to find what makes Chelsea so good and so dominant and so ‘Chelsea’, while also evolving and adapting, because that’s what you have to do.”

That hampered them last season, Bronze thinks: “The first year everything kind of went smoothly. As things started to change, we were so desperate to win because we are Chelsea – we need to win – but at the same time, it was about [how] we do that while evolving and I think that’s maybe what we struggled with in the second half of last season.”

There have been big changes off the pitch too, with all Women’s Super League games to be played at Stamford Bridge, starting with Aston Villa next Saturday, and cup games at AFC Wimbledon’s the Cherry Red Records Stadium. “It’s a statement of intent on the future of Chelsea’s women’s team,” says Bronze.

“Chelsea have been this dominant team on the pitch but now we need to dominate in every aspect. Not just in winning the league six times in a row – that is fantastic – but we need to win the Champions League, we need to grow as a team, we need to grow in the way that we play and the people that we bring in and we need to have a stadium that represents that ambition. Everything contributes.”

This article was amended on 29 August 2026. An earlier version said Chelsea would be playing their home cup games at Kingsmeadow, Norbiton; in fact, they will play at Wimbledon’s the Cherry Red Records Stadium.

There is clearly trouble ahead for Harry and Meghan on their return to the UK. Here are five ways to avert it

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 06:00:21 GMT

With a sceptical public and hostility from a lot of the press, the Sussexes face quite a challenge. Still, they really could help themselves

They’re back! Harry and Meghan’s quiet return to England this week, via Birmingham airport, was much anticipated but scarcely celebrated – no bunting or street parties.

So far there are many questions but very few answers: not just “why return now?” and “why so suddenly?”, but also questions of security: who pays if not themselves, given that they are not working royals? And where will the money come from to keep them in the style to which they are accustomed?

The bills are mounting: not just the Daily Mail’s legal costs incurred by Harry’s ill-fated court action, but even the upkeep of their nine-bedroom Montecito mansion, which, with property taxes, mortgage and upkeep (including looking after their chickens), could cost about $80,000 (£60,000) a month. That’s to say nothing about the house in Portugal. Meghan will have to get some pretty meaty and regular acting jobs – and fast.

Maybe all will be well, they will readjust to British life and Britain will readjust to them, but on past experience this seems highly unlikely. Can they avert it? Here are five tips that might help.

1. Find capable advisers. Not necessarily the pin-striped courtiers who serve at the palace and know a great deal but whom Harry hated, nor the subversives like Mark Bolland, the PR guru, who once advised Charles as prince and seems to have initiated rows with half the rest of the family. Young smart-alec briefers are not required, nor perhaps Americans who don’t have a feel for Britain and its generally pro-royalist population. There are considerable bridges to be rebuilt with the people who feel Harry and Meghan let them down, and especially with the rest of the royal family. The couple need careful guidance over how they should present themselves, when they should speak and what they should say – or not say. No more interviews with Oprah Winfrey slagging off the relatives. It makes a splash, but thereafter, it doesn’t exactly help.

2. Make peace again with the family, especially William and Catherine. It may be difficult and arduous to restore trust, but they need to do that as quickly as possible. And no setting up a rival court: they must know by now the obligation to choose discreet friends wisely.

3. Help out a bit. Not necessarily with the washing-up but with attendance at public events, visits and charities. Not by freeloading, the public hates that, but by generally doing good – not for a few minutes or a day or two between flips to California, but regularly and humbly.

4. Breathe deeply and make nice with the media – and not just the networks that have previously been prepared to pay them mega money. Wiser members of the royal family face challenges too, but they know that they need the so-called dead tree media, including newspapers, for their popularity. A smile goes further than a snarl. Remember that you need them more than they need you – they have businesses to run, you have a public perception to shape via their products. If they stop reporting on the royals or all the coverage is negative, the institution’s days of crisis will never end.

Think hard about what to communicate and what you try to keep secret. The “secret” – private – christening of Archie was unnecessary as was William’s attempt to hide the name of a family dog from an avid press and public. The media will always ferret even more important things out – such as their new home and the children’s school (especially if, as reported, Harry wants to watch young Archie play rugby every Saturday) and a defensive, sneering approach gains nothing. It just makes ever-fragile media/royal relations even worse. Better to be as open as possible and broker an arrangement for the media to thereafter leave Archie and Lilibet alone – it has worked for William and Catherine’s children. Harry and Meghan must face up to the fact they will always be newsworthy and isn’t that partly what they want to publicise their ventures?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

5. Above all, smile, for God’s sake. Harry and Meghan are both in a very privileged position. People won’t like it if they appear to despise or patronise them, or to feel too sorry for themselves. They have the opportunity to be identified with the great cause of cheering people up. Cometh the hour … perhaps.

Steve Bates is a former Guardian royal correspondent

Faster, higher, funnier: what we learned from China’s robot games

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 05:00:19 GMT

Five-day showcase reveals leaps Beijing has made in humanoid tech, but also its limitations as US rivals come up from the rear

With exploding pelvises, enough comic pratfalls for a Buster Keaton show reel and the odd moment of ruthless violence, the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing gripped the world this week with an unsettling mixture of hilarity, trepidation and relief.

The five-day showcase staked out China’s claim to undisputed leadership in humanoid robotics as android martial artists landed knockout roundhouse kicks and robot teams marched into the arena heralded by flag-waving captains astride giant robotic dogs. The games’ blue-riband event, the 100m, did not disappoint when the robot-sprinters ran quicker than Usain Bolt before slamming mindlessly into a padded wall in a blaze of sparks, flames and flying mechanical limbs.

There, in a 10-second clip perfect for the games’ global online audience, was proof of what onlooking international experts described as the superpower’s “staggering” engineering progress, combined with comfort that the disintegrating robots might not yet be ready to become humanity’s overlords.

“Ready for another big day of fail,” read a typically schadenfreude-laced comment from one of millions who tuned into viral social media clips and livestreams of events from boxing to breakdancing in which the humanoids displayed a jerky mix of ruthless effectiveness and pathetic failure.

Others caught themselves experiencing unexpected empathy. One captioned a robot struggling through the 400m obstacle race: “after drinking 4 bottles of wine at 2 a. m”. Another found a weightlifting contest “way more emotional than I expected” as the bots strained to achieve their sporting goals.

If the games had a slogan it might be: faster, higher, funnier. The obstacle course involving humanoids scrambling under nets, down stairs and over stepping stones reminded the comedian Charlie Higson of Monty Python’s Upper Class Twit of the Year sketch: “It’s only lacking ‘taking the bra off the debs’ and ‘shooting themselves’.” He came back the next day for more. “They get better and better,” he tweeted as a cheerleader robot wielding glittery pom-poms flailed around like it was having a fit.

But the games were not intended to only entertain. Involving over 2,000 humanoids built by more than 660 mostly domestic tech companies, it was a propaganda flex of China’s robotics muscle just weeks before its president, Xi Jinping, lands in Washington DC for a summit with Donald Trump, where the superpowers’ race to tech supremacy will be high on the agenda. Only last month Trump banned imports of Chinese humanoids and four-legged robot dogs, citing cyber and national security concerns. The event was also a billboard to boost global sales of Chinese robots as US rivals prepare their own launches, notably Elon Musk’s long-hyped Optimus humanoid which is reported to have finally gone into production this month. Last year China produced 12,800 humanoids, about 90% of the global total, according to the Mercator Institute for Chinese Studies, a dominance which perhaps gave China the confidence to candidly broadcast so many comic failures, which surprised some onlookers.

The event reflected the fact that, for the Chinese Communist party, humanoids are a high priority, offering solutions to a looming demographic crunch in the labour market, rising military ambitions and, as they walk more widely among the people, the state’s desire to tighten its surveillance web. Beijing is fuelling an intensely competitive robot industry by seeding hundreds of companies to create an evolutionary survival of the fittest dynamic, with the games creating a hard deadline for competitors to deliver measurable progress. Xi’s latest five-year plan, approved in March, was studded with pledges to boost robotics industries; accelerate the “practical application of … humanoid robots” and explore “embodied AI in roles experiencing labour shortages or high-risk environments” which likely include war. The military potential of the humanoids on display worried some onlookers.

“Fascinating, and honestly, a little scary,” said Arun Bothra, a senior police officer in India, which shares a tense border with China. “Watching robots run, play football and compete like humans is one thing. Seeing them on borders someday, carrying guns and making decisions, will be something else entirely.” Or as another viewer concluded while watching a humanoid hoist a loaded barbell in the weightlifting contest: “Humanity is preparing its own end”.

Of course China is not alone in pursuing robotic warfare. As the Beijing games progressed on Monday, Ukraine was staging a novel military parade in Kyiv made up entirely of robotic weaponry and defence equipment.

But how to explain the numerous crashes and fits in the Olympic speed skating arena where the competition took place? Experts said the games revealed how China was making the most rapid strides in developing humanoids’ bodies rather than their minds.

“The progress they have made from last year is staggering,” said Thrishantha Nanayakkara, a professor of robotics at the Dyson school of design engineering at Imperial College London. “Everything seems to be coming together …. by 2030, it will be a very different world.”

The fastest sprinter, Tiangong Ultra, completed the 100m more than twice as fast as last year, while the peak standing jump rose from 0.96 m to 3.40m. Liquid cooling has allowed Chinese engineers to increase the torque of the motors that drive their limbs creating more twitchy and powerful force.

“This execution is incredible,” said Ingo Keller, head of robotics at the National Robotarium, based at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh. “You would not have expected the speed of development. [But] does it move the goalpost in utilising humanoids? Not necessarily.”

Experts stress the games revealed progress in specialist, not generalist, humanoids: the robots were fast runners or good boxers, not both, partly because the AI models that govern their decisions are yet to be able to process the physical world’s full complexity. The industry talks about reaching a ChatGPT moment – a tipping point when humanoid technology becomes generally useful and explodes into the mainstream. By one definition, that comes when a robot can succeed at 80% of tasks in an unfamiliar home, instructed by voice or text. The event coincided with a sobering speech from Wang Xingxing, founder of Unitree, one of China’s leading robotics companies, who said it could be a decade before that ChatGPT moment.

“Humanoids are not yet capable enough for mass deployment,” he said. “The limitations in the AI models that power robots’ decision-making and interactions remain the industry’s biggest bottleneck.” Amid uncertainty about the impact of robotics and bubble fears, his company’s share price has been oscillating wildly since it listed in Shanghai earlier this month.

Georg Stieler, a consultant who advises multinational companies on robots, said he did not see much progress on robots’ autonomy when he was in Beijing this week. He reported that some Chinese robotics companies were also privately cynical about the five-day showcase, complaining about a lack of funding for commercial long-term pilot projects “to do something useful in a factory”.

“It’s not so difficult to make a stunt, which people will share on LinkedIn or X,” Stieler said. “The major challenge is to do something that’s really useful.”

Humanoid robot dexterity requires much more work and there was little focus on the events testing it. There was little obvious coverage of a Monty Pythonesque category that included power tool assembly, powder weighing, bottle opening, cap prying, box unpacking and tweezer bean-picking. One such challenge was briefly featured on Wednesday when the race track was occupied by the unspectacular sight of a humanoid struggling to pick up a small object from a table and spilling water in a pouring challenge. The cameras panned away to find a humanoid martial artist carving the air with kicks.

From The Dog Stars to Erykah Badu: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 05:00:19 GMT

Jacob Elordi stars as a post-pandemic pilot in Ridley Scott’s sci-fi adventure, while the celebrated soul singer returns with a long-trailed collaboration

The Dog StarsOut now Ridley Scott has got to be one of the most prolific octogenarians working today. The director’s latest, a sci-fi drama based on the 2012 novel, stars man of the moment Jacob Elordi as a former pilot surviving the aftermath of a pandemic, with Margaret Qualley as a medic/love interest and Josh Brolin as a pugnacious former marine.

ColonyOut now Welcome to a Korean zombie horror where the twist is that the undead share a hive mind, making them a formidable threat to the not-so-merry band of survivors hoping to pull through against the odds. Train to Busan director Yeon Sang-ho returns with more gore and action thrills.

One Night OnlyOut now Will Gluck writes and directs a romcom starring zeitgeist-friendly actors Callum Turner and Monica Barbaro. It hit the headlines for not having any explicit sex in it despite its The Purge-meets-romance premise: premarital sex is illegal in the US, apart from on one no-holds-barred night each year.

I Want Your SexOut now Another new release with banging on the brain sees Olivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman playing, respectively, a provocative artist and the assistant with whom she enters into a BDSM relationship. Being a Gregg Araki film, this one is rather bolder, with the young man soon finding himself in over his head, so to speak. Catherine Bray

ForwardsThe Downs, Bristol, 29 & 30 August The likes of Tems, Little Simz and Amyl and the Sniffers headline this two-day festival in one of the UK’s foremost music cities. The eclectic bill also includes UK legends (Tricky, Goldie) and electronic experimentalists (Oklou, Wesley Joseph). Michael Cragg

Gesualdo Six and the Colin Currie GroupRoyal Albert Hall, London, 2 September Two British musical trailblazers – a Renaissance-focused vocal consort and a new-music ensemble headed by one of the world’s leading percussionists – join forces for this late-night Prom. The programme mixes centuries-old Christian choral works with Steve Reich’s Tehillim to mark the composer’s 90th birthday. Flora Willson

A$AP Rocky30 August to 5 September, tour starts London In the eight years since his last album, Testing, rapper A$AP Rocky ventured into acting, designing and modelling, before releasing his fourth album, Don’t Be Dumb, in January. He now brings that expertly curated shapeshifting record to UK arenas. MC

Swansea international jazz festivalVarious venues, 3 to 6 September Swansea not only hosts the UK’s longest-running weekly jazz club, but a prestigious weekender too. Guitar maestro Nicolas Meier splices Turkish music, flamenco, jazz and more (3 September), while ever-cool vocalist Claire Martin duets with bass virtuoso Laurence Cottle (4 September). John Fordham

Selected 16 Nottingham Contemporary, 2 September Touring art venues across the UK, this exhibition celebrates incredibly diverse new moving image work by early-career artists including Rhiana Bonterre, Rosanna Lee, Jack Guariento and Viviana Almas.

Mike NelsonLeeds Art Gallery, to 30 August It’s your last chance to see M62 (East, West) by the ever brilliant English conceptualist Mike Nelson, a minimal display of blown-out car tyres, collected from the verges of the M62 motorway that runs south of Leeds.

John AkomfrahWalker Art Gallery, Liverpool, to 31 August Listening All Night to the Rain is a multichannel immersive video installation all about diasporic lives in the UK, dealing with ideas of racial injustice, the climate crisis and colonial history, all in Akomfrah’s signature dramatic, cinematic style.

Richard TuttleModern Art, London, 3 September to 3 OctoberThis American minimalist once filled the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall with vast reams of yellow and red fabric, but this show gives viewers a chance to see him operating at a much smaller, but no less radically experimental, scale. Eddy Frankel

Kimberly AkimboHampstead theatre, London, to 7 November This five-time Tony award-winning musical is about a 16-year-old girl who, due to a rare genetic condition, looks 74. It’s all a bit barmy but heartfelt and truthful too. Starring the mighty Maria Friedman. Miriam Gillinson

Henry Paker3 September to 30 May; tour starts Norwich Many comedians moonlight as artists, but few do both jobs at the same time. In Pencil Case, Paker – one-third of beloved podcast Three Bean Salad – combines standup with live drawing in what promises to be a gratifyingly clever and gently novel evening’s entertainment. Rachel Aroesti

Ballet NightsTheatre Royal Glasgow, 2 & 3 September Husband-and-wife dancers Harris Bell and Sae Maeda take a break from their day jobs at the Royal Ballet to perform on tour with Ballet Nights. The gala-style show is a smorgasbord of dance from classical pas de deux to new contemporary pieces, compered by ex-Scottish Ballet dancer Jamiel Devernay-Laurence. Lyndsey Winship

King LearCrucible, Sheffield, 29 August to 19 September Ian McDiarmid returns to Sheffield to play Shakespeare’s Lear – a king on the wane, surrounded by his scheming daughters, thoughtful fools, fears and frailties. Directed by Titas Halder. MG

VigilBBC One & iPlayer, 30 August, 9pm You may still think of Vigil as the sickeningly stressful Suranne Jones submarine drama, but these days the thriller takes place largely above ground; series three transports Jones’s intrepid detective to an Arctic research station where a British special forces operative has been murdered.

The GentlemenNetflix, 3 September Guy Ritchie’s other gangster streamer series (the one that hasn’t been generating a slew of headline-grabbing behind-the-scenes gossip) re-enters the fray, as aristocrat Eddie (Theo James) expands his drug dealing business into Italy. Alabama Shakes – I Must Be DreamingOut now As their 2018 hiatus extended it was assumed the Grammy-winning US soul-rockers would stay on their own musical journeys. Ansel Adams: US National ArchiveOnline In 1941, photographer Ansel Adams was commissioned by the US National Park Service to create a vast mural. Although never completed, his fascinating reference images are now available to view on the National Archives webstie.

Untold Raygun: Breaking BadlyNetflix, 1 September Following her chaotic breakdancing performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics, Rachael Gunn became a viral internet celebrity. Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 05:00:19 GMT

As a war correspondent, I worked with photographers who said the camera was a buffer between them and reality. It is much the same now as we snap and scroll

I was sitting on a rooftop in Athens at sunset looking up at Filopappou hill. Athens in August is burning hot. Not so much hotter than London or Paris any more, but the sort of hot that makes it foolish to step out into sunlight before 6pm. Emerging from the air conditioning at dusk, I saw a dense line of silhouettes on the ridge above me. Almost every one of these shadows had its arm raised, holding a cameraphone towards the sunset.

Of all the pretty hills in the Greek capital, Filopappou arguably has the best view. The Acropolis stands directly to its north. To its south, where I sat, the city sprawls out towards the sea and a dark horizon of islands – Aegina, Salamina, Agistri.

Looking up, the wall of tourist photographers reminded me of something: war zones.

I worked as a correspondent covering conflicts and disasters for the Guardian and other newspapers for more than a decade. Over time, every new disaster came to resemble the last: another catastrophic tableau of buildings and bodies with a dense ring of telephoto lenses pointed at it.

Print reporters like me could stay at a distance from the gore and the horror because we could describe it. The photographers had to get as close as possible because they needed a clean shot.

Later, when I asked them about their work over beers at the American Colony hotel bar or tea at Gaza’s now-destroyed Al Deira hotel – how could they do it? Spend their days gazing at suffering? – most said the same thing. The lens was a buffer, a sort of protective forcefield. They weren’t looking at the fatally injured child, they were looking at the image of one.

The illustrious war photographer Don McCullin was wise to the danger in this distance. “I operate not as a photographer but as a human being,” he said in 1983, 16 years before the first cameraphone. “I try to balance what I photograph not as a photographer but as a person, a man, and photography has got nothing to do with it. It is just something I have learned, it is just a way of communicating.”

Now it’s 2026 and almost every one of us – bar the kooks and the luddites – clutches a distancing device.

I was late to Instagram, but it quickly became second nature. Now, when an attractive dish is put in front of me, an animal does something cute, a fight breaks out on a ferry, a helicopter lands to race some poor person to hospital, I pull out my phone and record it alongside everyone else.

Like the people on the hill, most of us live our lives through lenses: camera first.

And they aren’t always pointing outwards. Multi-billion-dollar industries have been built on people photographing themselves. Much has been written about the psychological perils of our narcissistic age, but increasingly, the danger is more than psychological.

Earlier this month, five teenagers were killed in a car driving the wrong way down a motorway in Ireland. They crashed into another car carrying four members of a family, all of whom were seriously injured. It seems they died taking part in an online trend in which masked young men film themselves driving recklessly at high speed, baiting police into giving chase. The camera is not incidental to the danger: the danger is created for the camera.

Forensic cyberpsychologist Mary Aiken describes this as “hybrid behaviour”: filming and driving simultaneously, with “one foot in the real world and one foot in cyberspace”. While the physical car accelerates down a motorway, part of the driver’s mind is watching the finished video, the audience, the likes from other picture-sharers around the globe.

This could also explain the fatal selfie phenomenon. A study identified 332 selfie-related deaths between 2014 and 2021, most commonly caused by drowning, falling or some form of transport. These tragedies can’t all be blamed on vanity meeting the smartphone – people have always taken stupid risks – but phone cameras have changed how we perceive danger: a cliff edge becomes a backdrop, death is content.

In Afghanistan in 2009, Associated Press photographer Julie Jacobson took nine frames over two and a half minutes of 21-year-old US L/Cpl Joshua Bernard lying fatally wounded after a Taliban ambush as he was treated by his fellow marines. Jacobson didn’t help them, she photographed.

The resulting image of Bernard’s dying face and horrific injuries provoked bitter debate. His family asked for it not to be published. The then US defence secretary, Robert Gates, called AP’s decision to release it “appalling”. The news agency argued that the photograph performed an essential public function: it forced people at home to see the reality of a war being fought in their name.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Jacobson’s defence was that in the moment she couldn’t help him and she decided the most helpful thing she could do as a photographer was to document a painful truth.

I suspect that for the average smartphone user, their cameras serve the opposite purpose. The world has become too difficult to look at directly.

Every day, those same screens show us bombed homes in Gaza, burning forests everywhere, celebrities in psychological anguish, self-harming in front of millions of TikTok followers. After reels of influencers slurping “the best cacio e pepe ever”, we are shown executions, assaults, maimed and dying children. Phone users are exposed to more suffering than a human nervous system is built to absorb, and we keep scrolling.

We’re addicted to our cameras because they have the magical capacity to turn much of what is frightening, painful or just intensely beautiful into something we can frame, edit, caption and share. They allow us to be present but absent.

It’s this sort of moral confusion I tried to explore in my novel, Vulture. Its protagonist is a British correspondent in Gaza who finds that documenting other people’s suffering gives her not only purpose but somewhere to hide. Horror becomes a picture byline; every dead body a pull quote. Bearing witness becomes absolution.

Not that we should, can or will stop recording. In Gaza, Palestinian journalists filming on their phones have provided an indispensable record of a war foreign reporters have largely been prevented from entering. There, picking up a camera is an act of extraordinary courage.

“Photography for me is not looking, it’s feeling,” the great McCullin said, an approach that has produced some of the most affecting images ever taken in conflict zones.

The rest of us may just have to work to remain human behind the lens; to remember to engage with reality once the image is posted.

Phoebe Greenwood is a former Guardian correspondent, and the author of the novel Vulture
