The battle over RAF Barnham: how ominous anti-asylum protests engulfed a small Norfolk town

The Guardian Sat, 29 Aug 2026 04:00:16 GMT

Thetford has a welcoming history. So why have there been so many demonstrations this summer over plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby military base – as well as nights of violent disorder?

‘I don’t talk to mainstream media,” says a young man in an Arsenal shirt. I’ve just asked what brought him to the latest protest against the housing of asylum seekers in Thetford, Norfolk, and his disdain is clear as he goes to warn other protesters of the Guardian’s presence. This isn’t exactly the unity promised by the flyer advertising today’s march: “Everyone welcome: families, friends, dogs. Including the media.”

The protest is planned as a two-mile march from Thetford’s market square to RAF Barnham, a site just over the border in Suffolk, which is due to house asylum seekers while they progress through the system. It is the latest part of a campaign that has lasted the whole summer. Banners line the square, the largest succinctly describing why people are gathering here today: “Thetford and Barnham says no to asylum seekers.”

Some of the protesters are from Thetford, others from farther afield, but mostly Norfolk or Suffolk. I have been visiting Thetford in the weeks before the protest and, while the reasoning of the protesters varies, many say it comes down to numbers. How can this site house 1,250 people when the nearest village has a population of only 600?

Some say the country can’t afford to keep housing asylum seekers as they wait to be processed, or that there are simply too many coming in, or that we don’t know who they are. Asylum seekers are referred to by some here as “boat people” and “invaders”. The suggestion that Britain has lost control of its borders is nothing new. But new theories still materialise. At a protest the week before the march, one attender suggested that people may be being sent intentionally from Iran. “They say that they are sending some of the terrorists over to the UK and we have no idea who comes off the boats,” a protester, David Goulty, told me. “There’s no control on who comes into the country.”

In opposition, Labour criticised the Conservative policy of housing asylum seekers on military bases. But in October last year, now in government, it changed tack. The sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl by a resident of the Bell hotel in Epping, Essex, had prompted months of angry local protests against the housing of asylum seekers in hotels. Keir Starmer announced that military bases would be used once again.

Labour was explicit about the reason for the U-turn: “We know that communities don’t want asylum seekers housed in hotels, and neither does the government, and that’s why we are determined to fix the mess that we’ve inherited by getting a grip of the issue and committing to close every single asylum hotel, saving the taxpayer billions of pounds.”

Typically of Starmer’s time as prime minister, the people he was trying to appease with this policy responded: “Thanks, we hate it.”

Now, the Home Office is actively working to expand or open five sites, two of which are already active. MDP Wethersfield, a former RAF airfield in Essex, houses 800 asylum seekers, but could increase its capacity to more than 1,200. Crowborough training camp in East Sussex plans to increase its numbers from 350 to 540; a volunteer vigilante patrol group has been set up in the area to “protect” locals from migrants. Three large military sites are being readied with a reported capacity of 1,250 each: MOD Bicester in Oxfordshire; RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire; and RAF Barnham.

Much of the classic sitcom Dad’s Army was shot in Thetford, including the external shots of the episode that ends with the show’s most famous joke: “Don’t tell ’em, Pike!” The Guildhall on the market square, where the protesters congregate to start the march today, was often used as a backdrop.

The Dad’s Army museum is on the other side of the Guildhall. One of the protesters is an 80-year-old US air force veteran who thinks the UK should emulate Trump’s immigration policy. He sees a group of tourists being led on the Dad’s Army guided tour and invites them to join the march. It’s clear they would rather hear more tales of Jones, Mainwaring and Pike.

On the other side of the square, Anwar Noor, 63, is selling ice-creams from his truck to people gathering for the march. Noor came to Thetford from Kenya in the 1980s and worked in the Thermos factory for 17 years, before being made redundant when it closed. (Thermos moved manufacturing to Asia in 2000. Other big employers, such as the factory that processed Danepak bacon, have since closed, leading to the loss of hundreds of jobs.) Noor started another business, a scrapyard, before joining the ice-cream trade a couple of years back as he started his semi-retirement.

You could argue that Thetford is East Anglia’s capital of integration. In 1903, it elected the first black mayor in the UK, Allan Glaisyer Minns, who was born in the Bahamas and had trained as a doctor at Guy’s hospital in London. There is an established Portuguese community, congregating this morning at a cafe near the square, drinking bottles of Super Bock beer as a very loud wildlife documentary about porcupines plays on TV. The community moved here in their hundreds in the 2000s, after big East Anglian agribusinesses, including the turkey giant Bernard Matthews, set up recruitment offices in the country.

There is a statue of Duleep Singh, the last maharaja of the Sikh empire, who was exiled to Britain from Punjab and became a favourite of Queen Victoria, living in Elveden Hall, just over the Suffolk border. His son, Prince Freddy Duleep Singh, became a scholar of Norfolk life and gave Thetford the Ancient House, a home thought to have been built in about 1490, which is still used as a public museum.

But, as Ian Jack wrote in 2007, during a visit in which he marvelled at Thetford’s burgeoning Portuguese community, while suggesting the town was already paranoid about immigration statistics: “To compare Prince Freddy with the immigrant ham-slicer or turkey-gutter is of course ridiculous.”

There had already been unrest around immigration when Jack visited the town. In 2004, as New Labour’s second of three terms was nearing its end, Thetford was topping tables for deprivation and child poverty while coming bottom for skills and education. That summer, after England lost to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the European Championship, the Red Lion pub on the market square was besieged by more than 200 hooligans, trapping about 120 people – mostly Portuguese – inside the pub. They pelted the building with bottles and stones, smashed windows and tried to force their way in. Police called in reinforcements from all over Norfolk and several officers and pub customers were said to have sustained cuts from flying glass. It was more than two hours before those inside could leave.

The Red Lion, now a Wetherspoons, feels more sedate today. It sits on the edge of the market square, which, in the sun, feels like a piazza with added pints. And yet Noor, as he doles out ice-creams, says he can understand why people are angry. “You probably noticed as you walked through the town how many shops are closed, post offices gone. All the banks are gone. You can see the centre hollowing out.” Noor says he understands local people’s frustration and that he has never experienced racism in Thetford. But he believes that blaming asylum seekers is “all wrong. We’re all in the same boat.”

At times this August, what has happened in this small Norfolk town has seemed portentous, at risk of provoking another summer of unrest in England, after events in Southport in 2024 and Epping in 2025 led to protests around the country.

At the start of this month, the addresses of some houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) used to house asylum seekers in Thetford were leaked. This led to crowds of vigilantes targeting the properties on 4, 5 and 6 August.

During the second night of unrest, hundreds of people descended on a terrace house on Clover Way in the 70s-built Fairfields estate. Some threw rocks and eggs, smashing an upstairs window, while others attempted to get inside. During these days of disorder, police officers were spat at, while one was hit by a rock and another was bitten. According to police, some of the vigilantes even entered a property and forced out a resident, stealing their mobile phone.

More than 20 people were arrested on suspicion of a variety of offences, including racially aggravated public order, inciting racial hatred and conspiracy to commit aggravated burglary, as well as possession of cocaine with intent to supply, possession of cannabis and driving without insurance.

On the day of the Thetford to Barnham march, I visit Clover Way. The house that was once home to asylum seekers is immediately identifiable by the dried yolk that remains on the windows, almost three weeks after the eggs were thrown.

One of the neighbours comes out to have a cigarette. She tells me she had to flee to a friend’s house over the road on the night the crowds came; since losing her husband last year, she lives on her own. She suggests I speak to her neighbour, John Finch, 91. He says the people who sold the house that was besieged were initially going to sell it to a family, but they were gazumped by a company, which offered more money.

On the night the protesters arrived, the crowds stood on Finch’s flowerbeds and trampled his plants. He saw the melee out of his window, but decided to go to bed. “I slept through it,” he says. He was in the RAF police branch that served in Cyprus when Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots started firing at each other. “I’ve seen worse.”

When the disturbances went viral online, it brought infamy to this quiet street. The next day, film crews arrived, as did people keen to see the newly famous house covered in egg. “There were a lot of people coming,” says Finch. “They were coming in cars and stopping and just looking at it. And I think: it’s an empty bloody house, for Christ’s sake.” He shrugs. “Perhaps it was the highlight of their life.” Thankfully, after those three ugly nights, the violent disorder in Thetford fizzled out. But the anti-asylum protests continued.

The first protest against the use of RAF Barnham to house asylum seekers was in June 2026. Now, every Sunday, they happen like clockwork at 2pm. The week before the march from Thetford town centre to RAF Barnham, I visit the protest camp at the military base.

I park on the dry grass verge and walk towards the protest, noticing a makeshift shed offering drinks to protesters for whatever they can afford. A shirtless fortysomething man with a tan greets me and asks if I want a drink. Clinton Warner grew up across the road from the site and knows its history. He runs a used-car company and each weekend he moves his stock out of the way, so that there is parking space to accommodate the protesters.

Warner tells me a contract worker, tasked with servicing the sewers on the RAF Barnham site, gave him a tipoff about the plan to house asylum seekers there. He decided to blow the whistle. “They were asked to recommission it, so the contractors knew about it seemingly before the councillors,” he says. “We put it online.”

RAF Barnham has been used in many ways over the years. It has been a logistics hub for the RAF, and during the second world war it was a mustard gas and munitions storage facility. After the war, it was commissioned by Churchill to store nuclear bombs and everyone forgot about the mustard gas stored underground. Warner remembers being warned: “Do not remove wildlife from these ponds, do not pick the lilies, do not remove the flowers, leave everything, because it’s all hazardous.”

The use of sites such as Barnham to house asylum seekers isn’t only controversial with concerned residents. Two years ago, the UK parliament’s home affairs select committee wrote that the use of large military sites to house asylum claimants had “generally proved more costly to deliver than hotel accommodation”. Military sites cost more because of the cost of refurbishing them; they are often in a poor state of repair.

When it comes to the asylum issue, the UK government seldom learns the lessons published by parliament. Rather than respond to the evidence, the government seems trapped in a reactionary loop, apparently keen to be seen to do something punitive.

“In policy discourse, there’s this concern about how some asylum accommodation can function as a pull factor,” says Nuni Jorgensen, a researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. “Politicians often say hotels can work as a pull factor because people imagine that these are fancy hotels and that’s why they come to the UK. But the evidence that we have on that is not very clear.” That hasn’t stopped politicians such as Reform UK’s Nigel Farage making hay with the suggestion. Jorgensen adds, however, that there is a lot of evidence showing that larger sites negatively affect asylum seekers’ wellbeing.

When it comes to housing, asylum planning boils down to three choices. Hotels are cheaper when it comes to housing many migrants at one site. HMOs seem a good option when it comes to integration and infrastructure, but are hampered by the reality of house prices. And then there are military sites, which are notoriously difficult to use for this purpose.

Hotels are easier to source than HMOs, says Jorgensen, but they “have been linked to very poor mental-health outcomes among residents”, as the conditions are often cramped and unclean and isolate them from the community. Dispersal to neighbourhood HMOs has, historically, been the Home Office’s preferred option. “They tend to be cheaper than hotels. They tend to produce the best wellbeing outcomes for asylum seekers. The problem is that they are very hard to find in some areas.”

The failure of the hotels policy and suspicion around private management of HMOs are among the issues that have led to the use of large military sites.

It is clear that these sites are controversial. Along with the volunteer vigilante patrol group in Crowborough, a village near RAF Bicester has voted symbolically to leave the UK over the policy. The use of military sites to house asylum seekers has, in a way, united left and right in opposition, but on very different grounds. Human rights campaigners say they amount to a form of “open-prison camp”, while Reform UK likens them to holiday camps.

after newsletter promotion

On my first visit to RAF Barnham, I meet Terry Curtis, 40, one of the protest movement’s organisers. He was present at the HMO protests in early August, he says, but left “when things escalated … because it’s not what we’re here for”. He says the police were heavy-handed in their tactics; he mentions that a woman on a mobility scooter was pepper-sprayed. No one I speak to who was present at the HMO protests seems to have considered how afraid those living in the affected properties must have been.

Curtis moved to Thetford from south London when he was 15 and still supports Millwall. London accents can be heard all over Thetford. In the 1950s, the town’s population was 5,000. By the end of the 1960s, due to overspill from the capital, it had more than tripled to 17,000. In that booming decade, when new towns were referred to as “pram towns” because of the amount of children being born, Thetford was the fastest-growing in the country.

The Abbey estate was the last to be completed in that period of great expansion. In 1968, it was opened by Labour’s minister for housing, Tony Greenwood, who said the design was “exceptional”. The estate is today the poorest area of Thetford and was one of the locations of the violent protests in early August. Regeneration plans were announced in 2019, which were deeply unpopular with many residents and scrapped by Reform UK when they took over Norfolk county council in May. This was part of a Reform UK surge across the county, except in liberal, urban Norwich.

Curtis says he knows what it’s like to go through hard times: “I’ve been homeless myself … I’ve been in hostels.” The movement isn’t affiliated with any political party, he says, which feels like a stretch. Local Reform UK politicians mingle with the protesters each week, including the councillor Scott Hussey, a former Sun journalist who has moved back to his home town and seems fully committed to the anti-immigration agenda.

It is clear that the rise of Reform, and Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain, in East Anglia has put the wind in the sails of movements such as these. Reform UK now runs the county councils in Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex, in each case unseating the Conservatives, while Restore-backed candidates swept all 10 contested seats they stood for in the May 2026 local elections.

“I feel like we’ve got more inequality than we have equality these days,” says Curtis. “Everybody should be treated the same. And, unfortunately, we’re not. Everything’s going up. Prices are going up. Taxes are going up. But, yeah, people are able to come over here, you know, on boats, seek asylum and then get a home, get a house, get what they want – fed, gas, electric, all paid for by the government, which is inadvertently [sic] the taxpayers. Personally, I think we should close the borders to everybody. Get our own country sorted first.”

A failure of political communication, and the rise of social media that reward extreme content, has led to the anti-asylum narrative in UK politics becoming overwhelming. This isn’t lost on Terry Jermy, the Labour MP who represents South West Norfolk, the constituency that includes Thetford.

Some MPs parachute into a constituency with barely any knowledge of it. Not Jermy. He shot up the ranks of local politics, from town councillor in 2008 to mayor in 2016, before giving Liz Truss her Portillo moment in 2024, when he was unexpectedly elected MP at the expense of the former prime minister.

Jermy’s family has lived in Thetford for hundreds of years. In his maiden speech, in October 2024, he alluded to the fact his dad was one of 13 and his mum had seven brothers. “With nearly 40 aunties and uncles and over 100 cousins, I am sure that I owe at least my first election victory to my grandparents’ love for one another.”

After the HMO attacks, Jermy said the violence was “scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked”.

Jermy says he can see why the hotels policy had to change – “it’s not a good use of taxpayers’ money” – and isn’t against the use of military bases in principle. But he strongly opposes the use of Barnham. “I get branded a hypocrite when I say that Barnham’s not appropriate,” he says. “But if you’ve been to Barnham [the village rather than the military base], you will see that it’s relatively small. It’s in the middle of nowhere and it’s going to cost the government a fortune to put in the sewage and electricity and everything else that’s needed to make it work. I suspect, once they’ve done their calculations, they will realise that the cost-benefit rules it out.”

He points out that Barnham was only ever an overflow base for Honnington, a much bigger base nearby. Barnham has been empty for a long time and Jermy says a lot of the buildings are in a state of disrepair, “so new modular units will have to be built” to accommodate people.

The truth is, like a lot of asylum policy, this plan doesn’t feel very well thought-out. Meanwhile, the language used by the Home Office has been sloppy to the point of stoking rage, he says. “In the official government factsheet about Barnham, they referred to the people due to be based there as ‘illegal migrants’. They are asylum seekers. They are waiting to be processed.”

Jermy has flagged this with Home Office ministers, but he is facing an uphill battle with his constituents over a subject that is confusing at the best of times. “Most people don’t understand the difference between refugee, asylum seeker and economic migrant. And we’ve got a lot of work to do in this country to educate people about that, but also to talk more positively about immigration and its contribution to society.”

He doesn’t blame local residents for being angry. “These people have been failed,” he says. “They’ve been failed by decades in which people don’t shop in town centres any more and manufacturing is on the decline. And the vast majority of jobs locally are minimum wage. Our schools are rubbish and our healthcare system is rubbish. They’re going to be grumpy and they’re looking for somebody to blame. And rather than us, as a Labour government, articulating, actually, that it’s greed and austerity that are driving this, a lot of the language that we have used, trying to out-Reform Reform, has aided and abetted a lot of those concerns.”

At 1.30pm on Sunday, the march from Thetford to Barnham is due to begin. A group of women assemble behind the main banner. The march starts and passes through town. Shoppers stop and stare at the collection of union and St George’s flags.

The protesters move past a golden statue of Thomas Paine, the Thetford-born autodidact, founding father of the US and author of Rights of Man. The statue glints in the sunshine as Louis Armstrong’s What a Wonderful World drifts out of a speaker on wheels, being pulled by a female protester. The next track is Vera Lynn’s The White Cliffs of Dover. As we turn a corner, a horse-drawn hearse, crewed by three funeral directors in traditional garb, arrives out of nowhere, carrying a cardboard coffin with “DEMOCRACY” written on its side.

A handful of people watch the protesters pass. One or two are clapping. I don’t come across anyone who is vocally against the protests, despite talking to scores of people. It occurs to me later that I didn’t meet anyone who wanted to say anything in support of asylum at all.

And yet, the turnout of 130 people or so tells its own story. Although the march was billed as a community event, it hasn’t attracted a big crowd. One of the main chants as we walk out of town is distinctly un-family-friendly: “Deport, deport, deport the fucking lot.”

Jermy isn’t here because, although he agrees that Barnham should not be used to house asylum seekers, the protests have attracted gestures of support from not only Reform UK and Restore, but also the far-right party Britain First. During the protests at RAF Barnham, says Jermy, “there have been speeches on the stage which have basically been outright racist and disgusting and my presence would be seen as condoning that behaviour”.

We are on the straight road out to Barnham when the crowd starts cheering for a young man who is standing on the side of the common, setting off a flare attached to a St George’s flag. Acrid smoke spreads across the march. As two police officers approach the young man, an accomplice on a motorbike arrives, speeding him off towards a housing estate, to more cheers.

The march crosses the border from Norfolk to Suffolk, exiting Jermy’s constituency and entering the Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket constituency of his fellow Labour MP Peter Prinsley. “It’s affecting the whole country,” says Jean Glasdale, 73, who has come to the march from just outside Bury St Edmunds. What does she want the government to do? “I want them to deport them,” she says. “I want to be able to walk safely. I mean, they’re not just raping children, they’re raping pensioners like me. I want to feel safe in my own country.”

Talk of rape, amplified and distorted, fills the air at events like this. After we reach Barnham, male speaker after male speaker from Reform UK and smaller fringe parties follow each other on to the small stage with ever greater claims about what rape statistics suggest about migrant behaviour, generating fear about the threat posed by “undocumented, fighting-age men”.

What is clear from the statistics is that most rapes are perpetrated by men already known to the victim. But the image of men marauding the countryside and making women unsafe is potent and heavily exploited. I talk to a 38-year-old woman who lives near RAF Barnham and is on the protest with her small children. She is full of fear, she says, about what she sees as the threat posed by asylum seekers. She is so scared, in fact, that she thinks they should be held in detention offshore: “The safety of people is paramount. If they’re off from the main island – you know, if they’re off, say, Shetland or wherever – it’s another barrier and it’s another bit of protection for us.”

Safety concerns trump talk of specific ideologies – and sometimes reality. “No, there’s no far right,” says Curtis, the organiser. “It doesn’t matter whether you’re left or right wing. This is not what it’s about. It’s just about the community – all the communities getting together to feel safe. You know, everybody’s concerned for the safety of the whole area. Because the people that are going to be put here are going to be able to do whatever they want, whenever they want.”

It’s a message that magnifies the threat of foreign-born men. “It’s been going on since for ever,” says Vron Ware, author of Return of a Native, of the exploitation of these primal fears of rape by “others” and “invaders”. Ware’s book is a reckoning with rural England and chancers such as Lowe and Farage who try to exploit its insecurities.

In the 1980s, Ware was the editor of the anti-fascist publication Searchlight. “I’ve got a poster of an old fascist march in the 70s where someone’s got a placard that says: ‘75% of rapings are done by immigrants.’ It’s just a trope that never goes away.”

After the march, I ask Curtis how he thought it went. He seems a little disappointed with the turnout. He says he is going to take some time out from organising, which has taken its toll.

I leave RAF Barnham with Harry Murray, who has been taking photographs for the Guardian. We trudge along the side of the road, articulated lorries rushing past, until we reach a footpath through a field. As we make our way towards town, passing a few cows, I think about how angry everyone is – not just at events like today, but everywhere and all the time – and how draining it feels.

Will the rage blowing through East Anglia eventually die down? I think back to Glasdale, to whom I was talking as the march neared the protest camp. When I asked her if she thought the populist party she leaflets for, Restore, could make a dent in the next general election, maybe even win it, she was very positive. “We’ve only got to look at today,” she said. “These people are so … incensed.”

Five Great Reads: Building cities from wood, ancient rock art and Dolly Parton’s legacy

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 22:12:32 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to this week’s Five Great Reads. Settle into your weekend with some truly inspirational stories – from the incredible life of Dolly Parton, to a vision for greener cities, and life-affirming reflections on grief. Plus, a little bit of gossip.

As the tributes to Dolly Parton flowed in, so did the quotations. From her wisdom: “Don’t get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life,” to her best interviews, to her sharp wit. The country star will be remembered for her lyrics, her philanthropy, and for pioneering a new vision of femininity.

Notable quote: “People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don’t know, I’m never there.”

‘I’m not a fashion icon, I’m an eyesore’: Parton often said she modelled her look on a woman others called the “town tramp” but who held a glamorous appeal for her. She never failed to poke fun at her own appearance. Her hair was a “fire hazard”, she would say, or “I’m not a fashion icon; I’m an eyesore” – but her look was highly deliberate.

How long will it take to read: Just over two minutes

Further reading: Sian Cain looks at how Parton’s philanthropy focused most on helping children. Unabashedly herself, Parton was an icon to LGBTQ fans, Joe Stone writes. And from Jolene to Islands in the Stream, here are Parton’s 10 best recordings.

Thousands of years ago, Indigenous hunter-gatherers in a west Texas valley spent weeks pulverising gypsum, hematite, limonite and manganese to make paint. Using teamwork and precision, they painted tall figures on a rock wall. But Donald Trump’s administration is now dealing these rare treasures a potentially fatal blow.

How – and why? Last year, Republicans in the US Congress heaped a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into Trump’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. Now the longest remaining unwalled stretch of the US-Mexico border in west Texas, a remote region that includes some of the state’s most-visited public lands, is under threat. And with so much money behind it, Customs and Border Protection is moving ahead at speed, despite almost universal opposition from locals, business leaders and a growing number of political leaders from both parties.

How long will it take to read: Five minutes.

Further reading: ICE arrested 50,000 people in July – quietly the biggest month in Trump’s second term.

For author Hannah Richell, one crashing wave on one single day more than 10 years ago changed everything for her and her family, when her husband Matt died at Sydney’s Tamarama beach. Here, she describes beautifully, but heart-wrenchingly, how she kept going.

A profound journey: From their beginnings at a London publishing company, to travel, marriage and babies, Richell gives a moving account of the life she and Matt built before it was horribly cut short, and then her moving and profound journey through grief and acceptance.

Notable quote: “The waves still come, yet we carry on, living lives illuminated by wonder and grief, the duet of both.”

How long will it take to read: Eight and a half minutes

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Everyone loves a bit of gossip. But when the gossip is about you, and playing out in the pages of a bestselling novelist’s new book, things can get complicated. Critically acclaimed author of metafiction Rachel Cusk’s new book is alleged to be a thinly veiled portrait of Natalie Portman. And real-life movie star Portman is reportedly not happy about unwillingly being the author’s conduit for interrogating “fame, power, beauty and truth”.

Is Portman really the book’s subject? While not named, identifying details jump off the page. Cusk’s movie-star main character M is identifiable as Portman in all but name. While one writer was the first to draw the link, Great Rainbow wrote this week “she simply finished her advance copy sooner than the rest of us”.

What has Portman said? Was she a willing collaborator? It is still unclear whether Portman was involved. But it is known that Cusk and Portman are friends, and both live in Paris, leading to speculation that all this literary drama playing out in the press is a marketing ploy crafted by Cusk and Portman together. Whatever the truth is, Elle Hunt writes that “it’s worked”.

How long will it take to read: A breezy three minutes. Much shorter than the novel in question, which comes in at 192 pages.

Further reading: Life of M is “a book to admire enormously, but not one to love”, reviewer Clare Clark writes.

Our modern towns and cities are not environmentally friendly. They are, sadly, monuments to extraction and emissions, formed out of materials that have been extracted, smelted, superheated or synthesised through the intensive use of fossil energy. But what would happen if our town planners and builders aimed to replace these structures with wood?

The need for green change: “About 10 years ago I had to wake up a little bit myself,” the Norwegian developer Arthur Buchardt says. “About the importance of the environment, about what we are doing to it.” It was in 2015, in the wake of the Paris climate agreement, that he drew some pictures on a napkin and took them to an architect and asking: “How big is it possible to go with a high-rise wooden building?”

Isn’t it also bad to chop down trees? Consider these stats: when you fabricate a typical mid-rise building out of steel and concrete, its construction alone generates about 1,500 to 2,000 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions. That same building, when made out of wood, sequesters anything from 600 to 1,000 metric tonnes of CO2. And that is before you even factor in the additional absorption that comes with the planting and regrowth of the harvested trees.

How long will it take to read: Just under eight minutes.

Further reading: We asked our climate reporters to highlight one idea for positive change. We got a chronicle of global transformation.

The Guardian view on political donations: Labour should curb the power of big money

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:56:00 GMT

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistake

On the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham told a democracy activist that he favoured a political donations cap of around £500,000 and wanted it reduced over time. His government is now resisting amendments that would move in precisely that direction. Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now. It is difficult to argue that restricting a single person to giving half a million pounds a year to a political party would damage democracy. Such a cap would only affect the mega-rich. Reducing the cap would force parties to wean themselves off the present regime that allows the rich too much say.

There are two contra arguments swilling around Labour. The first is that there should be room for wealthy, progressive donors – whose cash helps rebut claims that Labour is in the pocket of the trade unions. The second is the warning from unions that a cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.

Neither of these arguments holds much water. Whatever benefit Labour might derive from rich friends is dwarfed by the wider damage caused by parties being bankrolled by a few rich individuals. Mr Burnham has registered £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,000 from billionaire Lord Sainsbury. In comparison, Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK a single £9m donation in August 2025 – a sum which exceeds the £8m in trade union donations that Labour will get this year.

The timing makes Labour’s retreat baffling. This newspaper’s revelation of Nigel Farage’s undisclosed £5m gift from Mr Harborne in 2024 has turned big money in politics from an abstract concern into a live issue. Reform’s support has fallen markedly in recent months.

Mr Burnham could recover the situation by backing amendments from two Labour MPs. Stella Creasy’s changes, which have cross-party support, start with a £500,000 cap – Mr Burnham’s own figure – before reducing it, while allowing parliament to alter the level. She proposes to exclude trade union political funds, recognising that money aggregated from thousands of members differs fundamentally from a donation controlled by a single billionaire or company. The former represents many individual contributions; the latter concentrated economic power. Unions warn that a cap might restrict their political activity. But Ms Creasy explicitly protects their member-funded campaigning cash. Opponents should explain why that safeguard is inadequate.

Anneliese Dodds, a former Labour cabinet minister, asks the right question: if ministers believe the growth of big money in politics is a risk, why retain the Conservatives’ sharply increased election spending limits? A donations cap limits how much concentrated private wealth can enter party politics; lower expenditure limits reduce how much money parties need to raise in the first place.

Instead of backing these measures, tabled as amendments to the representation of the people bill at next week’s report stage vote, ministers are pressing ahead with elaborate rules governing where political money comes from and how it reaches parties. Yet this year’s Rycroft review, which ministers are responding to, urged parliament, “if it wishes to restore confidence in the political process and to keep big money out of UK politics”, to consider spending limits. Given the scandals of recent years, it is astonishing that Labour is declining to regulate how much political influence any single wealthy donor can purchase.

The Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft power

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:55:09 GMT

The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France

“Harold Rex interfectus est”: King Harold is killed. As every British schoolchild knows, the Bayeux tapestry depicts a turning point in the history of these islands: defeat at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which would lead to the ascent of William the Conqueror to the English throne. Its return to the UK for the first time in nearly 1,000 years is being hailed as a hugely historic moment in its own right. The loan of the tapestry (technically an embroidery of wool on linen) to the British Museum in exchange for UK treasures from Sutton Hoo is the ultimate manifestation of soft power – a 70-metre symbol of post-Brexit Anglo-French rapprochement in comic-strip form.

Ticket sales for the exhibition, which opens on 10 September, were the biggest in a single day in the museum’s history, with online queues of 80,000. Radio 4 is devoting a day of special broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry, including a new drama with verse from the poet laureate Simon Armitage. The museum’s videos explaining this tale of ambition, friendship, betrayal and revenge are fittingly narrated by Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. Norman-mania is here.

“It probably took more years to deliver this project than all the Brexit talks,” Emmanuel Macron joked in a speech to the British parliament last year. To the list of 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs and only three women depicted on the tapestry, one might add a 21st-century British king, a French president, and three British prime ministers who have helped to bring it here – not to mention the millions of pounds it has cost.

Two previous attempts – one for Queen Elizabeth’s coronation in 1953 and another in 1966 – failed. It would not have succeeded this time if the tapestry had not needed to be moved for renovations to the Bayeux Museum in Normandy. Many curators and restorers still believed the risks of bringing it to London were too great. The late David Hockney called the transferral “madness”. One of his final works, the 90-metre iPad frieze A Year in Normandie, on display this summer at the Serpentine gallery in London, was testament to his lifelong fascination with the tapestry. An online petition against the move attracted nearly 80,000 signatures. However, political will won.

From poetry to parody – from Tennyson’s 1876 epic verse drama Harold to an episode of The Simpsons – the tapestry has enjoyed a rich cultural afterlife. But its message has always been political. Napoleon and the Nazis recognised its potential as a propaganda tool. In 2014 Nigel Farage, then leader of Ukip, sported a Bayeux tapestry silk tie during the Rochester byelection, as a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. The tie sold out in 24 hours.

In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story. The Bayeux tapestry is a devastatingly human saga. With war raging in Europe, this medieval masterpiece is a reminder of conflict’s brutality, human suffering and the importance of collaboration between countries. The tapestry will return to France for the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth next year. According to Philippe Bélaval, Mr Macron’s former culture adviser: “Such a loan will only happen once and never again.” This is truly a once-in-a millennium event. Hopefully, its success will pave the way for equally ambitious cultural exchanges in the future. Vive l’entente cordiale!

US Open tennis, Premier League and Itauma v Hrgovic – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:51:02 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

With another round of Premier League fixtures coming up and the imminent closure of the transfer window, Luke McLaughlin and Sarah Rendell will be keeping pace with all the day’s breaking news from around the grounds. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Day three of the latest round of county fixtures sees Tanya Aldred at Scarborough as Yorkshire face Leicestershire, but there’s so much more to our county blog. Expect updates from all the day’s action as Division One leaders Nottinghamshire take on third-placed Warwickshire at Edgbaston, while title-chasing Somerset face Sussex at Hove.

We head over to Lord’s for day three of the second Test. Our blog hosts Tim de Lisle and James Wallace will be providing over-by-over coverage. Pakistan were woeful in all departments during an innings defeat in the first of a three-Test series at Headingley last week and are fighting to avoid another loss to keep the series alive. Ali Martin and Simon Burnton report.

Andoni Iraola is still trying to instil his methods on Liverpool’s players as he takes charge of his first competitive home game following his move from Bournemouth in the summer. Oliver Glasner has started his reign with two home defeats to Leeds, but Forest have won their last two visits to Anfield without conceding a goal. Sarah Rendell helms our live blog with Andy Hunter our match reporter for a tough contest to call.

Saturday’s pair of top-flight 3pm kick-offs are the focus of Barry Glendenning’s blog. Bournemouth lost their opener after conceding two late goals at Manchester City, and Marco Rose’s side meet an Everton side seeking to start a league season with back-to-back wins for the first time since 2020. Elsewhere, Coventry host Hull in a meeting of promoted teams who began their seasons in contrasting fashions – and we’ll have live updates from the Championship, Bundesliga and beyond.

South Africa seek to level the Greatest Rivalry series in Cape Town, where the All Blacks have played their hosts 11 times since 1928, winning seven. The scrum was a potent weapon for the Boks last Saturday at Ellis Park until the 56th minute, when the All Blacks forced a defensive scrum penalty in front of their posts. New Zealand quickly turned a three-point lead into 10 and went on to win 33-16 in a thrilling upset. But the main theme of this week’s buildup has been about a backlash from South Africa, who haven’t lost two home Tests in a row at home since August 2015. Daniel Gallan helms the blog as the two giants of the game collide in the second of this four-Test series.

Scott Murray provides the overview on the pick of Saturday’s Premier League matches. Spurs were bludgeoned 3-0 by Brentford last weekend, a torrid start to the season for Roberto De Zerbi’s new-look side. Matthias Jaissle’s team were only denied by a 99th-minute penalty equaliser against Liverpool, and both teams enjoyed morale-boosting Carabao Cup wins in midweek. Paul MacInnes and Jonathan Liew report from the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

The IBF belt relinquished by Oleksandr Usyk will be on the line in London and the 21-year-old Moses Itauma (14-0, 12 KOs) could become the second-youngest heavyweight champion of all time. Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic (20-1, 15 KOs) will be the toughest challenge of Itauma’s fledgling career. There is plenty of expectation surrounding the British prospect, with Prince Naseem Hamed claiming Itauma is a “million times better” than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury and could become the best of all time. Bryan Armen Graham hosts the big fight blog and Donald McRae reports from the O2 Arena.

Emillia Hawkins clocks on bright and early to preview Sunday’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for another engaging set of Premier League fixtures, with four games on offer. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your notions and queries.

Tanya Aldred has all the best of day four’s county action as the battle at the top and bottom of both divisions heats up.

If there’s day-four play in the second Test, Tom Davies and James Wallace will be on hand with over-by-over coverage of the action from Lord’s.

Chelsea take on a Brighton side buzzing from their opening 4-0 battering of Aston Villa, while Xabi Alonso launched his reign with a 3-2 win over west London rivals Fulham. Leeds and Brentford also began their seasons with victories – so at least one perfect record has to go at Elland Road. Elsewhere, Sunderland host Fulham with both teams yet to get a point on the board. John Brewin is your go-to guide.

Follow events in New York live with our rolling blog as the final grand slam of the season gets underway. Carlos Alcaraz will open his title defence against Roman Safiullin in his first singles match since April. The world No 3 returned to play with Serena Williams in the mixed doubles tournament and looked rusty. He may have to be sharper against Safiullin, who reached the fourth round at Wimbledon. Tumaini Carayol reports from Flushing Meadows.

Ipswich gave Gary O’Neil the perfect start by beating Sunderland and they travel to Old Trafford in confident mood. Given Michael Carrick’s United were given a bloody nose by Championship playoff winners Hull in their opener, facing another confident promoted club comes with added pressure. Tim de Lisle helms the blog, with Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin reporting from pitchside.

An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 16:10:15 GMT

Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come

Follow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – just look at its share price. It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.

To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.

For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed to a series of changes in the way young people use their platforms. There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be “a good day”.

But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts to less than a month’s revenue. And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth of the $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the $1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up. No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.

Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings to Mark Zuckerberg directly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.

As for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal, Meta will not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.

No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting book Careless People, the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.

Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.

It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”

What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

There are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.

More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.

This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Russ Abbot: a class act, on stage and off

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:33:38 GMT

Readers respond to Simon Hattenstone’s interview with the retired actor and comedian

Simon Hattenstone’s wonderful interview with Russ Abbot (‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away, 24 August) brought back a treasured story that leaves my family eternally grateful to him.

During the summer of 2010, we travelled from Scotland on holiday, staying in Windsor, and attended Oliver! at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. When the show ended late at night, I had to set off on a 30-minute walk just to retrieve our car.

With my wife in a broken-down electric wheelchair and our two daughters, aged just eight and six, beside her, they faced a long, vulnerable wait on the pavement. Making matters worse, I then got caught in a central London driving nightmare, desperately trying to navigate back to them with a broken satnav, no map, and no knowledge of the city streets.

When Russ walked out of the stage door, he didn’t just pass by. Seeing my stranded family and my young daughters deeply distressed, he stayed and went to work comforting them, running through multiple Fagin monologues right there on the street. The girls were so completely sidetracked that they forgot anything was amiss. They were absolutely buzzing to meet “Fagin”, and it became an overriding memory they talked about all night. He turned a stressful situation into pure magic.

Our evening was saved not only by Russ’s incredible warmth, but also by the extraordinary humanity of two Polish doormen from a nightclub across the street. They rushed over to assist, letting my children stay warm in the back of one of their family cars until I finally found my way back.

To my family, the man who stepped out of the Drury Lane stage door that night was a true class act, both on and off the stage. Philip ShowellHamilton, South Lanarkshire

Simon Hattenstone’s interview with Russ Abbot took me straight back to our living room in the early 1980s – Saturday evening, dinner over, and all of us settling into that post-dinner golden hour of family television.

Russ always seemed such a happy chap, and his humour was wonderfully infectious. I can still hear my dear mother’s uncontrollable laughter one evening in particular as he launched into a gloriously over-the-top Bruce Forsyth, complete with cries of “higher! Higher!”

More than 40 years on, the memory still makes me smile. Thank you, Simon, for taking me back to that very happy time and place. And to Russ and his wife, Trish, after 60 years together, may the laughter continue. Noel HineyDublin, Ireland

Reading the Russ Abbot interview reminded me of a time when Saturday afternoon telly into the early evening would be a gathering force for our family.

Wrestling and Big Daddy and the latest American show like The A-Team or Airwolf, followed by gameshows hosted by the big comedian of the time and then the sketch comedy series. It didn’t matter if it was a repeat such as The Two Ronnies or Russ Abbot’s Madhouse.

Strict timings were adhered to and tea worked around a Radio Times-driven schedule – that, or you mastered the recording settings on your VCR.

Something’s been lost in an era where each of us has an individual screen and streaming services, meaning we can watch as and when we like. My father had the remote, and dictated the narrative on the box, but at least we were all in the same room at the same time, laughing simultaneously.

It’s never as good as you remember – but I do miss it. Lovely article. David Howes Hebden Bridge, West Yorkshire

Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:31:20 GMT

Jill White responds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure status

I write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial (The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars.

Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority.

Charmouth is a key part of the designated Jurassic Coast world heritage site, but I can’t think of any others where visitors are allowed, or even encouraged, to bring or rent hammers to wreck the protected features and/or remove them from the site unrecorded. If we want to protect our fossil heritage for future generations to study, we could make a start by regulating this geological vandalism. Jill WhiteMusbury, Devon

There can be huge comfort in end-of-life preparation

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 15:30:06 GMT

Gill Empson says her husband wanted to make sure that the family would not have a mess to sort out after his death from a terminal illness

Sarah Phillips’ article struck such a chord (What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work, 13 August). My husband, Dick, died last month with pulmonary fibrosis. His last few months were physically very difficult, but he gained an enormous amount of comfort from sorting out his affairs; he said it was so that the family wouldn’t have a mess to sort out when he had gone.

He changed everything into my name and prepared lists of passwords for our three sons. He passed on his watch to our grandson and his rings to our sons. To do this himself gave him tremendous pleasure.

Dick regarded himself as very lucky to have had 80 years largely free of illness, and he spent his last three years, when he had a terminal diagnosis, making sure that those left behind would be able to manage without him. Gill EmpsonAston-on-Trent, Derbyshire

The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that

In June 2013 Peter Francis, a former Metropolitan police officer, broke a 20-year silence about the role he had played in surveilling the family of Stephen Lawrence in a documentary jointly made by the Guardian and Channel 4’s Dispatches programme. Two years later, thanks in part to the programme, the Home Office established an undercover policing inquiry, commonly known as the spycops public inquiry, to shed light on the scale of surveillance of activists and trade unionists. That inquiry is now under threat.

Francis had served in the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Met unit founded in 1968 whose officers lived for years at a time inside political and campaigning organisations under false names.

In the months after Stephen Lawrence’s murder in 1993 Francis had been deployed to pose as an anti-racist campaigner. His superiors pressed him to find “dirt” that could be used against the Lawrence family and their supporters. Stephen’s mother, Doreen, told the Guardian and Channel 4 that nothing she had heard since her son died had topped the revelation that police had been spying on her while she grieved. She had always suspected the police were watching. She never had proof.

The Lawrences were not an isolated case. Justice campaigns and trade unionists across the country were also monitored.

At least 139 officers adopted fake names, pretending to be political activists, to spy on people between 1968 and at least 2010. Dozens of anti-racist campaigners, family members of victims of police violence and leftwing activists have been surveilled by police.

Suresh Grover, whose Monitoring Group stood behind many of these victims of police surveillance, has told the inquiry that the suspicion directed at Black campaigners was rooted in racist stereotyping. Complaints from Black communities were treated as a public order threat in a way that identical complaints from others were not.

The government has justified the consultation they launched on 16 July into the future of the inquiry on the grounds that it has gone on for more than 11 years and cost £137m. The figures are accurate but their explanation is missing.

Applications for anonymity and restriction orders, the vast majority sought by police officers, have slowed down this inquiry. Litigation over cover names, and a persistent unwillingness among former officers and their commanders to say what they did has also hampered the process. The Met, which ran the SDS, made the inquiry slow and expensive. The same government department that funded and served the squad now cites the inquiry’s slowness and expense as reasons to cut it short.

Despite a push to wind up the inquiry, it is still producing revelations about the conduct of England’s police forces. Just last year, it revealed that an undercover officer, James Thomson, who had deceived two women into intimate relationships, was suspected of fabricating an elaborate plot to link an anti-foxhunting activist to a gun that he told managers the activist intended to collect in France.

Before the inquiry, Thomson’s managers admitted that in order to protect the SDS, nothing was done either about his intimate relationship with women he was surveilling or his possible fabrication of evidence. The unit, it seemed, trumped almost anything.

The inquiry also exposed numerous instances in which managers appeared to have knowledge of undercover officers having had sexual relationships that continued long after undercover deployments ended, in one case even after the announcement of the inquiry.

Another shocking discovery from the inquiry is that the Met spent £2.5m hiding an officer – John Dines – from his former lover, going as far as to relocate him from New Zealand to Australia for that purpose.

after newsletter promotion

For the spycops scandal to be possible courts had to be misled. Officers were arrested alongside activists, appeared in court under false names and in some cases gave evidence under them without the court being told.

Surveillance was not limited to political activists and victims of racist violence. The Met’s own investigation concluded that special branch and the security services fed material to construction companies that blacklisted more than 3,000 workers suspected of being members of trade unions.

More instances of misconduct may come to light in the future, which is all the more reason to keep the inquiry running. The consultation is scheduled to end on 20 September, but there is still time to write to the Home Office to make sure that the government knows your views.

An inquiry that was set up because the state spied on the parents of a murdered child should not be closed down because the state has heard enough about itself. Doreen Lawrence has been told for 33 years that the truth is coming if she will wait just a little longer. She – and other victims of spying – have waited long enough. The inquiry should finish the job it was given.

Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitor

Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis

The Guardian Fri, 28 Aug 2026 10:56:29 GMT

Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states

Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal

As a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of the catastrophic flash flood that thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.

Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.

On 26 August, a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.

The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal and Tibet and greater investment in preparedness.

But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.

The warning system in the high-mountain Bhotekoshi valley illustrates the problem. The sudden, debris-laden flood destroyed upstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert. The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.

Preliminary assessments indicate that a large glacial collapse triggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow, temporarily blocking the river before a massive surge travelled downstream. The precise sequence is still being investigated. Whatever the final scientific explanation, the event shows how quickly hazards can cascade in a warming mountain environment.

By the time authorities received information about the flood and warnings were sent downstream, communities closest to the source had virtually no time to respond. The monitoring infrastructure did not simply fail to communicate the warning. It was destroyed before it could see the flood coming. That distinction matters. An early warning system designed around yesterday’s floods can be dangerously inadequate for tomorrow’s extremes.

This does not make early warning futile. It means we need to be honest about its limits. A warning is useful only if there is time to act. It cannot stop a mountain of ice and rock from collapsing. It cannot protect infrastructure in an increasingly hazardous corridor. And it cannot bring back a home, a hydropower station or a livelihood once it has disappeared.

Adaptation has limits, too. For years, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have been ramping up efforts to adapt: by strengthening infrastructure, improving preparedness, and protecting livelihoods – but often without financial support from the countries that historically contributed most to the climate crisis through historical emissions.

Nepal needs much greater international support for adaptation: early warning, mountain monitoring, climate science, anticipatory action, resilient infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Because Himalayan hazards originate beyond national borders, this must also include stronger cross-border cooperation and timely sharing of information.

The Nepal Himalaya is changing rapidly. Glaciers are retreating, while warming is altering the conditions in which glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes remain stable. The climate in which these hazards occur is changing, and continued warming will make an already difficult risk landscape harder to manage. That is why the global response cannot stop at adaptation.

The first task must be to stop making the crisis worse. The countries that benefited most from decades of fossil fuel-driven growth have a particular responsibility to cut emissions rapidly. They also have far greater resources to do so. A just transition away from coal, oil and gas towards renewable energy is therefore a matter of global justice.

The fossil-fuel industry cannot be separated from this conversation. Companies have made enormous profits extracting and selling the fuels that have driven global heating, while communities on the climate frontline are being asked to prepare for increasingly destructive impacts with far fewer resources. Even rapid mitigation cannot undo the warming already baked into the climate system or immediately reverse changes already taking place in the Himalaya.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is also a lesson for Nepal. It should not copy the economic model that created the climate crisis and call it development. We have an opportunity to build something different: an economy that puts people, livelihoods and ecological resilience before extraction.

The second task requires historical polluter states to pay for loss and damages. Nepal has contributed less than 0.1% of historical global greenhouse gas emissions. Its per-capita emissions remain among the lowest in the world. Yet we are increasingly paying for a crisis we did almost nothing to create. There is something profoundly unfair about this.

The cost of such an event is not an abstract figure in a post-disaster risk assessment. It is the lives of people killed by the flood; a hydropower station that took years to build and disappeared in minutes; livelihoods; public money that must now be spent on recovery instead of health and education.

Nepal and other vulnerable countries have repeatedly called on developed countries for compensation. The country should not be forced to borrow to recover from disasters to which it contributed so little. Nor should its scarce domestic resources repeatedly be diverted to repair damage caused by emissions of the global north.

Loss and damage finance must therefore be additional to existing official development assistance, adaptation and mitigation finance. It needs to be accessible and predominantly grant-based. But it cannot substitute for mitigation. No amount of compensation will be enough if the world continues to burn fossil fuels at the scale it does today. No adaptation programme can keep pace indefinitely with a climate that becomes more dangerous every year.

The people living along the Bhotekoshi river did not choose a warming Himalaya. They did not choose the fossil-fuel economy that drove most of the warming. However, with enough support, they can prepare better and build more resilient livelihoods. Sadly, they cannot adapt their way out of every disaster. This is why loss and damage finance is not charity – it is an obligation to people already paying the price.

Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, Nepal
